declarations.ethicsApproval: Sessions were approved by the HSE IRB (Moscow) and the University of Amsterdam EBEC; no separate approval was required at the University of Bari Aldo Moro. All participants gave informed consent.

detail.abstract: Extortionary ("harassment") bribery can persist even when widely condemned, consistent with a coordination problem sustained by beliefs about what others do and what others consider acceptable. We study whether a minimal institutional featurethe presence of a third-party monitor empowered to punish-shifts (i) normative expectations about extortion and compliance and (ii) empirical expectations about their prevalence. We implement a preregistered laboratory experiment with two phases in the Netherlands, Italy, and Russia. In Phase I, participants play a harassment bribery game with or without monitoring. In Phase II, using an independent sample we elicit social appropriateness judgments using a Krupka-Weber coordination game and empirical expectations about Phase I behaviour. We report preregistered within-country comparisons and complementary exploratory pooled specifications that increase precision while allowing country-heterogeneous effects. Overall, the findings are consistent with monitoring operating not only through deterrence but also as an institutional signal that can reshape the belief environment sustaining harassment bribery, with heterogeneous responses across settings.

title: Who cares about Excess CEO Compensation? Evidence from Overpaid CEO Designations
affiliations: The University of Texas at El Paso,  and Eller College of Management, University of Arizona

detail.title: Who cares about Excess CEO Compensation? Evidence from Overpaid CEO Designations
detail.abstract: For decades, there has been a controversial debate as to whether CEOs are overpaid and how stakeholders should respond to excess CEO compensation. We shed new light on the question as to which investors care about excess CEO pay. Using nine years of data from a report of the 100 most overpaid S&P 500 CEOs, we find that equity investors, on average, respond negatively when CEOs are designated as overpaid. The announcement returns are the most negative when the reports receive substantial attention shortly after publication and when firms first appear on the overpaid CEO list. We find, however, that institutional investors exhibit nuanced responses to the overpaid CEO designations. Specifically, non-ESG-oriented investors rebalance their portfolios towards the listed firms' shares, whereas ESG-oriented investors exhibit relatively muted responses. Additional tests indicate that investors who rebalance towards listed firms do so to course-correct excess CEO pay via their governance influence.

title: Entropy Pooling with CVaR and EVaR Views
affiliations: Universidad Nacional de Ingeniería

detail.title: Entropy Pooling with CVaR and EVaR Views
detail.abstract: This work presents an extension of the entropy pooling approach to handle views on the tails of the distribution of random variables. First, we provide formulations that allows to incorporate absolute and relative views on conditional value at risk into the traditional formulation of entropy pooling. Second, we provide formulations that allows to incorporate absolute views on entropic value at risk into the traditional formulation of entropy pooling. Also, we develop the sample formulas for weighted comoments tensors. Then, we run some numerical examples that shows how these formulations allows to transform a prior distribution into a posterior distribution that incorporate tail views.

title: How Artificial Intelligence LLM Engines Shape the Global Conflict Information Environment

detail.title: How Artificial Intelligence LLM Engines Shape the Global Conflict Information Environment
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) answer engines now field a growing share of the questions that analysts, scholars, and the public ask about issues of peace and conflict. Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to hallucinate under certain conditions, but do these errors have discernible patterns when they are asked about conflicts, and if so what can that teach us about the changing global conflict information environment? To answer, we first asked a battery of questions about 28 conflicts to five leading answer engines and scored their 5,460 answers against documented evidence. We found that the thinner the retrievable record around a given conflict, the more the engines invent, misattribute, and miscount. Thin records don't just encourage hallucination, but create structural exposure to mis-and disinformation, because they are the easiest records to warp through Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to bias engine responses. Through an analysis of 1,048 websites that the AI LLMs pulled conflict facts from, we found that GEO source optimization is already happening, and while state-partisan digital capture remains incipient it is rapidly growing. We explain what these findings mean for scholarship with the rise of GEO information warfare, and for policy argue for a return to the deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI tools cannot replicate, closing with a discussion of future research opportunities and challenges in this fast-moving space.

title: Oil Price Shocks, Supply Chain Disruptions, and the Speed of Post-COVID Recovery: A VAR Analysis for the U.S. Economy
affiliations: , Texas Tech University and Texas Tech University

detail.title: Oil Price Shocks, Supply Chain Disruptions, and the Speed of Post-COVID Recovery: A VAR Analysis for the U.S. Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study because it uses publicly available, aggregate secondary data and does not involve human participants or personally identifiable information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the transmission of oil price shocks has changed in the post-COVID period. Using a reduced-form VAR estimated on monthly U.S. data, we compare impulse responses of inflation, industrial production, employment, and monetary policy to an oil price shock across two subsamples: a pre-COVID period (2000–2019) and a post-COVID recovery period (2020–2024). Our approach follows the broader VAR literature on oil shocks, including the structural VAR oil market models in Baumeister and Hamilton (2019) and Kilian (2009), and recent high-frequency identification work such as Qureshi and Ahmad (2025). By estimating the model separately for each subsample, we evaluate whether the post-pandemic economic environment exhibits stronger or more volatile responses to energy price disturbances. The contribution of this study is twofold. First, we provide new evidence on how oil shocks propagate in the post-COVID U.S. economy, which has been characterized by supply-chain fragility, elevated inflation, and aggressive monetary tightening. Second, by contrasting these results with the pre-COVID period, we provide insight into whether the transmission of oil price shocks differs between the pre-COVID and post-COVID periods. This comparison helps clarify how supply chain disruptions, geopolitical uncertainty, and changing policy regimes may have altered the sensitivity of the U.S. economy to energy-related disturbances. We find that the pre- and post-COVID economies react differently to oil price shocks, and our results suggest that the post-COVID economy exhibits stronger responses in several key macroeconomic variables, particularly the federal funds rate.

title: No Spoilers: A Contamination-Free LLM for Brand Perception Analysis
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business

detail.title: No Spoilers: A Contamination-Free LLM for Brand Perception Analysis
detail.abstract: Brands are focal objects of marketing, and how consumers perceive them shapes positioning, consumer choice, and firm performance. These perceptions are often not directly observed but reflected in the large volume of unstructured text consumers produce about brands, making language models a scalable tool for measuring them. Tracking such measures over time, however, raises two challenges. First, model parameters may encode information from after the measurement date, producing lookahead bias. Second, changes across model versions undermine comparability. We address both with Data-Restricted Incremental Pretraining and Projection (DRIP^2), a workflow that builds a lightweight temporally bounded sentence encoder from pre-sample data, constructs quarterly brand representation vectors, removes platform-wide language shifts, and projects the vectors onto researcher-defined dimensions. Applied to more than 60 million tweets from 2016-2022, DRIP^2 generates interpretable maps of brands, sports teams, and actors. The measures respond to major real-world events, predict future profit-margin growth, and reveal short-lived shifts in the intended direction following marketing campaigns and movie releases.

title: India's Soft Power Diplomacy during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Vaccine Diplomacy for Global Solutions

detail.title: India's Soft Power Diplomacy during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Vaccine Diplomacy for Global Solutions

detail.abstract: This paper examines the extent to which India's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, through its health and vaccine diplomacy, affected its soft power and global standing. Building on a history of cultural and civilizational diplomacy, India leveraged its pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity to supply medicines, medical equipment, and vaccines to over 150 countries, most notably through the "Vande Bharat" evacuation mission and the "Vaccine Maitri" initiative. By positioning itself as a first responder and reliable healthcare provider, India sought to project itself as a responsible global actor and reinforce its regional influence in South Asia. Situating this response within Joseph Nye's theory of soft power, the paper traces India's diplomatic trajectory from the onset of the pandemic through 2024. The findings show that India faced a significant setback during the pandemic's second wave, marked by domestic infrastructural collapse, a vaccine export ban, and a temporary decline in its soft power ranking, but ultimately recovered, with its Global Soft Power Index ranking rising to 29th by 2024. The paper concludes that despite ongoing internal challenges and the spread of misinformation, India's medical diplomacy had a net positive, if uneven, effect on its international standing.

title: Combining Target and Bonus Discretion: An Experimental Investigation
affiliations: University of Bern - Institute for Accounting, Georgia State University and University of Bern - Institute for Accounting

detail.title: Combining Target and Bonus Discretion: An Experimental Investigation

declarations.ethicsApproval: All data collections of this paper were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the authors’ universities.

detail.abstract: In this study, we use an experiment to investigate whether ex ante managerial discretion over targets alters the effectiveness of ex post managerial discretion over bonuses in motivating performance. We predict and find that when managers do not have target discretion, bonus discretion decreases employee performance because employees' incentives and perception of fairness are impaired. In contrast, when managers have target allocation discretion, such that the sum of employees' targets must equal manager's own unit target, bonus discretion increases employee performance because managers use target discretion together with bonus discretion to motivate effort and performance, while keeping unfairness perceptions under control. Thus, our results suggest that having a "fit" between target and bonus discretion is more effective than granting only one type of discretion. We also find that when managers have full target discretion and can set targets without restrictions, employee performance is relatively low and bonus discretion has little effect on it as managers often set overly difficult targets, thereby undermining employees' financial incentives. Our results underscore the interrelated nature of different types of managerial discretion and the need for considering performance evaluation systems in its entirety rather than analyzing single components in isolation.

title: Revisiting the Cancer Metaphor in Organizations: A Critical Lens on Gareth Morgan
affiliations: University of Portsmouth

detail.title: Revisiting the Cancer Metaphor in Organizations: A Critical Lens on Gareth Morgan
detail.abstract: Gareth Morgan's Images of Organization (1986) introduced the cancer metaphor as a powerful analytical tool for understanding organizational pathology. Nearly four decades later, this metaphor remains influential yet critically underexamined. This paper offers a revisiting lens that integrates three traditions: medical oncology, cultural history, and organizational theory. Drawing on Smithers' (1962) argument that "cancer is a disease of organization," Sontag's (1978) ethical critique of illness metaphors, and contemporary organizational scholarship, I argue that Morgan's metaphor illuminates systemic pathology and internal threat but obscures agency, collapses benign/malignant distinctions, and carries problematic ethical baggage. I propose refinements including an autoimmune disease alternative, a "pre-cancerous" framework, and attention to environmental "carcinogens." The paper concludes that the metaphor remains valuable-provided it is deployed with critical sophistication, ethical reflexivity, and interdisciplinary depth.

title: Impact of Patient Portal Outreach and Hybrid Trial Model on Screening Volume and Trial Enrollment in Diabetic Kidney Disease: A Single-Site Operational Evaluation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Northeastern University, Northeastern University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Impact of Patient Portal Outreach and Hybrid Trial Model on Screening Volume and Trial Enrollment in Diabetic Kidney Disease: A Single-Site Operational Evaluation
detail.abstract: Background:Recruitment inefficiency remains a persistent barrier in clinical trials involving patients with chronic kidney disease, who often have comorbidities and logistical constraints that limit sustained participation. We evaluated whether sequential implementation of patient portal-based outreach and a hybrid recruitment and follow-up model was associated with changes in screening and enrollment counts and geographic reach at the Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH) site of an ongoing multicenter randomized trial in diabetic kidney disease.Methods:We performed a retrospective, single-site operational evaluation of prospectively collected data from the BWH site. Data was analyzed across three sequential recruitment phases: conventional recruitment, patient portal-based outreach transition, and a hybrid recruitment and follow-up model incorporating remote screening, off-site laboratory testing, and flexible in-person and remote follow-up visits. Outcomes included monthly screening and enrollment counts, the phase-level enrollment yield, patient portal-based engagement, and distance from participants’ residences to the study site. Differences across recruitment phases were evaluated using nonparametric tests and negative binomial regression.Results:The BWH site enrolled 123 of 156 participants randomized across all three participating sites. Median monthly screening increased from 3.5 during conventional recruitment to 20.5 during the hybrid phase, and median monthly enrollment increased from 1 to 9. Phase-level enrollment yields were 26.4%, 48.6%, and 29.7% across the three phases, respectively. Among enrolled participants, the median distance from home to the trial site increased from 7.8 to 19.9 miles.Conclusions:Patient portal-based outreach followed by a hybrid model was associated with higher screening and enrollment counts and greater geographic reach.

title: The Double-Edged Sword of AI Hallucinations: Experimental Evidence on Creativity Across Idea Generation and Refinement
affiliations: Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University, Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University and Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California

detail.title: The Double-Edged Sword of AI Hallucinations: Experimental Evidence on Creativity Across Idea Generation and Refinement

publicationDetails.detailsText: Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support creative work, yet little empirical evidence exists regarding how AI hallucinations influence creativity. Prior research has largely treated hallucinations as errors that undermine accuracy and reliability, leaving their role in creative tasks underexplored. In this study, we conduct an experiment in which participants use LLM assistance to generate, select, and refine product ideas based on real-world patents under varying levels of AI hallucination. Our findings reveal that the creative consequences of AI hallucinations depend on both hallucination severity and the stage of the creative process. During idea generation (divergent thinking), moderate and high levels of hallucination enhance originality, diversity, and elaboration, whereas during idea refinement (convergent thinking), higher levels of hallucination improve originality but come at the expense of feasibility. We further identify AI hallucination-induced recombinant search as a key mechanism through which AI hallucinations enhance creativity, whereby hallucinated AI outputs enable the discovery and recombination of previously disconnected knowledge elements, providing empirical support for the creative potential of AI hallucinations. Overall, this study provides one of the first empirical investigations of the creative consequences of AI hallucinations, offering a more nuanced understanding of hallucinations as barriers and enablers of creativity. More broadly, our findings suggest that the value of AI hallucinations depends on the cognitive demands of the creative process and provide practical insights for designing more effective human-AI creative workflows.

title: Taxing Money Holdings: Periodic Recoinage in the Middle Ages

detail.title: Taxing Money Holdings: Periodic Recoinage in the Middle Ages

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: I gratefully acknowledge financial support from the Sven Svensson Foundation for Numismatics, the Gunnar Ekström Foundation, and the Sven and Dagmar Salén Foundation.

detail.abstract:
This chapter analyses periodic recoinage (renovatio monetae) as a distinct and systematic monetary regime that was widely applied in medieval Europe between approximately AD 900 and 1400. Under periodic recoinage, local coins were valid only for a limited time and were regularly withdrawn and replaced by new issues at pre-announced exchange rates and at fixed, recurring intervals. This mechanism constituted a transparent form of monetary taxation, fundamentally different from hidden debasement strategies.
The chapter develops a theoretical framework explaining why periodic recoinage emerged, which institutional and economic conditions were required for it to function, and why it eventually broke down. Particular emphasis is placed on the interaction between low monetization, small currency areas, exchange monopolies, and minting technology—especially the role of bracteates as a cost-minimizing and enforcement-friendly coin type.
The theoretical analysis is followed by extensive empirical case studies from England, Germany, Scandinavia, Poland, and Bohemia, supported by numismatic evidence, written sources, and coin-hoard data. The chapter concludes by examining enforcement problems, distributional effects, temporary price-level dynamics, and the political and fiscal mechanisms behind the system’s eventual breakdown, linking periodic recoinage to later developments in long-lived coinage systems, token coinage, and representative money.

title: The Audit Trail of Impulse: A Framework for Detecting Behavioral Trading Errors in Retail Execution Records

detail.title: The Audit Trail of Impulse: A Framework for Detecting Behavioral Trading Errors in Retail Execution Records
detail.abstract: Four decades of behavioral finance research have established that retail traders systematically exhibit the disposition effect, overconfidence-driven overtrading, and loss-chasing behavior. Nearly all of this evidence is top-down: researchers observe large brokerage datasets and document biases in aggregate, while the individual trader — the agent who would benefit most from detection — has no published framework for identifying these patterns in their own records. This paper proposes such a framework. I develop a taxonomy of seven 'impulse signatures': measurable markers in a trader's own execution data (fills, timestamps, position sizes, and realized P&L) that map onto documented biases, including revenge re-entry after stop-outs, position-size escalation across consecutive losses, trade-frequency spikes late in losing sessions, and holding-time asymmetry between winners and losers. I argue that self-auditing of execution records constitutes a behavioral intervention in its own right, connecting the framework to the literature on commitment devices, feedback, and self-control. The taxonomy is designed to be computable from standard broker export files without proprietary data, making it directly testable; I outline the empirical validation program it implies. The framework inverts the traditional research posture of behavioral finance: from documenting that traders err, to specifying how an individual trader can detect the errors as their own.

title: Suffer Not the Economist to Live: What Warhammer 40,000 Gets Right About Institutional Dysfunction
affiliations: Trinity Business School, Trinity College Dublin

detail.title: Suffer Not the Economist to Live: What Warhammer 40,000 Gets Right About Institutional Dysfunction
detail.abstract: For nearly four decades, Warhammer 40,000 has sustained a dedicated community. This paper argues that much of its appeal derives from the institutional coherence of the Imperium of Man, a dystopian empire whose apparent dysfunction resembles durable extractive systems. We develop the concept of constraint convergence: Games Workshop's commercial and narrative pressures independently generated features comparable to those identified in North's transaction-cost framework, Acemoglu and Robinson's account of extractive institutions, and Scott's theory of state legibility. Coercive extraction, bureaucratic sclerosis, and technological conservatism thus appear not as inconsistencies but as load-bearing responses to structural constraint. Yet these institutions are not simulated in tabletop play. The rules privilege tactical agency and clear causality, while paratext carries institutional complexity. Drawing on paratext theory, procedural rhetoric, and participatory culture, we argue that this division of labour allows fans to co-produce coherence across an inconsistent, multi-authored canon without burdening the game with mechanics.

title: A Scalable Portfolio Model for Market Basket Choices
affiliations: and Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Marketing and Logistics

detail.title: A Scalable Portfolio Model for Market Basket Choices

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: Sparse market baskets create a fundamental challenge for multicategory choice models: nonpurchase need not indicate low product value, and co-purchase need not indicate consumption complementarity. We develop a scalable portfolio choice model in which households first face product-group opening costs and then choose categories within opened groups. The model uses within-category inclusive values to control for product attractiveness, allowing category entry to be modeled separately from product appeal. A product-group opening cost generates same-group co-entry because the fixed cost of opening a broader product group is paid only once. This mechanism provides an access-cost explanation for co-purchase and yields a diagnostic implication: conditional on the product group being open, the opening cost cannot create residual pairwise attraction. Computationally, the model factorizes the basket likelihood by product group, avoiding unrestricted enumeration over all category portfolios. Using NielsenIQ household panel and retail scanner data for a 32-category grocery system, we find that the model improves fit primarily in portfolio moments-basket size, group openings, and same-group co-entry-rather than in marginal category-entry rates. The results show that product-group opening, household routines, and trip-level shopping missions are distinct sources of basket dependence. For category management, the findings imply that high co-purchase lift should not be read mechanically as complementarity; it may instead reflect that shoppers have crossed a product-group opening margin.

title: Toward a Systematic Integration of Digital Technologies in Facility Management Organizations and Services
affiliations: , Polytechnic University of Milan, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Students and Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Students

detail.title: Toward a Systematic Integration of Digital Technologies in Facility Management Organizations and Services
detail.abstract:
Purpose-This article focuses on the complex relationship between digital technologies (DTs) and Facility Management (FM), aiming to develop frameworks to systematically integrate DTs into FM organizations and services. 

Design/methodology/approach-We conducted workshops with academics and industry representatives, focusing on (i) the classification and conceptualization of DT applications in FM, (ii) the effects of DT on FM, and (iii) the standardization and scaling of DTs within organizations and across the industry. 

Findings-This article, classifies DTs from the perspectives of information systems, business development, and the value chain. This article identifies key technology considerations, including positive and negative effects, risks and myths, barriers and enablers, and coping strategies. This article addresses opportunities and challenges related to the standardization and scaling of DTs.

Practical implications – The conceptualizations co-created by industry and academia help establish a relevant research agenda and support the implementation of DTs.

Originality/value – These categorizations advance the understanding of DTs in FM and lay a foundation for further research.

title: Reinvestment as Revealed Confidence: Reading Vietnam's Foreign Direct Investment Beyond the New-Licence Headcount

detail.title: Reinvestment as Revealed Confidence: Reading Vietnam's Foreign Direct Investment Beyond the New-Licence Headcount

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and Managing Partner of Lotus Investment Group, a boutique M&A and investment advisory firm active in cross-border transactions in Southeast Asia, including Vietnam. The paper reflects a practitioner perspective, draws solely on publicly available data, and does not constitute investment advice. detail.abstract: Foreign direct investment into Vietnam is conventionally read through the headline volume of newly registered projects. This paper argues that the headline is the weaker signal, and that a more informative variable is what investors already on the ground choose to do once they have lived with the operating environment: top up registered capital, raise equity stakes, and lengthen the horizon on commitments they have already made. A firm chooses where to break ground partly on expectation; it chooses where to add capital on evidence. Following the literature on reinvested earnings (Lundan, 2006; Zélity, 2025) and on the developmental quality rather than quantity of FDI (Alfaro & Charlton, 2007; OECD, 2022), the paper treats incumbent reinvestment and equity acquisition as revealed confidence. Using official Vietnamese data for 2015-2025, firm-level case evidence, and UNCTAD balance-of-payments data for regional comparison, it documents a consistent pattern. Adjusted (additional) registered capital from existing investors rose from USD 7.9 billion in 2023 to USD 14.1 billion in 2025, its highest level in the eleven-year series and roughly 37% of total registered capital, even as newly registered capital fell for two consecutive years; the surge is concentrated in named incumbents (Samsung, LG, Amkor, Foxconn, Hyosung) expanding existing sites. Realized (disbursed) FDI rose almost monotonically to a record USD 27.6 billion in 2025. And on a like-for-like UNCTAD basis, Vietnam was the only one of five major ASEAN recipients whose inflows rose in every year from 2021 to 2024. The paper is deliberate about what the data cannot say: Vietnam's "adjusted registered capital" is an administrative measure, not the balance-of-payments concept of reinvested earnings, which Vietnam (unlike Thailand, Malaysia or the Philippines) does not separately report in the harmonized IMF data at all; the country runs a large investment-income deficit as profits are repatriated; and reinvestment is not monotonic, with documented pull-backs (Intel, Hana Micron). It also examines a forward-looking complication: the 2024 adoption of the global minimum tax, which neutralises the tax incentives that historically anchored reinvestment and shifts the lever to non-tax support. These qualifications narrow the claim without dissolving it. The argument carries practical consequences for how policymakers measure progress and how cross-border acquirers price the destination.

title: Trade Without Capital: Reading Australia's Investment Gap with Southeast Asia

detail.title: Trade Without Capital: Reading Australia's Investment Gap with Southeast Asia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and Managing Partner of Lotus Investment Group, a boutique M&A and investment advisory firm active in cross-border transactions between Australia and Southeast Asia, including Vietnam. The paper reflects a practitioner perspective, draws solely on publicly available official data, and does not constitute investment advice. No client relationship or commercial engagement influenced the analysis.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses only publicly available, aggregate official statistics and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Australia treats Southeast Asia as a strategic priority and trades with it heavily, yet invests in it barely at all. This paper documents the gap and asks why it persists. Using Australian Bureau of Statistics data for 2025, it shows that Australia's entire outward direct-investment stock in ASEAN is A$26 billion, just 2.1% of its total, less than it holds in New Zealand alone, and that almost two-thirds of that sits in Singapore. Australia's direct-investment stock in Vietnam is A$490 million, roughly one five-hundredth of its position in the United States and, on one estimate, smaller than a single Danish toymaker's factory in Binh Duong. Set against an annual two-way trade flow of A$197.5 billion, the investment relationship lags the trade relationship by an order of magnitude; and the capital that does move runs the "wrong" way, with ASEAN holding more direct investment in Australia (A$67 billion) than Australia holds in ASEAN. On a comparable basis, Australia is not among ASEAN's top ten sources of foreign investment and has de-ranked over the past decade even as the region's inflows doubled. The paper reads this through the literature on the gravity of bilateral FDI and on information frictions, which predict that direct investment, being stickier and more information-intensive than trade, under-responds to proximity when familiarity is low. It then examines Australia's policy turn, the 2023 Invested strategy and the A$2 billion Southeast Asia Investment Financing Facility, as the gap's mirror image, and assesses what would have to change for the corridor to thicken. The argument carries practical consequences for cross-border investors and advisers positioned between the two economies.

title: Quality over Closure in Agentic Procurement: BATNA-Aware Reward Design for LLM Agents in Buyer-Supplier Negotiation
affiliations: Arizona State University, Arizona State University, W. P. Carey School of Business and Arizona State University

detail.title: Quality over Closure in Agentic Procurement: BATNA-Aware Reward Design for LLM Agents in Buyer-Supplier Negotiation

keywords: Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement

detail.abstract: Negotiation is a core procurement mechanism for determining prices, allocations, and contract terms when private information is present. As artificial intelligence moves from decision support to autonomous agency, buyer-supplier bargaining can increasingly be delegated to autonomous procurement agents that converse, reason over constraints, and commit to offers at scale. This shift creates a governance problem: an agent optimized merely to close deals may accept contracts a manager would reject relative to the firm's Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA). We address this problem through reinforcement learning by designing BATNA-aware rewards for large language model negotiation agents. The reward introduces a tunable utility floor that represents a package-level resistance point, penalizes agreements below that floor, and is applied selectively to multi-issue bargaining tasks where no natural structural floor exists, while surplus rewards are retained for single-issue price bargaining. We train a single unified agent across four benchmarks spanning price bargaining and multi-issue bargaining and evaluate it against both its frozen training opponent and stronger frontier models, including transfer to a held-out hybrid task. The proposed reward achieves the highest average bargained ratio, reduces deal-closing bias, and offers an interpretable control for calibrating walk-away behavior in agentic procurement systems.

title: The Global Minimum Tax and Foreign Direct Investment in Southeast Asia: Adoption, Incentive Redesign, and the Turn from Tax to Cash

detail.title: The Global Minimum Tax and Foreign Direct Investment in Southeast Asia: Adoption, Incentive Redesign, and the Turn from Tax to Cash

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and Managing Partner of Lotus Investment Group, a boutique M&A and investment advisory firm active in cross-border transactions across Southeast Asia, including Vietnam. The paper reflects a practitioner perspective, draws on publicly available official releases and reputable summaries, and does not constitute tax or investment advice. No client relationship influenced the analysis.

detail.abstract: Southeast Asia built its foreign-investment model on tax: corporate-income-tax holidays and preferential rates that pulled the effective rates of large multinationals well below the statutory level. The OECD's Pillar Two global minimum tax, applied across the region from 2024-2025, removes that lever, because any effective rate below 15% is now collected as a top-up tax somewhere, and the host that granted the holiday is usually the one that must collect it. This paper documents how the five largest ASEAN economies, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, have adopted the minimum tax and, more importantly, how each has redesigned its investment incentives in response. Two models have emerged. The first, adopted by Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, replaces forgone tax breaks with cash grants and qualified refundable tax credits that are treated favourably under the global rules and sit outside the top-up-tax base. The second, adopted by Thailand, recycles a large share of the top-up revenue the minimum tax itself raises back to investors through a competitiveness fund. The paper reads this turn from tax to cash through the literature on tax incentives and FDI, which finds that tax holidays were an expensive and only partially effective instrument to begin with, and argues that the reform may improve the quality of the region's incentive competition even as it raises its fiscal cost and shifts it toward discretion. It closes with the implications for investors and advisers, for whom the binding incentive is now a grant to be accessed rather than a rate to be negotiated. Every legal instrument is cited by type, number and date; the region's adoption is summarised in a single comparative table.
