declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The review uses only publicly available, aggregate official statistics and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The review received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This is the first edition of an annual, data-first review of foreign direct investment in Vietnam, intended as a standing reference for investors, advisers, policymakers and researchers. It compiles the official record for 2025 and sets it in an eleven-year context (2015-2025), covering registered capital and its three components, realized (disbursed) capital and the implementation ratio, sector composition, provincial distribution, source economies, the position of Vietnam against its ASEAN peers on a comparable balance-of-payments basis, and the policy environment, including the 2024 adoption of the global minimum tax and the compensating Investment Support Fund. Vietnam attracted USD 38.42 billion of registered FDI in 2025 and disbursed a record USD 27.62 billion; the defining structural feature of the year was the continued rise of reinvestment by existing investors, with adjusted capital reaching USD 14.07 billion, roughly 37% of the total. This edition adds a decomposition of what drives each year’s change in the total, a cumulative “pipeline” view of registered against realized capital, size-adjusted regional comparisons on FDI intensity and share, a regional comparison of the post-minimum-tax incentive transition across the ASEAN-5, and an account of the trade-investment nexus and the 2025 United States tariff shift that now bears directly on the investment data. The review is descriptive rather than argumentative; every figure is sourced to official Vietnamese statistics and international data, and the full series is provided in the data appendix. The intention is that each annual edition updates the same tables and charts, so that the series becomes a continuous reference on Vietnam's inward investment.

title:
Social Entrepreneurship, Value Creation, and Sustainable Impact:
An Integrative Review of the Literature up to 2022 and a Conceptual Framework Proposal

detail.title:
Social Entrepreneurship, Value Creation, and Sustainable Impact:
An Integrative Review of the Literature up to 2022 and a Conceptual Framework Proposal
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the conceptual evolution of social entrepreneurship through an integrative review of literature published up to 2022. Its objective is to examine the field's main theoretical tensions and to propose a conceptual framework for understanding social entrepreneurship as a hybrid form of sustainable social value creation. The review shows that the concept has been approached from several traditions, including social innovation, social enterprise, the social economy, institutional theory, social value creation, hybrid organizational models, and impact measurement. Despite this conceptual diversity, the literature converges around four critical dimensions: social value, economic sustainability, mission governance, and measurable impact. On this basis, the VSGI Framework is proposed as an analytical tool for evaluating social entrepreneurship initiatives, distinguishing them from traditional philanthropy, peripheral corporate social responsibility, or cause-related marketing, and guiding future research. The article concludes that social entrepreneurship should not be defined solely by the intention to generate welfare, but by its capacity to address relevant social problems through sustainable models, coherent governance mechanisms, and proportional evidence of results.

title: Bargaining Power and the Optimal Sequence of Negotiations
affiliations: University of Cologne and Frankfurt School of Finance & Management - Economics Department

detail.title: Bargaining Power and the Optimal Sequence of Negotiations

declarations.funderStatement: Funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy −EXC 2126/2− 390838866.

detail.abstract: In most bargaining situations with multiple parties, the negotiation sequence is crucial for the efficiency of outcomes and the parties' success. However, the driving forces behind the socially and privately optimal sequences are poorly understood. To study these issues, we consider a general framework of bilateral negotiations between a principal and two agents with bargaining externalities. We show that the agents' bargaining strengths are essential for the determination of the sequence. The surplus is highest if the principal negotiates with the stronger agent first, regardless of externalities being positive or negative. The principal always chooses the efficient sequence if externalities are negative. Instead, if externalities are positive, the principal often prefers to negotiate with the weaker agent first. We show that our results extend to a general number of agents, demonstrate that the sequence can be non-monotonic in the externalities, and provide conditions for simultaneous negotiations to be optimal.

title: The Carbon Odyssey: Value-chain Carbon Flows, Demand Reallocation, and Dynamic Low-carbon Upgrading
affiliations: , University of Science and Technology of China and University of Science and Technology of China

detail.title: The Carbon Odyssey: Value-chain Carbon Flows, Demand Reallocation, and Dynamic Low-carbon Upgrading

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it does not involve human participants, patients, animals, or personally identifiable data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We develop an infinite-horizon dynamic general-equilibrium model with a production network to study value-chain carbon flows, demand reallocation, and dynamic low-carbon upgrading. The model traces how carbon is measured, priced, and transmitted through the production network, and how this transmission affects welfare. Low-carbon preferences generate carbon premia that reallocate final demand toward cleaner varieties and propagate upstream through supplier choice. Carbon permits operate through a distinct channel: permit scarcity raises the cost of carbon-intensive energy and production, and these costs propagate downstream through intermediate and final-good prices. In the dynamic economy, firms decide each period whether to upgrade by comparing current adoption costs with future gains from demand expansion, cost reductions, and lower carbon exposure. We show that low-carbon preferences and carbon regulation accelerate firms' low-carbon adoption; by reducing embedded carbon in intermediate inputs, these upgrades create positive network spillovers along the value chain. The welfare analysis compares the benchmark economy with a counterfactual without low-carbon preferences or cap-and-trade, focusing on a common allocation-based channel rather than a direct comparison of utility levels across different preferences. Low-carbon demand and cap-and-trade improve welfare by accelerating low-carbon adoption, beginning with high-appeal firms and generating technological gains that extend beyond consumers who directly value lower carbon content.

title: A Cross-Jurisdiction Crosswalk of Machine-Learning Model-Risk Regulation, with an Open Compliance Benchmark for Quantitative Finance
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: A Cross-Jurisdiction Crosswalk of Machine-Learning Model-Risk Regulation, with an Open Compliance Benchmark for Quantitative Finance
detail.abstract: Machine-learning model-risk regulation in finance has fragmented across jurisdictions. The U.S. SR 11-7 / OCC Bulletin 2011-12, the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), the U.K. Prudential Regulation Authority's SS1/23, Singapore's MAS FEAT principles and Veritas assessment methodologies, and Canada's OSFI Guideline E-23 each impose overlapping but non-identical obligations on model documentation, data provenance, independent validation, per-prediction logging, record retention, monitoring, and governance. A firm deploying one model into several markets must currently reconcile these texts by hand, and a researcher auditing the published literature has no common yardstick. This paper makes two paired contributions. First, we construct a cross-jurisdiction crosswalk that maps twelve audit-trail and model-risk-management requirements onto the specific provision of each regime (and onto the voluntary NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 frameworks), making explicit which obligations the regimes share, which are unique to a single jurisdiction, and which have no analogue at all. Second, we release an open compliance benchmark that scores a machine-learning pipeline against the union of these requirements, with a reproducible scoring harness and a public leaderboard. Both artefacts are released under permissive licences and versioned against the regulations' effective dates, so that practitioners and researchers can extend them as the law evolves.

title: From Diversification to Consolidation: Supply Chain Reconfiguration across Repeated Tariff Episodes
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Operations Area, Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management, , , Santa Clara University - Leavey School of Business and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: From Diversification to Consolidation: Supply Chain Reconfiguration across Repeated Tariff Episodes
detail.abstract: Most prior academic research examines how firms respond to a single tariff episode. Yet firms increasingly operate in an environment characterized by recurring tariff shocks. Whether successive tariff episodes lead firms to continue diversifying their supply chains or instead prompt a different mode of adaptation remains largely unknown. We study how U.S. importing firms reconfigure their global supply chains across two major tariff episodes: Trade War 1.0 in 2018 and Trade War 2.0 in 2025. Using firm-product-level import transactions from Panjiva matched with Compustat, we track changes in sourcing locations, supplier networks, and shipment flows. We first show that both tariff episodes divert sourcing away from China toward a similar set of alternative countries. However, the magnitude of reallocation is substantially weaker during the second episode, and the nearshoring shift toward North America that emerged in the first episode is largely absent. We then document a fundamental shift in firms’ adjustment behavior across episodes. The initial tariff episode induces broad-based diversification: firms expand the number of sourcing countries and suppliers while reducing average shipment volumes per supplier, consistent with an explore-and-test response under uncertainty. In contrast, the repeated tariff episode does not further broaden supplier networks. Instead, firms reduce the number of active suppliers and concentrate sourcing within networks established during the first episode. Moreover, supply chain reconfiguration following the second episode occurs more rapidly and is driven primarily by supplier exits rather than new supplier entry. This pattern suggests that firms draw on knowledge accumulated during the first trade war to make more targeted and decisive adjustments. The consolidation effect is particularly pronounced for differentiated products, where coordination-intensive inputs are less amenable to fragmented supplier networks. Repeated tariff episodes do not lead to further diversification. Rather, an initial episode prompts firms to build supply chain optionality by expanding their sourcing networks, whereas subsequent episodes trigger selective pruning and consolidation within those expanded networks. These findings offer guidance for managers seeking to design resilient global supply chains in an era of recurring trade-policy uncertainty.

title: The Impact of Digital Payment Systems (UPI) on Economic Growth :  A State-Level Panel Data Analysis

detail.title: The Impact of Digital Payment Systems (UPI) on Economic Growth :  A State-Level Panel Data Analysis
detail.abstract: The landscape and structure of India’s digital economy have changed significantly over the last decade. One possible reason for this transformation is the rapid growth of the Unified Payment System, or UPI. People use it for a wide range of transactions- in local shops, cafés, supermarkets, and even for very small purchases. The increase after 2018 was phenomenal. UPI transactions have risen year after year during the period from FY 2018 19 to FY 2023–24. Today, UPI handles nearly 75% of India’s retail digital transactions (Dev et al., 2024). More than 2/3rds of payments being channeled through only one app underscores how quickly digital settlements have become part of the everyday life of the citizens of India. In many cities, paying through UPI now feels routine (Dev et al., 2024).  The primary research question of this study is to find What is the impact of UPI adoption on state-level economic growth in India? The question focuses on examining whether the use of UPI is linked to higher levels of economic growth across the States in India. Since the States differ widely across many aspects, such as income, infrastructure, and development, which needs to be accounted for, becomes an important rationale for conducting this study in a more detailed and disaggregated way. In addition to the previous question, the study also aims to uncover if UPI acts as a ‘leapfrog’ technology, meaning that it benefits less developed States more than 'more developed' ones. This question is of great importance because some studies argue that newtechnologies are expected to help weaker regions grow faster by allowing them to skip the traditional stages of development (Steinmueller, 2001). If UPI works in this way, it can help reduce inequalities among States by supporting faster growth in less developed States. However, an opposite outcome is also possible, as argued by Acemoglu (2002). It is also possible that States with better infrastructure, stronger governance, and higher digital readiness benefit more from using UPI (Acemoglu, 2002).

title: A Model for Business Ethics in the Sharing Economy
affiliations: Student

detail.title: A Model for Business Ethics in the Sharing Economy
detail.abstract:
The cornerstone of this study is business ethics.

A review of the literature about business ethics in the digital economy at the initial stages of the research process confirmed a surge in academic research about management and organisational issues in the sharing economy. In contrast, research about business ethics in the sharing economy was lacking, which is why the editors of a November 2019, Special Issue of the Journal of Business Ethics expressed the need for business ethicists to address ethical problems in the sharing economy.

Although the concept of business ethics has existed since the 1970s in the US, corporate scandals and unethical behaviour occur globally on a regular basis. The analysis of the review of literature about business ethics revealed several fundamental issues regarding the failure of business ethics to curtail ongoing unethical behaviour, including the disconnect between academia and business. Therefore, after critically evaluating the literature, it was suggested that there is a systemic problem in business ethics.

After an initial assessment at the inception of this study, it was concluded that, because of the shortcomings in business ethics in general and the uniqueness of the new and unfolding, digital and sharing economies, the current practices of business ethics would not be adequate for the sharing economy. As a result, the main research question for the study was: What are the main characteristics and features of business ethics for the sharing economy? Therefore, the purpose of the study was to provide a model for business ethics in the sharing economy.

Change has become the norm in business today, which is why an interpretative approach, with phenomenology as a qualitative research methodology, was adopted for this study. Semi- structured, in-depth interviews with 19 participants provided the data for this study.

All the research objectives in the study were achieved. Firstly, the analysis of the participants’ experiences confirmed the assessment that current business ethics practices are not sufficient for the sharing economy. Secondly, the characteristics of a sharing economy company were identified, using Airbnb as an example. Thirdly, based on an analysis of the participants' experiences, a model for business ethics in the sharing economy was produced.

The authors of Blockchain Revolution recently provided a model of seven design principles for blockchain. Another recent study provided a model for governance principles for the blockchain economy. At the same time, a special issue of the Journal of Business Ethics was devoted recently to the impact of artificial intelligence on business ethics in organisations. The simultaneous occurrence of these events is one example of the convergence of the sharing economy, artificial intelligence and blockchain and illustrates the relevance of this study.

This study forms a credible basis for further research explorations about business ethics in the sharing economy and the related technologies of artificial intelligence and blockchain in future.

Keywords: Business ethics, digital economy, sharing economy, blockchain economy, artificial intelligence

title: Human Development as Pure Awareness: The Case for SDG 0

detail.title: Human Development as Pure Awareness: The Case for SDG 0
detail.abstract: This paper asks to what extent the human-development frameworks underpinning contemporary policy can accommodate pure awareness-a heightened, non-conceptual alertness, distinct from ordinary waking vigilance, on which neuroscientific, phenomenological and contemplative literatures converge. It advances two separable claims. The narrow, analytical claim is that pure awareness is conceptually compatible with the three leading frameworks (Sen's and Nussbaum's capability approaches and Wilber's Integral Theory) but paradigmatically compatible with only Wilber's, whose evolutionary (Aurobindo-Hegel) lineage admits the inner life as foundational rather than derivative. The broad claim is that this gap matters for the post-2030 development agenda, because paradigms-not parameters-determine what a system can deliver (Meadows, 2009; Kuhn, 1970). The argument is deliberately ontologically neutral: it does not assert that reality is ultimately consciousness, only that heightened awareness functions as an upstream precondition for the quality of human decision, wellbeing, freedom and action-a claim robust enough that even a reductive physicalist (Metzinger, 2009) endorses the practice. I close with a two-track set of recommendations, a proposal to treat pure awareness as the foundational enhancer of the SDG framework ("SDG 0"), and the conditions under which the thesis would be falsified.

title: Donors' Blended Finance Portfolio Optimization, A Variation on Modern Portfolio Theory

detail.title: Donors' Blended Finance Portfolio Optimization, A Variation on Modern Portfolio Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Executive PhD candidate at ESCP Business School and Deputy CEO at Climate Investment Funds, formerly Director of Blended Finance at IDB Invest.

detail.abstract: For a blended finance donor, is extending a grant different than extending a concessional investment of the same subsidy equivalent? If not, what drives a donor's choice of instrument and participation amount? More broadly, in the context of constrained aid budgets, is there room for donor-side financial optimization in blended finance, holding other decision-making factors constant? To address these questions, I draw on Modern Portfolio Theory to formulate and solve a donor optimization problem. I assume donors' decision-making is sequential: aid envelopes, broad policy objectives and project selection are set before the financial terms of individual concessional financings are determined. Assuming stochastic and correlated projects' returns, donor preferences at this final stage can be represented in terms of the donor's expected present cost and the variance of that cost. The model yields five main results. First, grants are preferred when donor risk tolerance is zero or close to it. Second, greater donor risk tolerance lowers the expected donor's cost, but only by increasing nominal donor participation and thereby reducing private capital leverage. Third, grants are also preferred for any asset for which the donor's cost of funding exceeds the investor's hurdle rate. Fourth, when optimal donor participation exceeds the aggregate subsidy equivalent, the same optimum can be implemented through different combinations of grants and investments. Finally, in the unconstrained interior case, donor risk tolerance affects the amount of the donor's participation but not the relative portfolio weights across assets.

title: Carbon Tariffs and Macroeconomic Adjustment in Emerging Markets: The Role of Exchange Rate Regimes
affiliations: and Mohammed V University of Rabat

detail.title: Carbon Tariffs and Macroeconomic Adjustment in Emerging Markets: The Role of Exchange Rate Regimes
detail.abstract: Unilateral carbon tariffs pose severe macroeconomic challenges to emerging market economies. We develop a repeated game-theoretic model featuring multidimensional policy strategies and macro-financial constraints governed by exchange rate regimes to study how emerging markets respond to foreign carbon tariffs. Our theoretical model demonstrates that exchange rate regimes critically shape these strategic incentives. In corner solutions, fixed regimes incentivize the unilateral adoption of domestic carbon pricing and weaken the credibility of trade retaliation, whereas floating regimes undermine standalone domestic carbon pricing but strengthen complementarities between carbon pricing and carbon-based retaliation. In repeated interactions, climate policy cooperation is easier to sustain under floating regimes and more fragile under fixed regimes due to structural shock-absorption and credible retaliation mechanisms that prevent deviations. To test these theoretical insights, we construct a novel continuous trade-weighted index capturing regulatory exposure to the CBAM shock across a panel of 25 emerging markets from 2010 to 2024. This indicator is embedded within a regime-dependent Double Machine Learning Local Projections (DML-LP) framework for nonlinear causal inference. Our empirical estimations reveal a severe, delayed real effective exchange rate depreciation following a carbon tariff shock under fixed regimes, whereas floating regimes smoothly absorb the shock, strongly aligning with our game-theoretic assertions.

title: Deepfakes And Identity Appropriation: Re-Examining The Limits Of Indian Criminal Law In The Age Of Generative AI
affiliations: Woxsen University

detail.title: Deepfakes And Identity Appropriation: Re-Examining The Limits Of Indian Criminal Law In The Age Of Generative AI
detail.abstract: Rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence have enabled the creation of highly realistic synthetic videos, audio, and images capable of imitating a person's face, voice, and likeness without consent. 1 Public discussions on deepfakes are usually about misinformation, but this paper argues the fundamental legal problem lies elsewhere: Indian criminal law which treats deepfakes as wrongful only when they produce a separate recognisable harm such as fraud, defamation, or fabricated evidence rather than recognising it as the theft of identity of an individual as an independently wrongful act. Drawing on recent Indian incidents which include Rashmika Mandanna deepfake controversy 2 , deepfake-enabled investment scams impersonating executives associated with Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) 3 , and AI-generated political content circulated during the Tamil Nadu Assembly Election 2026, this paper examines the Information Technology Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and finds that each statute applies only after a downstream consequence occurs. The paper then discusses Indian personality rights law, which recognises that using someone's identity without consent is independently illegal and can be enforced through civil courts. It argues that this principle should also be applied in criminal law, not just civil law. The paper further recommends creating a new law that specifically criminalises the non-consensual use of digitally created or synthetic versions of a person's identity such as deepfakes. Overall, the paper suggests that Indian law should shift from a reactive approach in which action is taken only after harm occurs to a preventive approach where unauthorized use of identity itself is treated as an offence. This paper's novel contribution lies in reframing deepfake regulation in India from a consequence-based harm model to an identity-based appropriation model, arguing that unauthorised digital replication itself should be treated as the primary criminal wrong.

title: From Prudence to Power in European and American Stablecoin Regulations
affiliations: Student

detail.title: From Prudence to Power in European and American Stablecoin Regulations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: "A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution.", S. Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, White Paper, October 2008, opening lines.

detail.abstract: Stablecoins now represent a combined market capitalisation of $310 billion and settle transaction volumes exceeding those of Visa and Mastercard aggregated. The MiCA Regulation in the European Union and the GENIUS Act in the United States constitute two concurrent normative responses to this phenomenon. This comparative study in banking and financial law reveals a remarkable convergence on the prudential front: the requirement for reserves at parity with issuance and the management of banking disintermediation risk feature as shared objectives, often pursued through similar legal techniques. However, divergence emerges on the monetary front: while the European Union erects a defensive framework in service of its monetary sovereignty, the United States instrumentalizes the private stablecoin as a vector for the hegemonic expansion of the dollar.

title: Decide or Default? How Defaults, Information, and Financial Incentives Influence Sustainable Delivery Choices in a Field Experiment
affiliations: , University of Groningen and University of Groningen - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: Decide or Default? How Defaults, Information, and Financial Incentives Influence Sustainable Delivery Choices in a Field Experiment

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical review was conducted by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the University of Groningen, which reviewed the completed research data management plan and ethics checklist and issued a statement of no objection for the study.

detail.abstract: E-commerce delivery choices matter for environmental sustainability, yet checkout designs often steer consumers toward faster, less sustainable options. Research on shifting these choices has focused largely on information and financial incentives, with evidence drawn mainly from stated-preference and controlled settings whose findings may not carry over to actual checkout behavior. This study reports a large-scale field experiment with an e-commerce retailer, in which three commonly studied interventions are varied: (i) the preselection of a delivery option (default), (ii) the provision of sustainability information, and (iii) a small financial incentive. The empirical design allows identification of both the individual and combined effects of these interventions on the uptake of sustainable delivery. The results show that the sustainable default is by far the most effective intervention. Financial incentives and sustainability information both raise uptake only modestly. Interaction effects are predominantly negative, suggesting that interventions partly substitute for one another. Taken together, the pattern of effects is consistent with delivery choices being made with limited deliberation at checkout, where interventions requiring minimal effort are especially effective.  For retailers, this implies that simple, low-cost changes to checkout design can substantially increase the uptake of sustainable delivery.

title: The Execution Economics Canon: Understanding Why Projects Succeed, Fail, or Stall

detail.title: The Execution Economics Canon: Understanding Why Projects Succeed, Fail, or Stall
detail.abstract:
Across Africa and many emerging economies, substantial resources are invested annually in projects, institutions, and industrial initiatives that fail to achieve their intended outcomes. Conventional explanations frequently emphasize insufficient finance, weak governance, limited capacity, or infrastructural deficits. While these factors are important, they do not fully explain why similar implementation failures recur across sectors, countries, and institutional settings despite varying levels of investment and institutional commitment.

This paper introduces Execution Economics, a conceptual research programme that examines execution as a distinct object of institutional analysis. It proposes that development challenges are often better understood as system failures rather than resource failures, arguing that the decisive constraint is frequently the institutional architecture that converts capital, policy, and organisational intent into measurable outcomes.

The paper establishes the foundational concepts, philosophical position, analytical boundaries, and research agenda of Execution Economics. Rather than competing with established fields such as institutional economics, project governance, or implementation science, it proposes a complementary interpretive framework for analysing why well-funded, technically feasible, and politically supported initiatives continue to stall or underperform.

Execution Economics introduces a doctrine-based analytical architecture designed to identify recurring structural mechanisms that influence delivery performance across projects and institutions. It positions execution capability as a measurable institutional variable distinct from financial, strategic, or technical capacity and outlines a long-term research programme for developing, testing, and refining these concepts through comparative institutional analysis.

As the first paper in the VitroScript Working Paper Series, this article establishes the conceptual foundation for subsequent doctrine papers examining specific execution mechanisms, governance patterns, and institutional design principles within the broader Execution Economics research programme.

title: From AI Readiness to Organizational Performance: The Mediating Role of AI Adoption in a MENA -Anchored Multi-Industry Study

detail.title: From AI Readiness to Organizational Performance: The Mediating Role of AI Adoption in a MENA -Anchored Multi-Industry Study
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly invest in AI readiness, yet evidence remains mixed on whether such readiness improves performance directly or only after AI is adopted in practice. This study examines how innovation and the structural determinants of AI affect perceived organizational performance, with AI adoption tested as a mediating mechanism. Drawing on the TOE/TOEH framework, dynamic capabilities theory, and the resource-based view, data were collected through a bilingual online questionnaire from 422 professionals, mainly from MENA organizations. The model was assessed using SPSS, SmartPLS 4, and PROCESS Model 4. Results show that structural determinants strongly predict AI adoption, and AI adoption significantly improves perceived organizational performance. However, structural determinants do not directly affect performance once AI adoption is included. AI adoption fully mediates the structural determinants-performance relationship, while innovation affects performance directly and is not mediated by AI adoption. The study clarifies how AI readiness becomes performance-relevant only through actual adoption.

title: Uncle Sam's Cut: A Century of the Federal Tax Drag on US Equity Returns
affiliations: Columbia University

detail.title: Uncle Sam's Cut: A Century of the Federal Tax Drag on US Equity Returns
detail.abstract: We estimate the Federal tax drag on US equity investors by simulating a taxable investor holding the market portfolio from 1926 to 2025, under the tax code in force each year with tax-lot accounting, holding-period rules, capital-loss limits, and carryforwards. Federal taxes reduce long-horizon equity wealth by more than one-third. Across overlapping 30-year windows, the annualized tax drag averages 347 bps, peaks at 538 bps in 1936-1965, and falls to 165 bps in 1996-2025. Dividend taxation is the dominant historical channel. The step-up in basis at death reduces embedded capital-gains liabilities, and for a 30-year-old investor, it lowers tax drag from 165 bps to 127 bps; by age 70, it lowers it to 103 bps.

title: The Stack Sovereignty Theorem: A Mathematical Framework for Strategic Economic Power in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Energy Scarcity, Quantum Risk, and Space Industrialization

detail.title: The Stack Sovereignty Theorem: A Mathematical Framework for Strategic Economic Power in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Energy Scarcity, Quantum Risk, and Space Industrialization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it is a theoretical and policy framework paper relying exclusively on mathematical derivations, economic modeling, and publicly available aggregate secondary data. No human participants, private personal data, or animal subjects were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted as independent, self-funded research by the author.

detail.abstract: For decades, standard economic models have compressed technological progress into a weightless, frictionless scalar of total factor productivity (A). This paper develops the Stack Sovereignty Theorem as a theoretical and policy framework for strategic economic power under geopolitical fragmentation. It makes three primary contributions. First, it provides a formal model integrating O-Ring bottlenecks, supermodular complementarities, and convex state-contingent dependence to derive the net condition under which a coherent capability stack dominates isolated technological specialization. Second, it operationalizes the model through a pre-registered Sovereign Stack Index Core (SSI-Core) linking artificial intelligence, compute, energy, and critical-mineral processing. Third, it specifies a pre-registered empirical and public-policy protocol, illustrated through the 2022 European energy crisis, that shows how to diagnose bottlenecks, estimate stress-dependent fragility, and translate the theorem into industrial-policy, strategic-capital-allocation, and alliance-design rules. The paper does not claim completed causal validation; it offers a falsifiable architecture for testing when technological leadership remains robust and when it is undermined by physical constraints, external dependence, or coordination costs. Contemporary strategic power is therefore defined not by isolated technological peaks, but by coherent capability net of supply fragility and integration cost.

title: Foreign Investment in Vietnam: A Review of the Evidence

detail.title: Foreign Investment in Vietnam: A Review of the Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and Managing Partner of Lotus Investment Group, a boutique M&A and investment advisory firm active in cross-border transactions across Southeast Asia, including Vietnam. This review compiles publicly available scholarship and official data and does not constitute investment advice. No client relationship influenced the compilation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The review synthesises published literature and public statistics and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The review received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Vietnam is one of the developing world's clearest foreign-investment success stories, yet the evidence on what that investment has actually done for the economy is scattered across four decades and a dozen sub-literatures that rarely speak to each other. This paper maps that evidence. It organises the empirical work on foreign direct investment in Vietnam into seven themes, growth, productivity spillovers, exports and value chains, location and provincial institutions, wages and labour, sector and source composition, and the policy frontier, and states, for each, what the literature can say with confidence and what it cannot. Three findings recur across otherwise unrelated studies and form the spine of the review. First, aggregate spillovers are not automatic: the gains from foreign presence flow through vertical supply-chain linkages, not through same-industry proximity, where the effect on domestic firms is often negative. Second, the origin of the investor matters, with several studies finding that Asian affiliates transmit larger backward-linkage benefits than Western ones. Third, everything is conditional on absorptive capacity, human capital, financial depth, and provincial governance decide whether foreign investment lifts the domestic economy or merely coexists with it. The review anchors on the field's most-cited work, provides two reusable classification tables intended as a reference scaffold, and pushes coverage past the existing narrow reviews into the two frontiers now reshaping the field: the global minimum tax and the China-plus-one relocation wave. It closes by naming the open questions, the sharpest of which is a rigorous treatment of how the minimum tax reshapes an incentive regime built on tax holidays.

title: The China-plus-one Paradox: Vietnam's Foreign-investment Boom and its Rerouting Vulnerability

detail.title: The China-plus-one Paradox: Vietnam's Foreign-investment Boom and its Rerouting Vulnerability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and Managing Partner of Lotus Investment Group, a boutique M&A and investment advisory firm active in cross-border transactions across Southeast Asia, including Vietnam. This paper reflects a practitioner perspective, draws on publicly available data and reputable analyses, and does not constitute investment or trade-policy advice. No client relationship influenced the analysis.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The paper uses only publicly available data and analyses and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Vietnam is the poster child of "China plus one," the strategy under which multinationals keep a China base but shift new capacity elsewhere to hedge geopolitical and tariff risk. On every visible metric Vietnam leads: it was ranked the single biggest mover in global business-environment terms, the top diversification destination across almost all manufacturing sectors, and the largest single beneficiary of the shift in the United States trade deficit away from China. Its exports to the United States nearly tripled between 2017 and 2024, and Chinese firms themselves have become one of its fastest-growing sources of investment, leading Vietnam by number of new projects. This paper argues that the boom carries a paradox: the very features that make Vietnam the leading China-plus-one destination are also its central vulnerability. The same investment and trade data that show Vietnam winning, roughly US$144 billion of imported Chinese inputs in 2024, a Chinese value-added content of some 16 to 25 percent embedded in its exports, a 314 percent surge in Chinese-owned firms rerouting through the country, and an export dependence on the United States equal to about 30 percent of GDP, are precisely the exposures that the 2025 United States tariff package, with its 40 percent levy on transshipped goods, was designed to hit. Drawing on the trade-rerouting literature, the paper decomposes Vietnam's export surge into genuine value-added, an estimated 84 percent, and rerouting, the remaining 16, and argues that Vietnam is a real winner rather than a mere laundering channel, but a winner whose gains are only as durable as its ability to convert assembly into domestic value. It closes with what that means for policymakers and for investors, for whom the location decision now turns on genuine local content rather than tariff arbitrage.

title: The Labor Market Impact of Economic Nationalism
affiliations: University of Melbourne and

detail.title: The Labor Market Impact of Economic Nationalism
detail.abstract: Administrative immigration policy can reshape who firms hire even when statutory visa supply is fixed. We study the April 2017 Buy American and Hire American order, which raised the expected cost of H-1B sponsorship while leaving statutory caps unchanged. This setting allows us to study economic nationalism through sponsorship risk rather than visa quantities. Comparing firms with different pre-policy H-1B reliance in the same industry and month, we find that exposed firms shifted new hiring toward inferred citizen/permanent-resident (IPR) workers: the IPR share of six-month entrants rose 0.966 percentage points, while lateral hires did not respond. Job postings reveal the mechanism: H-1B-sensitive roles became more likely to require citizenship and less likely to offer sponsorship. A dynamic stock-adjustment model attributes the persistent response mainly to the post-order administrative regime, not to anticipation. These hiring-flow changes accumulated to roughly 23,000 IPR worker-equivalents across exposed firms.

title: Choosing an Employer of Record: Infrastructure Models, Liability Chains, and a Provider Selection Framework for Cross-Border Hiring

detail.title: Choosing an Employer of Record: Infrastructure Models, Liability Chains, and a Provider Selection Framework for Cross-Border Hiring
detail.abstract: A previous paper (Schuchmann, 2026) proposed a taxonomy distinguishing four global employment intermediary models: Employer of Record (EOR), Professional Employer Organization (PEO), Global Payroll, and Contractor of Record (COR). That taxonomy answers the between-category question: which model applies to a given hiring scenario. This paper addresses the within-category question that follows: once EOR is the appropriate model, how should a company choose between providers whose legal structures, and therefore risk profiles, differ in ways their marketing does not reveal? The central problem is that the most consequential structural distinction in the EOR market, whether the provider employs workers through its own local entities or through a network of in-country partners, is discussed almost exclusively in vendor-authored content, where each provider argues for the superiority of whichever model it happens to operate. No neutral framework exists. This paper proposes one. It formalises three infrastructure models (owned-entity, partner-network, and hybrid), introduces the liability chain as the analytical device that reveals what the infrastructure question actually determines, and argues that the owned-versus-partner binary is a proxy debate: the operative question is not which label a provider carries globally, but who the legal employer is in each specific country and how many contractual steps separate that entity from the client. A six-dimension selection framework and a sequenced decision protocol are offered for practitioners. This is a conceptual paper. It evaluates structures, not vendors, and makes no empirical claims about the performance of either infrastructure model. Independent empirical evidence on comparative compliance outcomes does not yet exist and is identified as a priority for future research.

title: Sustainability Practices in Online Grocery Retail: A Case-Based Evaluation of Picnic and Implications for Vocational Training and Personnel Development

detail.abstract: The thesis examines the sustainability practices of online grocery retailers on a case-by-case basis with the example of Picnic and their implications for vocational training and personnel development. Online grocery retail has grown at a fast pace in Europe, presenting new sustainability challenges in the field of last-mile delivery, packaging waste, food waste, digital logistics and resource efficiency. The thesis examines documents of the company as well as relevant academic literature in the context of the case study of Picnic with a structured qualitative content analysis. The study has adopted the Triple Bottom Line approach of Elkington and the concept of competence by Weinert as well as the sustainability competence framework by Wiek et al. to gain insight into the environmental, economic and social aspects of sustainability and competence requirements of the employees. The results indicate that most of the sustainability efforts of Picnic are linked to electric delivery vehicles, logistics are route efficient and planning is demand-based on management of the packaging system, reduction of food waste and the use of digital operational systems. These practices are not only technological/organizational measures, but also rely on the knowledge, skills, attitudes, motivations, communication and problem-solving skills of employees. The thesis describes the areas of key competence such as sustainable awareness, resource-efficient working behaviour, sustainable logistics understanding, packaging and waste reduction competence, digital process competence, teamworking competence and continuous improvement competence. The results of these findings inform the proposed practice-oriented training model for HR managers, in-company trainers, captains, and supervisors. However, the study indicates that a more effective way of achieving sustainability in online grocery retail is to make corporate-level sustainability practices into competencies and training at the workplace.

detail.abstract: The persistent inability of rating agencies to foresee financial crises and systemic failures raises questions about their reliability, especially as their role expands in a globalised economy. Notably, some firms with AAA ratings have faced bankruptcy, highlighting delays in rating adjustments and the factors influencing them. This study examines the relationship between financial ratings and market indicators, uncovering instances of rating inertia. It distinguishes between "Investment Grade" and "Speculative Grade" ratings, focusing on the significant impact of transitions between these categories. Using a two-stage empirical approach, we first develop a prediction model to identify overrated firms, employing regression techniques to address errors and correlations. Next, logistic regression with repeated data estimates downgrade probabilities based on prior over-ratings. Findings reveal a strong correlation between over-scoring and ratings, with "Investment Grade High" firms exhibiting lower downgrade risks, challenging traditional assumptions about rating dynamics. This analysis underscores the need for more responsive and accurate rating mechanisms to enhance market reliability. Our findings challenge conventional assumptions about rating dynamics and highlight potential regulatory and market implications.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Cost Structure
affiliations: Shenzhen University, Fudan University - School of Management, University of Sussex and City University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Cost Structure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relation between artificial intelligence (AI) investment and firms' cost structures. Using a firm-level AI investment measure that captures AI-related skills in employee resumes, we find that firms with greater AI investment exhibit more elastic cost structures, consistent with AI improving prediction, coordination, and resource redeployment and thereby increasing firms' ability to adjust resources flexibly in response to demand uncertainty. This relation is stronger for firms facing greater supply chain uncertainty, covering a broader set of product markets, and approaching capacity, suggesting that AI is especially valuable when firms encounter greater difficulty aligning resources with demand and therefore have a greater need for flexibility. It is also stronger in environments that better support the effective use of AI. We further find that AI investment is associated with greater elasticity in cost of goods sold, lower reliance on vertical integration, and higher inventory turnover. These results suggest that AI also enhances firms' flexibility in adjusting production costs, coordinating supply chains, and utilizing assets more efficiently. Our results are robust to an instrumental variable approach and a change analysis. Overall, our findings suggest that AI is an important technological force that shapes firms' resource commitments, capacity choices, and cost structures.

detail.abstract: Southeast Asia is the developing world's leading destination for foreign direct investment, drawing a record US$225 billion in 2024 and holding that position among developing regions for four years running, yet comparing its economies against each other is a trap for the unwary, because the region's headline numbers are reported on three incompatible bases that are routinely, and wrongly, placed on the same axis. This compendium assembles the comparable evidence for the six largest ASEAN economies, Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines, and states, as its first contribution, the measurement rule that governs any honest comparison: balance-of-payments FDI is the only crosscountry comparable series, and national registered, approved or realised figures, several times larger and forward-looking, must never be benchmarked against it. On that comparable basis the picture is stark. Singapore alone accounts for about 64 percent of the region's inflows, a scale that reflects its role as a global holding and conduit hub rather than a host economy, and once it is set aside the real contest among the other five shows Vietnam as the only one rising every year since 2020. The compendium maps inflows, stock and intensity, the sources and sectors of the capital, the split between greenfield and acquisition, the region's weight in global flows, and the 2025 policy frontier of the global minimum tax and the China-plus-one relocation wave. It is built to be a standing annual reference, with every figure sourced, every measurement basis labelled, and the data gaps named rather than hidden.

title: When Can Bibliometric Evidence Be Trusted? Developing a Conditional Robustness Theory for Research Evaluation in Business Research

detail.title: When Can Bibliometric Evidence Be Trusted? Developing a Conditional Robustness Theory for Research Evaluation in Business Research

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis that did not involve any human participants, patients, or tissue sampling.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Bibliometrics has become one of the most widely used tools in management and accounting research, yet the method that measures scholarly impact is rarely asked to justify its own statistical footing. This paper turns the bibliometric lens on bibliometrics itself. Drawing on a Scopus and Web of Science corpus assembled through a PRISMA-guided identification and screening process (6,144 unique records, 763 retained at the eligibility stage), we combine science mapping (co-word analysis, thematic mapping and thematic evolution, co-citation analysis and a historiographic map) with a systematic reading of the 57 most influential works in the field to ask a single question: is bibliometrics a statistically robust and econometrically reliable research method, and why do some journals and researchers accept it while others do not? We find that the field's own most-cited literature is dominated by critical and nuanced positions (33 of 57 works) rather than unconditional endorsement (8 of 57), converging instead on a small set of recurring validity threats spanning data coverage, indicator construction, citer behaviour and research governance. From this evidence we develop the Contingent Theory of Bibliometric Robustness, which reframes bibliometric robustness not as an inherent property of citation counts but as an achievement that depends on triangulation with peer judgement, field normalisation, transparent construction rules and adequate sample scale. We discuss the implications of this model for research evaluation in accounting, finance and management, where journal-ranking lists such as the ABS Academic Journal Guide, the ABDC list and the Financial Times 50 sit at the exact intersection of indicator construction and institutional governance, and we close with a nine-point research agenda derived directly from the threats identified.

title: The Impact of Warehouse Expansion on B2B Procurement: Evidence from an e-commerce Pharmaceutical Supply Chain
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology - School of Management, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Indiana University Bloomington, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University and Huazhong Universtiy of Science and Technology

detail.title: The Impact of Warehouse Expansion on B2B Procurement: Evidence from an e-commerce Pharmaceutical Supply Chain
detail.abstract: Logistics responsiveness is a key driver of supply chain performance, yet its role in business-to-business (B2B) procurement remains underexplored. We empirically study how upstream warehouse expansion affects downstream purchasing behavior in an e-commerce pharmaceutical supply chain. Exploiting the upstream seller's opening of a new warehouse as a quasi-natural experiment, we use a difference-indifferences design to estimate the causal effect of shorter delivery lead times. We find that faster delivery leads to more purchases from downstream pharmacies, with monthly gross merchandise value increasing by 129.6%. Moreover, downstream pharmacies begin to place orders more frequently and in smaller quantities, with the number of orders placed per month increasing by 13.3% and the average quantity per order decreasing by 11.0%. These patterns are especially pronounced for smaller pharmacies and those facing higher demand uncertainty. Furthermore, the response varies by product price tier: for lower-and mid-priced products, pharmacies mainly reduce batch sizes, whereas for high-priced products they primarily increase replenishment frequency. These changes in downstream buyers' purchasing behavior, however, also carry costs for the upstream seller. The total product return rate increases by 24.1%, driven by a 90.0% rise in buyer-induced returns and a 289.2% rise in seller-induced returns. Overall, our findings highlight how logistics infrastructure reshapes downstream purchasing decisions, reallocates risk across supply chain partners, and generates both efficiency gains and operational frictions in B2B supply chains.

title: Reimagining Scotland's Golf Value Chain: Architecture, Operations, Social Impact and Regional Development in a Contemporary Multi-Case Study
affiliations: University of Edinburgh, King’s College London - King's Business School, , affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Edinburgh

detail.title: Reimagining Scotland's Golf Value Chain: Architecture, Operations, Social Impact and Regional Development in a Contemporary Multi-Case Study
detail.abstract: Golf holds a unique position within Scotland's cultural identity and economic structure. Whilst extensive scholarship has examined the historical significance of Scottish golf, considerably less attention has been paid to its contemporary value chain and the evolving interactions between course design, operational models, social contribution and regional development. This study addresses this gap by conducting an integrated qualitative analysis based on twelve elite interviews with architects, general managers, investors, and industry stakeholders across Scotland's most influential golf developments. These include historic championship venues, newly constructed destination courses, remote community clubs and modern multi-course resorts. Using a multi-case thematic approach, the paper identifies four interlinked dimensions shaping the modern Scottish golf economy: architectural innovation rooted in landscape heritage; evolving operational and business models that influence global competitiveness; the social and cultural value of golf as a tool for community wellbeing and employment; and, the role of new golf investments in stimulating economic growth, particularly in fragile or remote regions. The findings demonstrate that Scotland's golf sector now operates as a complex, adaptive system in which tradition and modernity reinforce and support rather than contradict each other. The study concludes with policy implications for sustainable development, regional regeneration and the future positioning of Scottish golf within the global sports-tourism marketplace.

title: The Provincial Geography of Foreign Investment in Vietnam: Concentration, the Northern Shift, and the 2025 Redraw

detail.title: The Provincial Geography of Foreign Investment in Vietnam: Concentration, the Northern Shift, and the 2025 Redraw

This paper is a data reference compiled from publicly available official statistics and reputable secondary sources and does not constitute investment advice.
