title: Tokenised Assets: Pathways for Emerging Market and Developing Economies
affiliations: University of Oxford, University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Students, University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Students, University of Cambridge - Judge Business School, Financial Conduct Authority, , University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Students, University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Students, University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Students and Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Cambridge Judge Business School, University of Cambridge

detail.title: Tokenised Assets: Pathways for Emerging Market and Developing Economies

declarations.funderStatement: This study is supported by Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO).

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (CCAF), UK

detail.abstract:
This research project – conducted with the support of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) – seeks to identify use cases and investigate the infrastructure and regulatory pathways for tokenisation of real-world assets in Emerging Market and Developing Economies (EMDEs).

 Recent initiatives have largely focused on modernising and addressing financial sector inefficiencies in advanced economies. But tokenisation could have meaningful implications for financial inclusion and access in EMDEs, for instance, by allowing increased investability for previously informal, illiquid or inaccessible assets or by mobilising domestic and international capital.

 Through a comparative analysis of the state of asset tokenisation in EMDEs, this report evaluates where tokenisation may offer a credible value proposition across stages of the asset lifecycle as well as different asset classes. Real estate, securities and commodities are the subjects of in-depth analysis.

The report offers vital insights for regulators, policymakers, market participants and development partners seeking to harness tokenisation responsibly to deepen capital markets and broaden access to investment in EMDEs.

title: The Market Response to Mergers and Nationalisation Announcements: Stock Market Evidence from the UK Banks

detail.title: The Market Response to Mergers and Nationalisation Announcements: Stock Market Evidence from the UK Banks
detail.abstract: In this paper I use standard event study methodology to explore two main issues in the UK banking industry. First, I attempt to show how the big five banks' domestic and cross-border mergers affected shareholders' wealth. Second, I present a timely empirical analysis of the Northern Rock bank crisis in which the effects of earnings, merger and nationalisation announcements are carefully examined. The event studies show no significant gains in either domestic or cross-border mergers. These results suggest a strong financial integration between the UK and Europe. For the Northern Rock case, the bank itself and the industry experienced a positive stock reaction when it announced an increase in earnings, but faced negative outcomes for the dividend cancellation. Interestingly, the nationalisation of Northern Rock appears to be unwelcome to the big five banks.

title: Windowed Temporal Alignment for Data-Driven Soft Sensing of Copper Matte Grade in Flash Smelting
affiliations: Northeastern University and Northeastern University (USA)

detail.title: Windowed Temporal Alignment for Data-Driven Soft Sensing of Copper Matte Grade in Flash Smelting
detail.abstract: Real-time measurement of copper matte grade in flash smelting remains challenging. The high-temperature, corrosive environment prevents direct inline sensing, and laboratory assays introduce substantial delays. Beyond point accuracy, matte grade exhibits strong temporal dependence, so the direction of grade change is as important as the estimated value for process operators. This paper presents a data-driven soft sensor based on a windowed temporal difference alignment (WTDA) mechanism integrated with gradient boosted regression trees (GBRT). WTDA compares grade variations between adjacent time windows and dynamically reweights training samples according to temporal sign consistency, penalizing estimates that are numerically close but directionally incorrect. The resulting soft sensor improves both point accuracy and trend fidelity. For industrial validation, a modularly enhanced sand cat swarm optimization (SCSO) scheme uses the soft sensor output to search for feasible parameter adjustments under ±15% operational constraints. On production data from a commercial flash smelting furnace, WTDA-GBRT achieves an R2 of 0.9379, representing a 4.1% improvement over the GBRT baseline, and reduces the mean absolute error (MAE) by 72.3% to 0.2272. The soft sensor transfers to a held-out smelting campaign with consistent accuracy, and the coupled optimization reduces grade deviation to 0.62%. A prototype platform integrates both modules to support operator decision-making.

title: Impact of Inventory Management on Profitability: Evidence from Selected Indian Textile Companies

detail.title: Impact of Inventory Management on Profitability: Evidence from Selected Indian Textile Companies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based entirely on publicly available financial data and did not involve human participants, personal data, or confidential information. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by the author and did not receive any external financial support.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates the relationship between inventory management efficiency and profitability among selected Indian textile companies. The Inventory Holding Period (Inventory Days) is used as a proxy for inventory management efficiency, while Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) serves as the measure of profitability. The study utilizes financial data covering the period from 2014 to 2025 for six major Indian textile firms: Arvind Ltd., Welspun Living Ltd., Vardhman Textiles Ltd., Trident Ltd., Raymond Ltd., and KPR Mill Ltd. Data were collected from publicly available annual reports and financial databases.

Using Pearson correlation and simple linear regression analysis, the study finds a moderate negative correlation (r = −0.42) between Inventory Days and ROCE, indicating that firms with shorter inventory holding periods tend to exhibit relatively higher profitability. However, the regression results reveal that this relationship is statistically insignificant (p = 0.41; R² = 0.18), suggesting that inventory management represents only one of several factors affecting profitability in the textile industry. A sensitivity analysis excluding an extreme observation from Raymond Ltd. (2024) further demonstrates the limited standalone explanatory power of inventory days in explaining variations in profitability.

title: Women Political Appointments and the National Gender Policy's Affirmative Action in Nigeria: A Case Study of Kaduna State (2015-2023)
affiliations: Federal University Gashua and Bayero University Kano

detail.title: Women Political Appointments and the National Gender Policy's Affirmative Action in Nigeria: A Case Study of Kaduna State (2015-2023)
detail.abstract: Affirmative action for women is a positive policy for gender mainstreaming into politics and decisionmaking process. There are several women friendly international treaties to which many countriesincluding Nigeria-are signatories. These treaties stipulate, among others, that women are to be allotted certain percentage in all appointments and elective positions in both public and private sectors. This is to ensure that women become more visible in politics and governance. Presence of women in politics is increasingly becoming a yardstick to measure levels of democratization and sustainability of democracy. Thus, Nigerian Government came up with its National Gender Policy (NGP) which allots 35% to women in all appointments. However, women are still being marginalized in Nigerian politics due to the age-long notion that the public domain is not for women. Using Kaduna State as a case study visa -vis women political appointment and leadership in governance, this paper assesses the National Gender Policy's affirmative action and its challenges in Nigeria with focus on Kaduna State. Its approach is both qualitative and quantitative. Though women in Kaduna State fared better within the timeframe of the study in terms of political appointments and leadership roles, findings revealed that women affirmative action was not implemented as widely thought. It concludes that unless women affirmative action is enshrined in the Constitution, its implementation would continue to be subject to governmental discretion on gender issues. This study recommends, among others, constitutionally backed affirmative action to facilitate women political appointment.

title: Anticipated Fuel Price Shocks and the Intertemporal Elasticity of Fuel Purchases
affiliations: and Universidad Nacional de Educacion a Distancia (UNED) - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Anticipated Fuel Price Shocks and the Intertemporal Elasticity of Fuel Purchases
detail.abstract: When consumers anticipate price increases, they may bring forward purchases to avoid paying higher future prices. We estimate the anticipation effects of fuel price shocks drawing on the price shocks generated by regional tax changes in Spain. Using this quasi-experimental setting, we estimate an intertemporal elasticity of fuel purchases of 1.25 for diesel and 1.39 for gasoline, indicating substantial substitution of purchases across time in response to anticipated price changes. We then examine fuel demand following the Russian invasion of Ukraine and find evidence consistent with the forward-looking behavior identified in our quasi-experimental analysis. Our results suggest that consumers partially mitigate the short-run impact of fuel price increases by shifting purchases forward. At the same time, anticipation effects may exacerbate temporary fuel shortages by increasing demand precisely when supply conditions are already constrained.

title: Beyond Market and State Failure: Private Digital Legal Orders and the and the Rise of Infrastructural Power
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Beyond Market and State Failure: Private Digital Legal Orders and the and the Rise of Infrastructural Power
detail.abstract: The traditional dichotomy between market failure and state failure has long dominated debates on financial regulation, yet it has become analytically insufficient for explaining contemporary digital economies. Financialized, platform-based, and AI-mediated markets are not autonomous arenas subsequently corrected by regulation; rather, they are legally constituted and infrastructurally organized power structures. Drawing on legal institutionalism, law and political economy, and theories of infrastructural power, we argue that governance is increasingly exercised through privately controlled digital infrastructures that organize payment systems, collateral regimes, platform architectures, and algorithmic decision-making. Artificial intelligence contributes to this transformation by embedding predictive objectives directly into digital infrastructures, thereby institutionalizing normative objectives that shape economic coordination across innumerable transactions. Rather than focusing on the quality or legality of individual algorithmic decisions, the paper examines the institutional conditions under which the normative objectives that guide AI-mediated decision-making become legally stabilized and embedded in durable governance structures. Under these conditions, financial regulation becomes structurally ex post, while private actors increasingly exercise sovereignty-like functions through what we conceptualize as private digital legal orders. These hybrid legal-infrastructural arrangements not only control access and enforcement but also stabilize the normative objectives embedded within digital infrastructures, transforming contingent political choices into durable architectures of governance. We conclude that effective governance requires a shift from regulating technological applications toward governing the legal and institutional architectures through which digital infrastructures organize economic life, reaffirming the primacy of law over technology as a constitutional precondition for democratic economic order.

title: From Periodic Review to Continuous Vigilance: A Framework for Real-Time, AI-driven Credit Risk Monitoring
affiliations: Ladoke Akintola University of Technology

detail.title: From Periodic Review to Continuous Vigilance: A Framework for Real-Time, AI-driven Credit Risk Monitoring
detail.abstract: Traditional credit risk management has long relied on periodic, backward-looking assessment cycles that leave lenders exposed during the interval between reviews. This paper develops a conceptual and operational framework for shifting credit risk monitoring from periodic review toward continuous vigilance, using artificial intelligence (AI) and high-frequency data streams. Building on emerging evidence that machine-learning models can ingest transaction-level and market-frequency signals to detect deterioration far earlier than quarterly reporting allows (Oyekola, Elikwu, & Odunaike, 2022), we articulate a layered architecture spanning data ingestion, feature construction, model inference, alerting, and governance. We situate real-time monitoring within the broader risk-management stack, arguing that continuous signals are complementary to-not a substitute for-scenario-based stress testing (Odunaike, Agbaakin, & Elikwu, 2024) and to the integration of slow-moving structural drivers such as climate exposure (Saadu-Ayuba, Elikwu, & Odunaike, 2019). The paper contributes a design taxonomy, a discussion of latency-accuracy trade-offs, and a governance checklist for institutions seeking to operationalize continuous credit surveillance responsibly.

title: The Transmission Mechanics of Monetary Policy: Analyzing the Federal Reserve's Dual Mandate and Structural Imbalances on Equity Valuations
affiliations: BlueCrest Capital Management

detail.title: The Transmission Mechanics of Monetary Policy: Analyzing the Federal Reserve's Dual Mandate and Structural Imbalances on Equity Valuations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest: Vishal Chopra is the Founder and CEO of BlueCrest Capital Investment Consulting LLC, an independent financial markets research, trader education, and fintech consulting venture. The research presented in this paper was conducted independently, and the author's commercial activities do not influence, nor are they influenced by, the findings and analysis contained herein. There are no other financial relationships or personal conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study relies entirely on publicly available macroeconomic indicators, historical market data, and simulated trading metrics. It does not involve human subjects, private patient data, or animal participants; therefore, ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: Funding and Disclosures: This study was self-funded by the author, who serves as the Founder and CEO of BlueCrest Capital Investment Consulting LLC. No external grants, corporate sponsorships, or third-party funding were received for this research.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the transmission mechanics of modern U.S. monetary policy through the lens of the Federal Reserve's statutory dual mandate-price stability and maximum sustainable employment. We model how structural economic shocks (e.g., geopolitical supply chain disruptions, energy sector volatility, and artificial intelligence-driven productivity shifts) create policy friction within the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). By analyzing the transition from a low-rate environment to the current 2026 regime under Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh-characterized by a federal funds target range of 3.50% to 3.75% and resurgent core inflation-we quantify the impact of central bank decisions on the U.S. equity market. Utilizing structural vector autoregression (SVAR) principles, we isolate the specific mechanisms through which unexpected rate trajectories, changing dot-plot projections, and shifts in aggregate equity duration compress or expand multi-asset valuation multiples.

title: Converging Regimes:NBFIs and Investment Screening in Asian Finance

detail.title: Converging Regimes:NBFIs and Investment Screening in Asian Finance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

contentType.other: accepted for publication with The University of Pennsylvania Asian Law Review

detail.abstract: Cross-border capital flows have drawn growing regulatory attention in recent years, amid the expansion of global investment and the rise of financial technology. Broadly from regulatory perspective, two regimes govern the movement of capital: investment screening and financial regulation. Both play an essential role in shaping how funds are allocated, yet their interaction and the challenges posed by emerging financial actors has become increasingly complex. On the investment side, many frameworks remain limited or unevenly developed, creating friction for investors navigating state-driven approval mechanisms. Review criteria typically focus on deal size, destination, sectoral sensitivity and technology. For example, a large foreign investment in strategic sectors may trigger enhanced scrutiny, while smaller transactions may proceed with minimal review. Yet, these criteria often intersect with broader market-access principles under trade and investment agreements, leaving uncertainty about how rules apply in practice. On the financial-regulation side, rapid fintech adoption has lowered transaction costs and shortened execution times, but also created oversight gaps. Traditional channels such as SWIFT and Western Union, historically monitored by regulators, now coexist with faster, non-bank mechanisms that operate at the speed of digital markets. Bank-centric regulatory frameworks struggle to keep pace, raising questions about outdated requirements and unnecessary barriers to entry. Regulators face the challenge of balancing market efficiency with adequate oversight, particularly where capital can move quickly and across multiple jurisdictions.The stakeholder landscape has also shifted. Non-bank financial institutions (Hereinafter NBFIs) have grown dramatically in both scope and systemic significance. These entities, which lend using investor funds to a wide range of borrowers, now account for approximately $250 trillion, or 49 percent of global financial assets, as of 2023. Their rise signals a gap in regulatory oversight: many NBFIs operate outside traditional banking supervision, yet their activities carry significant implications for capital stability and investment flows. These trends point to both convergence and friction between investment screening and financial regulation. When capital moves across jurisdictions, financial stability risks arising from geopolitical tensions and those linked to NBFIs sit at opposite ends of the spectrum. In the case of ASEAN+3, rising uncertainty in U.S. policies and persistent geopolitical tensions in 2024–2025 exert the greatest impact on the region’s financial systems. When the two regulatory regimes intersect, their interaction may reveal new market vulnerabilities. As scrutiny of cross-border flows intensifies, regulators should ensure that rules protect national interests without unduly constraining long-term investment. In Asia, where both state-driven investment approvals and rapidly evolving financial markets especially driven by financial technology innovations coexist, the challenge is particularly pressing. Policymakers should consider how to implement effective oversight while fostering a stable environment for capital allocation, particularly the systemic footprint of NBFIs. The paper aims to discuss how regulators can strike the right balance between controlling the flow of capital while facilitating frameworks that addresses the risks posed by NBFI. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing regulatory regimes that support both growth and stability in increasingly interconnected financial markets.

title:
Mission-focused Acquisition:

 A Stakeholder Briefing Series
affiliations: ASI Government, LLC

detail.title:
Mission-focused Acquisition:

 A Stakeholder Briefing Series
detail.abstract:
Part of the *Mission-Focused Acquisition* working paper series, which applies complex-adaptive-systems analysis to federal acquisition and the persistent tension between compliance culture and mission-outcome orientation. The series pairs a formal analytic core with practitioner-facing translation — No. 1 develops the information-architecture theory of why reform cycles regenerate the culture they target; No. 2 translates that diagnosis into role-by-role stakeholder briefings — with forthcoming companions providing the framework-and-glossary treatment and the agent-based simulation.

This stakeholder briefing series translates the information-architecture theory of federal acquisition — developed formally in the companion working paper — into practical terms for the people who work inside the system. It argues that acquisition's compliance-over-outcome bias is not a failure of individual courage or competence but the rational response of each role to the incentives it faces, so reform succeeds by changing the conditions rather than exhorting the people. Six briefings address the system's principal stakeholders in their own terms — Senior Acquisition Executives, Program Managers, Contracting Officers, Legal and Policy Counsel, Industry, and the technology function — showing each how the shared architecture shapes its choices and what each can do to move the culture from compliance toward mission outcome. Written for practitioners and policymakers, it is the applied counterpart to the framework's analytic core, and it situates recent statutory change — including the Portfolio Acquisition Executive established at §1802 of the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act — within a coherent account of what would make this round of reform last.

title: Trump v. Cook: What the Majority Missed
affiliations: Fein Law Offices

detail.title: Trump v. Cook: What the Majority Missed

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced my study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: No other person or organization funded this paper or the research reflected in it.

detail.abstract: The reasoning of the majority in Trump v. Cook is fundamentally at odds with Trump v. Slaughter and clashes with the reality that the Federal Reserve’s non-monetary regulatory functions are every bit executive in nature as those the Court said make the Federal Trade Commission subject to the President’s removal power. Although the Federal Reserve’s independence with respect to its monetary policy functions seems assured, the tension between the Cook and Slaughter cases creates potential vulnerability for Fed independence with respect to its bank regulatory functions. Hidden in footnote 6 of the majority opinion in Trump v. Cook is the warning that the Court’s view of the Fed’s constitutionality might change if Congress assigns the Federal Reserve “additional regulatory powers that are attenuated from monetary policy.” The majority did not elaborate on what additional regulatory powers might jeopardize the Fed’s constitutionality, not having any apparent knowledge of the Fed’s existing regulatory powers that are attenuated from monetary policy. This should be a matter of interest and concern to members of Congress, the Fed and other federal banking regulators when Congress next amends the banking laws.

title: How Does Monetary and Fiscal Policy Affect the Economy in the Face of Large Shocks?
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics and University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: How Does Monetary and Fiscal Policy Affect the Economy in the Face of Large Shocks?
detail.abstract: We build a model that combines (i) heterogeneous households with incomplete markets, and (ii) state-dependent pricing with strategic complementarities by firms, to analyze the effects of large macroeconomic shocks and policy interventions. Both features significantly influence the transmission of fiscal stimulus and monetary policy-heterogeneous households because of failures of Ricardian equivalence, and state-dependent pricing because of its nonlinear effects on inflation. We use our model to quantify how monetary and fiscal policy shaped macroeconomic dynamics in response to the large shocks of 2020, and how alternative policy choices could have led to different aggregate and distributional outcomes. We find large departures from Ricardian equivalence and strong stepping-on-a-rake effects of interest rate changes. The large unfunded fiscal transfer program helped prevent deflation in 2020 and significantly raised output throughout 2021 and 2022, but led to permanently higher prices. The monetary easing through 2020 and 2021 also contributed to preventing deflation, but had a minimal impact on GDP. The monetary tightening from 2022 lowered the maximum inflation rate, but contributed to persistently abovetrend inflation. These policies led to net welfare gains for low-wealth households and net welfare losses for high-wealth households, but those welfare effects are due to incomplete markets for idiosyncratic risk not aggregate stabilization. Alternative commitments to funding fiscal stimulus could have achieved similar short-term effects on inflation and output with a much smaller longterm increase in the price level.

title: Federalism Behind Closed Doors: Does It Serve the Public Interest?
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE)

detail.title: Federalism Behind Closed Doors: Does It Serve the Public Interest?
detail.abstract: To make federalism work, especially under parliamentary forms of political governance, a dense network of national and provincial political and bureaucratic interactions becomes a necessity. All federal countries have responded to this need by developing formal and informal mechanisms and processes of intergovernmental consultation and joint decision-making involving senior policymakers and officials-the so-called "institutions of executive federalism." These interactions typically take place behind closed doors but often yield decisions on the sharing of resources and on policy directions that differentially affect the lives of citizens in different parts of the country, with little opportunity for feedback. This chapter uses a neo-institutional framework to assess these arrangements for their impact on the efficiency, equity, and accountability of the federal system, and extends the analysis to the most significant recent test of executive federalism worldwide: the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Zoning: Externalities or Misallocation?
affiliations: Harvard University, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Academia Sinica and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: Zoning: Externalities or Misallocation?
detail.abstract: We study how residential-commercial zoning affects the allocation of urban space. Using propertylevel data from Taipei and 34 U.S. metropolitan areas, we infer neighborhood-level zoning wedges from the allocation of residents, workers, and floor space. We find substantially greater dispersion in these wedges in U.S. cities than in Taipei, where mixed-use development is pervasive. The inferred wedges increase neighborhood specialization and reduce welfare. We then evaluate whether zoning is aligned with the neighborhood characteristics that would justify intervention. Although zoning is systematically related to comparative advantage, comparative advantage explains only a small fraction of the variation in zoning. The dominant effect of zoning in American cities is therefore not to promote efficient land use, but to increase the segregation of residential and commercial activity across neighborhoods.

title: The Theocratic Agency of the Iranian Legal System at the Legislative and Judicial Levels

detail.title: The Theocratic Agency of the Iranian Legal System at the Legislative and Judicial Levels
detail.abstract: The Iranian theocracy is an exceptional form of Islamic polity in terms of the special role that sharīʿa plays within the theocratic legal system. The project of sharīʿatization triggered in the aftermath of the Islamic Revolution of 1979 has shaped the Iranian legal system into the world's most prominent theocracy, where revolutionary norms are married with Shiite jurisprudence. The legal analysis of the uneasy intersection between sharīʿaand the legal system, as entrenched within the Iranian constitutional framework, indicates that not only has the Islamicity of all laws firmly been guaranteed, any revision of theocratic elements of the Constitution has also been obstructed. The result is the formation of a theocratically frozen constitution. In addition to securing Islamicity at the legislative level, the Constitution safeguards the Islamicity of the legal system at the judicial level. In empowering judges to deliver sentences based on unwritten law (authoritative Islamic sources and authentic fatwa), even in criminal cases, the Constitution preserves the traditional role of Muslim judges and therefore deactivates the mechanism of codification, codification being considered a hallmark of modern Western legal codes. This has given rise to a systematic overlap between the scope of sin and crime and made the application of the last resort principle (ultima ratio) particularly complicated, if not impossible.

title: Supply and Demand with Market Heterogeneity
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, University of Chicago, University of Chicago, University of Chicago and Harvard University

detail.title: Supply and Demand with Market Heterogeneity
detail.abstract: We revisit the classic identification problem of separating supply and demand for a homogeneous good using data from multiple markets. We allow markets to be heterogeneous according to unobservables, a feature that arises if there are unobservable differences in consumer preferences or firm technology. We develop a new identification analysis based on hypothetical market types. We use this analysis to show how nonparametric, economically motivated assumptions carry empirical restrictions for a wide range of target parameters, including elasticities, but also welfare parameters, such as consumer surplus. Then, we develop computationally tractable methods for implementing partially identified linear random coefficients models in which the slopes of supply and demand are heterogeneous. We apply these methods to estimate the welfare impact and incidence of sales taxes in the United States.

title: The Unintended Consequences of Registration Reform When Informed Contracting Is Absent: Evidence from China
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Unintended Consequences of Registration Reform When Informed Contracting Is Absent: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how a market-oriented reform affects the earnings management behavior of firms raising capital through private investments in public equity (PIPE) under an institutional friction characterized by the absence of efficient informed contracting. We find that, contrary to the intended effect of China's registration-based reform, PIPE issuers simultaneously escalate both accrual-based and real earnings management during the issuance year. We further find that state-owned enterprises (SOEs) rely more heavily on sales-based real earnings management than non-SOEs following the reform. We extend the PIPE and earnings management literature by examining corporate behavior under this institutional friction. Our findings should be of interest to policymakers, suggesting that market-oriented reforms may be insufficient on their own to curb issuer opportunism, particularly for state-owned issuers facing weaker market discipline.

title: Reimagining Assessment of Learning in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Reimagining Assessment of Learning in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Introduction-The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) renders traditional, artifact-based higher education assessments obsolete. This study explores how institutions must transition toward evaluating the holistic learning process rather than static end products. Methodology-A Narrative Literature Review was employed to synthesize interdisciplinary evidence, encompassing quantitative AI adoption trends, qualitative cognitive judgment evaluations, and multidimensional institutional readiness frameworks. Results-Findings indicate that the GenAI disruption constitutes a "wicked problem" requiring a shift to a Postplagiarism Framework, where human-AI co-authorship is standard practice. Traditional assessment formats are highly vulnerable, necessitating structural redesigns such as interactive oral vivas and process portfolio audits. Furthermore, standardized models like the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) and the GENESIS framework are crucial for establishing explicit permissibility levels and executing systemic programmatic reform. Discussion-Higher education must abandon punitive detection strategies in favor of cultivating students' evaluative judgment and critical AI literacy. Implementing resilient, process-driven evaluations combined with synchronous checkpoints is essential to secure the validity of educational credentialing in an AI-saturated learning landscape.

title: DSGE as a Structured World Model: Benchmarking Counterfactual Generalization in Economic Worlds
affiliations: City University of Macau

detail.title: DSGE as a Structured World Model: Benchmarking Counterfactual Generalization in Economic Worlds
detail.abstract: Modern world models-Dreamer, transformer world models (IRIS, Genie), and JEPA / next-latent architectures-learn dynamics from observed trajectories but share a weakness: their transition map is disciplined only where data were seen, so it degrades under policy-induced distribution shift and on counterfactual states off the training path. We argue that a Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model is a structured world model: its state is a belief state-the very object a latent world model learns, but supplied with causal structure and hard cross-equation constraints. We introduce DSGE-Gym, a benchmark of eight DSGE environments with off-path counterfactual test sets, scaling to the ECB's 230-variable New Area-Wide Model. We find that (i) learned world models match the dynamics on-path but collapse off-path (5σ tail RMSE up to ∼40× the onpath level), and (ii) training the same architectures on data the DSGE generates across rare and counterfactual-policy states-coverage only a structural model can synthesize-roughly halves tail error and cuts policy-regime error 10-280× where the counterfactual rule shifts the ergodic support. Because such coverage cannot be sampled from any single history, this measures structure's ability to manufacture the missing distribution. DSGE-Gym and all code are released as a reproducible testbed for counterfactual generalization.

title: Forecasting Realized Variance using Echo State Networks

detail.title: Forecasting Realized Variance using Echo State Networks

declarations.funderStatement: Funding provided by the North West Social Science Doctoral Training Partnership (NWSSDTP), part of the Economic Social and Research Council (ESRC)

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates Echo State Networks (ESN) for realized variance forecasting of the S&P500 and 24 Dow Jones constituents, complemented by simulations from stochastic volatility models. In a large-scale horse race against econometric and ANN benchmarks, HAR-type models remain a hard-to-beat benchmark: although ESN variants achieve lower QLIKE and MSE losses, the HAR is consistently outperformed with statistical significance only by the jump-augmented ESN (ESN-J). This finding refines the evidence of Caporin (2023) that jumps contain little predictive power for RV: whilst the linear HAR-J corroborates their conclusion, the ESN-J delivers consistent and significant gains, suggesting the predictive content of jumps is nonlinear and state-dependent. ESN improvements are most pronounced in high-volatility episodes, whereas the LSTM deteriorates markedly when volatility is elevated. Taken together with an approximately 75% reduction in computation time relative to the LSTM and reduced forecast variability, these results position ESNs as a more reliable ANN for volatility forecasting. In Value-at-Risk applications, HAR remains the leading prudential benchmark, with ESNs broadly matching rather than surpassing it. The overall findings persist qualitatively across simulations, model specifications, and forecast settings.

title: The Nexus of Youth, Vulnerabilities, and Disaster in Nepal
affiliations: , Kathmandu University and Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Nexus of Youth, Vulnerabilities, and Disaster in Nepal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All the authors share no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The understanding of disasters in Nepal has evolved over time. Amid changing ideologies and response frameworks, youth-a demographic making up over 42% of Nepal's population-remain marginalized, seen as passive victims rather than active agents in disaster response and resiliencebuilding. However, recent trends show that young people are increasingly involved in disaster response initiatives, community awareness campaigns, and policy advocacy. Therefore, to bring attention to youth-led action, this article explores the nexus of youth, disaster, and vulnerability in Nepal by analyzing Nepal's current policy landscape to understand the current limitations placed on youth-led disaster response and recovery. Through policy analysis, it is clear that a multistakeholder, policy-driven approach is necessary to support the formal integration and inclusion of youth into national disaster governance frameworks. By actively acknowledging the importance of youth as pivotal agents in the sphere of disaster management and by empowering them to take a leading role, Nepal has the potential to significantly strengthen community resilience and to promote a more sustainable and effective methodology for disaster risk reduction initiatives.

title: Export Controls and Technological Redirection
affiliations: Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Peking University - Guanghua School of Management and

detail.title: Export Controls and Technological Redirection
detail.abstract: Export controls can weaken a country's position at the technological frontier by shrinking markets for incumbent technologies and redirecting firms innovation. We develop a model in which U.S. suppliers allocate R&D between incumbent and alternative technological routes following export control shocks. We construct a patent-level Technology Redirection Score from patent text. Exploiting additions of Chinese firms to the BIS Entity List, we find that both exposed U.S. suppliers and designated Chinese firms shift innovation away from the incumbent U.S.-supplier-led route and toward alternative technological routes. Following designation, alternative-route patents gain $6.80 million in value relative to incumbent-route patents.

title: Expectations and the Two Sides of Inflation
affiliations: Universidad del Pacifico

detail.title: Expectations and the Two Sides of Inflation
detail.abstract: Inflation is the difference of two gross margins — inflationary and deflationary pres sures — with sharply different persistence. Household and professional forecast errors load on both margins with the same signs across surveys and samples: underreaction to the persistent margin, overreaction to the transitory one. The deviations cancel inside aggregate inflation, so standard efficiency tests detect nothing. We prove why no processor of the aggregate escapes them: one signal cannot reveal two states, and both coefficients remain positive at infinite processing capacity. A single aggregate processing friction reconciles the two: sign-stable and recurrent across samples, though marginal against a harsh spurious-persistence null.
