title: The 2022 and 2026 Oil Shocks: Implications and Policy Options for Puerto Rico

detail.title: The 2022 and 2026 Oil Shocks: Implications and Policy Options for Puerto Rico
detail.abstract: This policy brief offers a data-driven account of how the 2022 oil shock moved through Puerto Rico’s economy—tracing its effects across gasoline and electricity prices, inflation, output, and the labor market—and uses that episode as an empirical template for anticipating how the more recent 2026 shock could unfold. Building on this comparison, the brief makes the case that the 2026 event is more macroeconomically dangerous: although larger in magnitude, its real threat lies in its timing, striking an economy marked by dual stagnation and mounting tariff pressures, and stripped of the federal stimulus and labor-market momentum that cushioned the 2022 blow. The brief then sets out a concrete slate of policy options and business strategies—pairing immediate relief that keeps money circulating in the local economy with structural reforms that reduce Puerto Rico’s exposure to global volatility—to help the public and private sectors protect growth over the short and medium term.

title:
From Formalization to Observation: Methodological Operationalization of the Palindromic Geopolitical Theory
A Methodological Bridge Between Analytical Formalization and Systematic Empirical Observation

detail.title:
From Formalization to Observation: Methodological Operationalization of the Palindromic Geopolitical Theory
A Methodological Bridge Between Analytical Formalization and Systematic Empirical Observation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study because it did not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
The transition from theoretical formalization to empirical observation represents a fundamental
challenge in cumulative scientific research. While conceptual frameworks and analytical models
provide structured interpretations of complex phenomena, they do not by themselves establish the
methodological conditions required for consistent empirical observation across heterogeneous
contexts. This methodological gap is particularly significant in geopolitical analysis, where
strategic processes evolve through multidomain interactions, adaptive behavior, and changing
spatial and temporal configurations.
Building upon the ontological foundations established in Working Paper No. 1, the scientific
validation developed in Working Paper No. 2, and the analytical formalization of relative power
variation (ΔP and δP) presented in Working Paper No. 3, this study develops the methodological
operationalization of the Palindromic Geopolitical Theory (PGT). Its primary contribution is to
establish explicit methodological principles for connecting analytical formalization with
comparative geopolitical observation while preserving conceptual consistency across diverse
empirical environments.
The study examines the methodological requirements for multidomain observation, comparative
consistency, analytical transparency, temporal interpretation, and the integration of formal
analytical categories into systematic empirical inquiry. Rather than extending the theoretical
structure of the PGT, the proposed operationalization strengthens the relationship between
conceptual definition and empirical investigation, providing the methodological foundation
necessary for cumulative comparison and subsequent empirical evaluation.
By establishing coherent observational criteria without introducing deterministic assumptions or
predictive claims, this Working Paper establishes the methodological transition between theoretical
formalization and empirical application within the PGT research program. In doing so, it provides
the analytical basis for the systematic empirical assessment of strategic reversibility developed in
the subsequent stage of the research program.

title: Financial Education and the Co-holding Puzzle
affiliations: Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and

detail.title: Financial Education and the Co-holding Puzzle
detail.abstract: We collect 36 RCT-studies with 213,000 participants that report results of financial education on both savings and borrowing. Financial education increases not just savings but also borrowing outcomes. These changes are positively correlated at the study and outcome levels, consistent with the individual-level results from related literature establishing the co-holding puzzle. However, the co-holding reverses away from a positive to a negative relation between changes in saving and borrowing when we exclude financial education programs delivered by financial institutions. This indicates that financial education can moderate the co-holding puzzle, if the implementing institution has no incentive on increasing borrowing.

title: Do Central Bank Financial Stability Reports Predict Macro-Financial Distress? A Text-Mining Analysis of Maltese FSRs
affiliations: Central Bank of Armenia

detail.title: Do Central Bank Financial Stability Reports Predict Macro-Financial Distress? A Text-Mining Analysis of Maltese FSRs
detail.abstract: I examine whether the tone of central bank Financial Stability Reports (FSRs) contains economically meaningful predictive information for macro-financial distress, using a corpus of Maltese FSRs. I construct a domain-specific Financial Stability Sentiment (FSS) index and combine it with lead-lag regressions, group comparisons, and rare-events models. Regular reports are significantly more negative than update reports (p = 0.005), and sentiment co-moves with GDP growth and crisis episodes, although lead-lag coefficients remain statistically imprecise. I conclude that FSR tone is a valid descriptive indicator of financial stress, but not, on its own, a reliable forecasting tool.

title: The Allocative Cost of Non-meritocracy: What a Country Pays for Putting the Right People in the Wrong Places

detail.title: The Allocative Cost of Non-meritocracy: What a Country Pays for Putting the Right People in the Wrong Places
detail.abstract:
Public debate on meritocracy has been dominated by a moral question — does merit deserve its rewards? — most influentially in Michael Sandel's The Tyranny of Merit (2020). This essay asks a different, complementary question: does a country recognize merit when it has it in front of it? Framed this way, meritocracy is not an ideology to be judged but an allocation problem to be measured: how well an economic system assigns its human capital to the positions where it is most productive. 
      The essay uses Italy as a documented case study, drawing exclusively on public and institutional sources (CNEL, Bank of Italy, OECD, Istat, ANVUR, CEPEJ, Court of Auditors) to reconstruct the mechanism by which proximity — family, faction, territory — systematically outranks demonstrated competence across nine selection contexts, from academia to the judiciary to the governance of family firms. Two anchor figures frame the account: €159.5 billion of human capital lost to qualified emigration between 2011 and 2024 (7.5% of 2024 GDP; CNEL, 2025), and five generations for a bottom-decile family to reach median income, against two to three in Denmark (OECD). 
     Methodologically, it reports full ranges rather than midpoints and refuses a single aggregate: a band of convergent independent estimates is harder to dismiss than any one number. It argues the mechanism generalizes to any system where selectors are not third parties, processes are opaque, and the talented hold an exit option the institutions do not — and closes with a policy instrument for polarized democracies: an annual, apartisan Meritocracy Atlas built from data the state already produces. Measurement, not moralization.

title: Decolonizing Digital Sovereignty: An Operational Framework and Policy Analysis of AI Governance in Sub-Saharan Africa

detail.title: Decolonizing Digital Sovereignty: An Operational Framework and Policy Analysis of AI Governance in Sub-Saharan Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes value-laden societal outcomes worldwide, the imperative for robust governance has become critical. Yet the global AI governance literature remains disproportionately Western-centric, frequently overlooking the structural and infrastructural realities of Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). This paper bridges the gap between theoretical critique and practical implementation by proposing a Five-Pillar AI Governance Framework tailored to SSA. The framework is substantiated through a qualitative documentary analysis of contemporary African policy developments, employing a most-different systems comparative design across the divergent regulatory pathways of Rwanda, Nigeria, and the African Union. Policy evidence is extracted and coded against three governance indicators - infrastructural sovereignty, stakeholder participation, and institutional enforcement - and mapped onto the proposed structural pillars to produce an operational governance matrix. The resulting architectural blueprint offers African policymakers a practical roadmap for harnessing AI safely while safeguarding local digital sovereignty.

title: What Drives Anomaly Premia around the World?
affiliations: Saarland University and

detail.title: What Drives Anomaly Premia around the World?
detail.abstract: We study the prevalence and economic sources of cross-sectional stock return anomalies across countries. Anomalies are more prevalent in developed markets and in countries with more individualistic cultures. Both investment theory and mispricing theory receive support as main drivers of anomalies. However, the crosscountry evidence supports mispricing theory only through an individualism channel, not through channels related to economic development or institutional quality. Across markets, proxies for mispricing, limits to arbitrage, and distress explain larger shares of anomaly premia than proxies for other economic concepts. Candidate mechanisms explain anomaly premia significantly better in developed than in non-developed markets.

title: Explaining Anomalies
affiliations: Saarland University,  and University of Reading - ICMA Centre

detail.title: Explaining Anomalies
detail.abstract: More than two-fifths of anomaly premia can be explained by a small set of proxy variables that capture key economic concepts. Using a decomposition approach that incorporates both the crosssectional and time-series dimensions of potential explanations, we analyze the return premia of a broad set of prominent anomalies in the cross-section of stock returns. The main drivers of anomalies are mispricing, limits to arbitrage, and lottery demand. Debt issuance, low-risk, profitability, short-term reversal, and value anomalies are explained relatively well, whereas accruals, momentum, profit growth, and quality anomalies are accounted for only to a limited extent.

title: Regional Income Inequality, Individual Household Leverage, and Housing Consumption
affiliations: , University of Washington, University of Washington and University of Washington - College of Built Environments

detail.title: Regional Income Inequality, Individual Household Leverage, and Housing Consumption
detail.abstract: This study examines how regional income inequality affects individual household leverage and propagates intertemporal housing polarization through the housing market. Using American Housing Survey (AHS) micro-level panels across fifteen major U.S. metropolitan areas from 2015 to 2023, we deploy a structural two-stage least squares framework using a Bartik-type instrument to address household sorting. We document a striking divergence that rising regional Gini coefficient, rather than the share of top households, significantly reduces individual loan-to-value (LTV) ratios but expands mortgage-to-income (MTI) ratios. Mechanism analysis reveals that the LTV reduction is not driven by lenders’ risk-screening, but by a structural compositional shift where middle- and low-income households are priced out of homeownership. Concurrently, high-income households bidding up high-end housing assets fuels a mortgage expansion that drives up MTI. Furthermore, analysis based on the life cycle hypothesis reveals that initial leverage, given the housing market conditions shaped by regional income inequality, produces a gradual but substantial drag on future housing value over an eight-year horizon. By establishing a post-Great-Recession empirical baseline, these findings demonstrate that, through protecting the housing consumption of homeowner households while blocking poorer households from even entering the homeownership market, regional income inequality polarizes housing over time.

title: Financial Crisis, Volatility Spillovers, And Contagion in Islamic and Conventional Equity Markets
affiliations: and Business School of Sfax

detail.title: Financial Crisis, Volatility Spillovers, And Contagion in Islamic and Conventional Equity Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, or animal subjects, as it relies entirely on publicly available financial market data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines volatility spillovers and financial contagion between the United States equity market and a broad set of Islamic and conventional stock markets covering the United Kingdom, Canada, Europe, emerging markets, and the Asia-Pacific region during the Global Financial Crisis. Using daily Dow Jones index data and a multivariate GARCH framework (BEKK, DCC, and ADCC-GJR-GARCH-t), we analyse volatility transmission and dynamic correlations across pre-crisis, crisis, and post-crisis periods. The results reveal strong volatility spillovers originating from the United States conventional market, with pronounced asymmetric transmission during the crisis and sharp, persistent increases in cross-market correlations. These findings challenge both the resilience and decoupling hypotheses, showing that Islamic equity markets do not provide safe-haven benefits under systemic stress. The dominance of the United States market in global volatility transmission emerges as a key structural feature of international markets. Consequently, any diversification benefits offered by Islamic equities are largely temporary and context-dependent, diminishing during periods of extreme stress. Overall, the study highlight the deep integration of Islamic markets into the global financial system, with important implications for international portfolio management and financial stability assessment.

title: Perpetual Futures, Payments, and Oracle Funding
affiliations: Stanford University and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Perpetual Futures, Payments, and Oracle Funding
detail.abstract: This paper studies perpetual futures as a payment-native way to hold a synthetic claim on a stock or a basket, and develops the estimation of the funding mechanism that keeps such a claim anchored. We build directly on our companion paper, Gupta and Polson [2026], whose no-arbitrage framework we review and take as given: a perpetual future is priced as the riskneutral expectation of the spot sampled at a random funding time, and for an equity with carry it trades at a fixed multiple of spot. Our first contribution is a model that makes precise a practical advantage of the instrument. A conventional exchange-traded fund is kept near net asset value by daily creation and redemption of shares against the physical basket, a lumpy, inventory-based settlement. A perpetual future instead holds its peg through a signed funding transfer whose direction flips at the oracle price, so the peg is maintained by payments rather than by inventory. We show that continuous oracle funding is the high-frequency, low-cost limit of partial creation and redemption, and that it settles far less gross cash for a comparable tracking error. Our second contribution is implementation. The funding intensity is latent and time varying, so we estimate it with generative Bayesian computation: we simulate the basis, learn an amortized quantile map from summary statistics to the posterior, and filter the funding intensity with a particle filter. In a controlled study the credible intervals are calibrated, and a de-anchoring monitor built on the estimated parameters detects a funding-stress regime almost as well as an oracle that knows the true parameters. We keep claims modest and flag limitations throughout.

title: Takeovers and Knowledge Worker Productivity
affiliations: Central European University (CEU), Central European University and University of Mannheim

detail.title: Takeovers and Knowledge Worker Productivity
detail.abstract: We study how takeover announcements affect the productivity of knowledge workers employed by target firms. Using data from GitHub to measure individual work output and a stacked event study specification, we find that work output declines by 14% following takeover announcements. We also find suggestive evidence that code quality deteriorates. The effect on quantity is more pronounced for acquisitions associated with a larger risk of layoffs, specifically within-industry takeovers. Also, the results are weaker in states where takeovers are likely to be motivated by the wish to acquire skilled employees. These patterns are consistent with stress and anxiety induced by takeover uncertainty. The findings highlight a previously under-explored channel through which takeovers can be costly for acquirers. More broadly, the welfare effects of takeovers might extend beyond capital and product markets to include non-trivial productivity and mental health costs for affected workers.

title: Measuring the Economic Optionality of Work: A Systems Thinking Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Measuring the Economic Optionality of Work: A Systems Thinking Approach
detail.abstract: This paper approaches the future of work as a problem in systems science: paid work sits inside a sociotechnical system in which a production subsystem (what machines can do) and a distribution subsystem (what people can afford) are coupled, and the optionality of work is an emergent property of their interaction, not an attribute of either subsystem alone. Most quantitative work on artificial intelligence and labor measures only the production side, asking whether machines can perform the tasks that constitute human jobs. The paper introduces the Optional Work Index (OWI), an instrument for observing the state of the whole system: a composite index that measures the degree to which paid work is becoming economically optional. Work becomes optional only when two conditions hold simultaneously: machines must be able to do the work (a supply condition, measured through AI capability, robotics deployment, and observed labor-market shift) and people must be able to afford to stop working (a demand condition, measured through economic abundance and wealth distribution). The two sides are combined by geometric mean, a non-compensatory aggregation under which strength in one subsystem cannot offset weakness in the other, formalizing the coupling the construct asserts. The paper develops the theoretical grounding of the optionality construct, the index construction, its data foundations, the companion National AI Compute Index, how the index is read, and the method's limitations.

title: Bridging Models and Justice: Participatory Multi-Modelling for a Just Energy Transition
affiliations: , Rathenau Instituut, Leiden University, Leiden University, Leiden University, Delft University of Technology, Delft University of Technology - Faculty of Technology, Policy and Management, Leiden University, Leiden University and Delft University of Technology - Faculty of Technology, Policy and Management

detail.title: Bridging Models and Justice: Participatory Multi-Modelling for a Just Energy Transition

declarations.funderStatement: This work was created as a part of the "JustETrans: Co-creating just and effective energy transitions: supporting decision-making through participatory multi-modelling" project, funded by the Dutch Research Council (NWO) grant number KICH1.ED03.20.002 https://justetrans.nl/

detail.abstract:
Local and regional energy transition planning requires meeting national and international climate targets while ensuring a fair and just transition for all.
Decision-makers often use computational models, which predominantly represent techno-economic aspects of energy systems and insufficiently address other societal values, such as energy justice.
While progress has been made in integrating various aspects of justice in models, bridging this gap remains challenging.
Main case is that 'what is just' is contextual across temporal, spatial and organisational dimensions, is contested and must be deliberated. Models, on the other hand, are fundamentally simplifications based on assumptions. They are mono-interpretable mapping machines, requiring a consistent ontological basis, and produce uncertain outcomes.
In this perspective, we explore tensions between justice and computational models, and identify opportunities to advance the integration of justice into energy models.
We argue, first, that multi-modelling approaches offer a way to do justice to justice's multidimensional nature. Second, participatory (multi-)modelling enables a more comprehensive inclusion of  justice issues. Third, a more reflexive setting needs to be enacted, moving the focus from the models themselves to the process of modelling and the institutional context within which models are created and used.
We acknowledge that all three proposals are broad, present challenges and are insufficient for bridging the gaps among the multiple worlds involved in an energy-related decision-making process. However, staying with these challenges and navigating the gaps and underpinning uncertainty can trigger a necessary shift for a better use of the models for just decisions in energy transitions.

title: Beyond Religious Practice: Spirituality, Karma and Subjective Well-Being
affiliations: Curtin University, Australian National University (ANU) - Crawford School of Public Policy and Independent

detail.title: Beyond Religious Practice: Spirituality, Karma and Subjective Well-Being
detail.abstract: As the interest in research on happiness and well-being gains traction, the influence of religiosity and spirituality is generating interest. In this study, drawing on data from three rounds of the Gross National Happiness survey, we find higher religiosity is strongly linked to greater happiness and higher life satisfaction. We estimate a 1 SD increase in religiosity is associated with a 0.142 SD increase in happiness and a 0.121 SD increase in life satisfaction. We find the overall positive relationship is largely driven by individuals' intrinsic religiosity, encompassing self-reported spirituality and the consideration of karma in everyday life. We examine mental health, emotional health, and social support as potential mechanisms. We find intrinsic religiosity is positively related to individual's mental health, positive emotions and social support. We find individuals with higher religiosity tend to report lower levels of anger, selfishness, and jealousy, but higher levels of fear, worry and sadness.

title: Forecasting a Conditional Orbital Bottleneck: Launch Capacity as a Planning Constraint for Off-Planet Computation
affiliations: Zhejiang University

detail.title: Forecasting a Conditional Orbital Bottleneck: Launch Capacity as a Planning Constraint for Off-Planet Computation
detail.abstract: Large-scale computation is becoming a sociotechnical infrastructure whose growth may be constrained by terrestrial heat rejection, electricity supply, and permitting. We develop a finite-horizon planner model that treats orbital computing as heat relocation and links compute expansion to launch mass, bidirectional communication feasibility, and evidence-tiered demand scenarios. Under explicit assumptions on terrestrial saturation, feasible orbital deployment, and positive net orbital value, launch capacity can acquire a shadow price once terrestrial limits bind or are anticipated. This multiplier measures the marginal system value of relaxing launch capacity; it is not automatically a private rent. At a reference launch-cost floor of $1,500/kg, the multiplier is negligible at the electricity-value anchor. For the 2026-2085 horizon, the reporting threshold lies near κ net = 9.16, approximately $0.418/kWh. The threshold is horizon-dependent, and expanding-demand rent windows remain right-censored. A demand-continuation stress test addresses this limitation: flat demand after 2075 remains censored, whereas 5% annual contraction produces an internal closure in 2075 that is stable under longer horizons. Lifecycle heat displacement breaks even after 13.7 years in the stated central check. The framework contributes an evidence-tiered forecasting method and a dated partial evidence-update protocol for screening when investment, management, or governance appraisal is warranted as public evidence evolves.

title: Economic Perspectives on Monetary History

detail.title: Economic Perspectives on Monetary History

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Sven Svensson Foundation for Numismatics. The Gunnar Ekström Foundation. The Sven and Dagmar Salén Foundation.

detail.abstract:
Economic Perspectives on Monetary History analyses monetary history as a sequence of recurring economic problems rather than as a purely chronological evolution from barter to modern money. The book brings economic reasoning into dialogue with historical, archaeological, anthropological, and numismatic evidence, including coins, hoards, minting techniques, inscriptions, weights, metal content, circulation patterns, written sources, and institutional settings. Its central argument is that money should be understood by the functions it performs rather than by its material form. Across different periods and societies, monetary systems have sought to reduce transaction costs in exchange, valuation, saving, taxation, and credit while preserving the trust needed for general acceptability.

The book examines commodity money, coinage, monetization, minting systems, debasement, seigniorage, small change, credit instruments, representative money, bimetallism, international currencies, fiat money, and hyperinflation. These monetary forms differed in substance and institutional context, but they faced similar problems: how to provide sufficient liquidity, how to prevent fraud and over-issuance, how to maintain credibility, how to balance fiscal incentives against monetary stability, and how to make money acceptable beyond local or political boundaries. The analysis emphasizes that monetary development was neither linear nor irreversible. Commodity money, coinage, token money, credit, banknotes, bullion, and fiat money often coexisted, serving different transaction niches.

The book’s main conclusion is that monetary history can be interpreted as a gradual shift from material credibility to institutional credibility. Commodity money relied on intrinsic value; coinage added standardization and public authority; token and credit money required legal, fiscal, and reputational support; representative money depended on convertibility; and fiat money rests on credible monetary and fiscal institutions. Monetary history is therefore best understood as a persistent trade-off between elasticity and discipline: successful monetary systems expanded the supply and usefulness of money without destroying the trust on which money ultimately depends.

title: Natural Water Drowning Deaths in the Houston Metropolitan Region
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Baylor College of Medicine and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Natural Water Drowning Deaths in the Houston Metropolitan Region
detail.abstract: Most drowning deaths in the United States occur in natural water. Natural water settings are diverse with a variety of risks. Drownings also impose economic burden on local governments. This study describes drowning deaths in natural waters in the Houston metropolitan region and identify associated risk factors.This was a cross-sectional study of drowning deaths involving persons of all ages in the Houston metropolitan region from 2016 to 2022. Information on drowning deaths was obtained from probabilistically-linked data. High-risk drowning locations were identified based on the number of drowning deaths per capita. Associated risk factors were examined. Fifty-two percent of drowning deaths occurred in natural water locations. More than one-third occurred in flood control structures. Next were drowning deaths along the Gulf of Mexico (the ”Gulf”), mostly beach drowning deaths, followed by those in bays, lakes, flood waters, and rivers. Drowning death risk was higher in recreational areas. Beach drowning deaths were more likely to occur along the Gulf coast while boat-related drowning deaths were more dispersed in the Gulf, bays and lakes. Eight high-risk drowning locations were identified. Poor swimming ability was identified among decedents at all eight locations. Alcohol or drug use among decedents was also documented. Local governments can work to reduce drownings. Actions include expanding swimming lessons for children, emphasizing life jacket use for children, boaters, and people with limited swimming skills. Targeting countermeasures at high-risk drowning locations is needed including better warning signage and community outreach. Better protective barriers are needed at flood control structures.

title: The Rural Electronics Manufacturing Opportunity: A Framework for Building Niche Electronics Production Zones in Underserved American Communities

detail.title: The Rural Electronics Manufacturing Opportunity: A Framework for Building Niche Electronics Production Zones in Underserved American Communities
detail.abstract: Manufacturing came back to America the hard way. Not through a policy announcement or a ribbon-cutting ceremony-through a shock that exposed, in real time, how completely dependent the world's largest economy had become on someone else to make things. In April 2021, Ford shut down a truck plant in Kansas City. Not because demand was soft-there was a six-month waiting list for F-150s. They shut it down because a microcontroller chip worth about a dollar fifty wasn't available in quantities large enough to keep the line running. GM idled plants in Michigan and Ohio the same week. Hospital purchasing managers in New York were quoting sixteen-week lead times on patient monitoring equipment. The supply chain for America's most critical industrial input had been built almost entirely overseas, and when it buckled, there was nothing behind it. sited, this paper argues, in the post-industrial rural communities-Butte and Bessemer and Helper and Hazard-that built the first American industrial economy and have been waiting decades for the next one. AI Disclosure Statement: Artificial intelligence tools were used in a supporting capacity during the preparation of this paper across three functions: (1) initial literature search and source identification across federal, academic, and industry databases; (2) assessment of source relevance and credibility against the paper's research questions; and (3) generation of data visualizations and infographics based on data inputs and design direction provided by the author. All AI-assisted outputs were independently reviewed, factchecked against primary sources, and editorially approved by the author, who assumes sole responsibility for all content, analysis, and conclusions in this paper.

title: SUEVAL: An integrated urban evaluation model incorporating semi-supervised temporal structures
affiliations: Chengdu University of Information Technology

detail.title: SUEVAL: An integrated urban evaluation model incorporating semi-supervised temporal structures
detail.abstract: Developing comprehensive urban indices is critical for urban governance and policy evaluation, yet prevailing approaches face notable limitations: rule-based weighting schemes are static and subjective, whereas data-driven machine learning models often lack interpretability and temporal comparability. This paper proposes SUEVAL (Supervised-Unsupervised Ensemble for Evaluation), a semi-supervised, structure-aware, and temporally evolvable framework for composite urban evaluation. Building on a pre-constructed D-S-A hierarchical structure, the framework jointly exploits (1) feature importance derived from multi-task supervised learning and (2) structural importance obtained through unsupervised learning. An uncertainty-aware adaptive fusion mechanism is then introduced to generate a baseline static anchor. (3) A three-layer state space (Evidence -State -Score) performs Bayesian filtering and incorporates a Kalman gain to update annual dynamic weights via exponential smoothing. Using a long panel dataset of Chinese cities spanning 2000-2023, we benchmark SUEVAL against rule-based weighting schemes and single-model approaches. SUEVAL consistently delivers superior performance in multi-step forecasting of exogenous proxy variables, reduces prediction errors relative to static and rolling-static indices, and produces more balanced and robust weight distributions and city rankings. The dynamic weights reveal substantively meaningful post-pandemic shifts: the relative importance of digital infrastructure, healthcare capacity, and local fiscal resilience increases, while traditional offline consumption and several industrial indicators exhibit declining explanatory power. These results demonstrate that SUEVAL can detect and interpret structural transitions in urban systems while preserving temporal stability. More broadly, the framework provides a transferable, data-driven methodology for constructing interpretable and updatable composite indices, thereby supporting technology-enabled urban sustainability and long-term policy evaluation.

title: Child Penalties in Personal Finances: Evidence from Bank Data
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School and Lund University

detail.title: Child Penalties in Personal Finances: Evidence from Bank Data
detail.abstract: We study how parenthood affects gender differences in personal financial behavior using comprehensive, high-frequency bank data covering roughly one third of the adult population in Iceland. Exploiting sharp changes around the birth of the first child in an event-study framework, we show that parenthood generates large and persistent financial child penalties for women. At childbirth, women abruptly reduce savings, draw down supplemental pension balances, increase reliance on consumer credit, and disengage from risky asset markets, while men show no comparable response. These effects persist for over two decades after the first birth. To assess whether these patterns are mechanically driven by income losses associated with parental leave, we decompose financial responses into components implied by income changes and behavioral adjustments conditional on income. Income-based mechanical effects explain essentially none of the observed responses; the financial child penalties are driven overwhelmingly by behavioral changes. We interpret these findings through a framework in which parenthood induces endogenous specialization in financial engagement under asymmetric time constraints and limited commitment within households. When separation risk is non-negligible and financial engagement is individual-specific, changes in personal financial behavior reallocate financial risk and control across partners in non-neutral ways. Our results identify parenthood as a central and previously underexplored driver of gender inequality in personal finances, even in a highly gender-egalitarian setting.

title: Degrees Without Returns? Wage Premiums, Underemployment, and Labor Market Mismatch among University Graduates in Nepal

detail.title: Degrees Without Returns? Wage Premiums, Underemployment, and Labor Market Mismatch among University Graduates in Nepal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial, professional, or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on secondary analysis of anonymized data from the Nepal Labour Force Survey 2023. No primary data were collected by the author, and no personally identifiable information was accessed. Therefore, formal ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant, funding, or financial support from any public, commercial, or non-profit organization.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether labour market outcomes among university graduates in Nepal are consistent with concerns about credential inflation accompanying rapid educational expansion. This study examines the responses from 450 university-educated participants of the Nepal Labour Force Survey 2023. The Empirical approach combines an analysis of descriptive statistics with ordinary least squares regression on wages and logistic regression on employment outcomes. The results show that there is an approximately 3.4% increase in wages for every additional year of schooling (p < 0.01) and that 34% of employed graduates would be considered underemployed. The employment benefit of education is relatively small and not statistically significantly different from unity (OR = 1.089, p < 0.10), and there is no statistically significant association between education and reducing underemployment. Such patterns would not necessarily support the notion of credential inflation but would be more indicative of concerns with labour market mismatch. The study is cross sectional, and a comparison of the results of this study with the concerns of credential inflation must be read as evidence, not as conclusive proof, of credential inflation. In conclusion, the paper points to the need for better linkages between the expansion of education, labour market demand and employability of university graduates in Nepal.

title: Searching for the Relationship between Emissions and Stock Returns: How Returns, Emissions and Firm Size Interact
affiliations: Stockholm University and

detail.title: Searching for the Relationship between Emissions and Stock Returns: How Returns, Emissions and Firm Size Interact

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest but acknowledges that the paper in an earlier version received an award from the Sustainable Finance Lab for the best master thesis pitch. However, the authors are not affiliated with the Sustainable Finance Lab.
declarations.funderStatement: The paper has not been funded.

detail.abstract: Despite climate change being a global problem, few studies have investigated how carbon emissions and stock returns relate to each other in a global setting. The few that have undertaken this empirical challenge have faced strong critique due to methodological concerns. Therefore, it raises the question; does a relationship between stock returns and carbon emissions exist? This question is investigated cross-sectionally with a dataset covering a substantial part of the world's total market cap of listed firms between 2015 to 2024. Methodologically the study contributes to earlier literature by using a pragmatic approach and incorporates; (i) firm reported emissions, (ii) filing dates from annual reports to avoid look ahead bias and (iii) test both unscaled and relative emissions. Further, by utilizing the Frisch-Waugh-Lowell theorem the paper takes a stance on how firm size affects the results, where the results suggest that both unscaled and relative emissions are highly related to size. Globally, when adjusting the size variable accordingly, no relationship is found between emissions and returns. However, some evidence is found regionally for the US, the UK and Japan but mostly limited to models using unscaled emissions.

title: Who Holds U.S. Bonds and How It Shapes the Yield Effects of QE and QT
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: Who Holds U.S. Bonds and How It Shapes the Yield Effects of QE and QT
detail.abstract: How much do quantitative easing (QE) and tightening (QT) move bond yields? The answer turns on the slope of aggregate bond demand: who holds bonds, how sensitive their demand is to yields, and how fast they rebalance. I estimate heterogeneous investor demand in the U.S. bond market across four asset classes, Treasuries, agency MBS, corporate bonds, and municipal bonds, from sector-level portfolio-share data spanning 1985 to 2025, using granular, QE-shock, and heteroskedasticity-based instruments. I measure each sector's demand against the non-bond asset it actually trades off against, and I let each sector rebalance at its own speed. Both elasticities and speeds differ sharply across sectors: financial intermediaries and foreign investors are inelastic, and the largest long-term holders, insurers and pension funds, barely respond within the quarter but reach a positive long-run slope over the following year. Because these sectors hold most of the market, aggregate demand is inelastic, and more so at low yields, which amplifies QE's price impact and dampens QT's. Feeding the estimated demand system through market clearing, I find that historical QE compressed yields substantially and spilled over to corporate and municipal markets. QT is smaller, a further $900 billion of runoff raising Treasury yields by about 15 basis points, because demand is more elastic at the higher yields prevailing during QT.

title: The gendered effects of reputational shocks in team-based production environments
affiliations: University of Bergamo - Department of Economics,  and Bocconi University - Department of Policy Analysis and Public Management

detail.title: The gendered effects of reputational shocks in team-based production environments
detail.abstract: This paper studies how reputational shocks are distributed within teams, using scientific article retractions as a setting in which a highly visible negative signal falls simultaneously on all co-authors while individual responsibility remains ambiguous. Linking retraction records to the complete publication histories of all involved authors (1993-2020), and applying document embeddings to over 490,000 abstracts, we assess both demand-side responses by the scientific community and supply-side adjustments by affected authors. We document large and persistent gender gaps in retraction penalties: female co-authors experience substantially larger citation losses than male co-authors from the same event and shift their research agendas significantly farther from the retracted topic. We interpret the citation gap as reflecting biased blame attribution by the scientific community: it concentrates in mixed-gender teams, larger groups, and mid-authorship positions, and it is higher for severe retractions and in male-dominated fields. The agenda shift reflects, instead, a differential behavioral response by women, who also experience a productivity slowdown, gain fewer new collaborators, and display higher inactivity rates. Importantly, women's behavioral responses do not fully account for the demand-side penalty.

title: Are Persistent Trade Deficits Problematic? Monetary Sovereignty, Capital Deepening, and the Keen Mechanism

detail.title: Are Persistent Trade Deficits Problematic? Monetary Sovereignty, Capital Deepening, and the Keen Mechanism

declarations.funderStatement: There are no funding interests to disclose.

keywords: data envelopment analysis JEL classification: F32

detail.abstract: Are persistent trade deficits problematic? The mercantilist instinct, its balance-of-paymentsconstraint descendants, and Keen's endogenous-money critique of Modern Monetary Theory answer yes; MMT's "imports are a benefit" position answers no. We test both poles in a five-year-window panel of up to 187 countries (1960-2024), pairing growth regressions with a world-frontier decomposition and a direct decomposition of Keen's mechanism into its money, credit, and ownership margins. The results discipline both sides. A linear association suggesting trade deficits predict faster subsequent growth (-0.032, p < 0.01) is an artifact of forced symmetry: a spline shows the deficit region is flat and the action lies entirely in the surplus region-large trade surpluses predict slower subsequent growth. Keen's money-drain prediction fails in both the world panel and 140 years of advanced-economy data; what operates instead is his own endogenous-money logic-trade deficits predict faster private credit growth in both panels, a result that survives cluster-bootstrap inference-relocating any harm to the leverage margin. The ownership margin is inert: the flow-to-NIIP passthrough is 0.21 (valuation effects absorb roughly four-fifths of flows), the NIIP level predicts nothing for growth, and foreign equity ownership shares predict faster growth. In the frontier decomposition, one channel survives frontier-re-estimating cluster-bootstrap inference: trade deficits predict faster capital deepening-crowding in, through imported investment goodsunder all six frontier constructions, though an Anderson-Hsiao instrument attributes the association to transitory co-movement rather than persistent deficit positions. Nor does the trade balance predict the composition shift its critics attribute to it: the aggregate balance is unrelated to changes in manufacturing's output or employment shares once composition is held, and the deindustrialization that does occur tracks the manufacturing-specific balance with a value-added/employment split that is the signature of productivity rather than hollowing-out. Every sovereignty differential-growth-level, efficiency-channel, and deepeningchannel-is statistically indistinguishable from zero under design-based inference. Estimates are conditional correlations, not causal effects.

title: Racial/Ethnic Differences in Household Debt Payment Delinquency Among Renters and Homeowners
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU) and

detail.title: Racial/Ethnic Differences in Household Debt Payment Delinquency Among Renters and Homeowners

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Financial Counseling and Planning

detail.abstract: We used the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances and Heckman's two-step procedure to examine racial/ethnic differences in household debt payment delinquency among U.S. renters and homeowners. Black renters were more likely to be delinquent than White renters, and Black homeowners more likely than White and Hispanic homeowners. Among renters, being in a couple was negatively associated with delinquency, whereas having children under age 18 was positively associated with delinquency; neither pattern appeared among homeowners. Racial/ethnic disparities in delinquency differed by homeownership status: Black households showed higher delinquency risk among both renters and homeowners, whereas Asian disparities emerged primarily among non-couple homeowners, who were more likely to be delinquent than White and Hispanic non-couple homeowners. These results suggested a strong association between racial/ethnic status, family structure, and debt delinquency among both renters and homeowners, informing targeted financial education and policy interventions to address persistent racial/ethnic disparities in debt delinquency.

title: Domestic Content Requirements and Global Collective Action
affiliations: New York University School of Law and Yale Law School

detail.title: Domestic Content Requirements and Global Collective Action
detail.abstract: Domestic content requirements (DCRs) are a common but controversial feature of clean energy tax credits and subsidies. These requirements distort production and consumption decisions, increasing the social cost of achieving climate goals. However, DCRs can also yield an underappreciated benefit: one country's implementation of a subsidy with a DCR may induce other countries to adopt similar subsidies, thus accelerating the global transition away from fossil fuels. This paper develops a game-theoretic model of clean energy policy choices, identifies conditions under which DCRs increase global welfare, and derives policy-relevant lessons for tax and trade law.

title: Greenwashing in Sustainable Finance: An Overview of the Literature, Future Research Directions, and a Case Study of Germany
affiliations: Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg

detail.title: Greenwashing in Sustainable Finance: An Overview of the Literature, Future Research Directions, and a Case Study of Germany

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that may have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, the study reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval and informed consent were not required because this research did not involve human participants, patients, personal data, or an individual- or company-based case study.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Charl Hugo & Cayle Lupton (Eds.), Annual Banking Law Update 2026. Juta and Company.

detail.abstract: Greenwashing has emerged as a key challenge to market integrity in sustainable finance, as sustainability claims function as investment-relevant signals under information asymmetry, costly verification and fragmented measurement of environmental performance. This chapter provides an overview and synthesis of greenwashing research in finance and law, integrating evidence from asset management (environmental, social and governance (ESG) labelling, mutual fund flows and hedge funds), corporate finance (green bonds, real-asset transactions, transformation narratives and valuation effects) and disclosure research (mandatory sustainability reporting, green taxonomy design and ESG ratings divergence). Building on these research strands, the chapter develops an integrated framework that explains greenwashing as an equilibrium response to investor demand salience, the pricing of carbon risk and climate tail risk, reputational incentives and enforcement constraints, while emphasising the role of green taxonomies and disclosure regimes in shaping incentives and verifiability. The chapter then outlines future research directions and a call to action on measurement, causal identification and comparative enforcement design. To demonstrate how anti-greenwashing norms can be operationalised through enforcement, the chapter presents a case study of the German legal and enforcement framework. It examines misleading environmental advertising and “climate neutrality” claims under the Act against Unfair Competition (UWG), capital-market disclosure and prospectus liability under the Securities Prospectus Act (WpPG) and Capital Investment Act (VermAnlG), collective redress via the Consumer Rights Enforcement Act (VDuG) and escalation pathways to administrative and criminal sanctions via the Act on Regulatory Offences (OWiG) and the German Criminal Code (StGB).

title: Monopolization After Microsoft

detail.title: Monopolization After Microsoft

declarations.declarationOfInterest: My research is funded only by NYU School of Law; my wife is an antitrust attorney in private practice.

detail.abstract:
United States v. Microsoft may be the most celebrated monopolization case of all time. No other modern antitrust decision has received so much praise from across the political sp ectrum, nor been so widely accepted as an authoritative guide to the law.

This Article proposes a modest reassessment. It argues that, while Microsoft contains much to admire, it is in some important ways overrated, both as a clear statement of monopolization doctrine and as a “pro-enforcement” precedent. Despite its many virtues, the opinion is embroidered with formulations and applications of law that are contradictory, confusing, or facially unreasonable. Today, as a wave of Big Tech monopolization cases moves through the courts, these features of the decision threaten to confuse and mislead judges and litigants alike.

As we celebrate Microsoft’s 25th anniversary, we should honor the decision by moving beyond it in some important respects, in search of clearer and more appealing accounts of monopolization doctrine. The “dangerous exclusion” framework—which distinguishes tests of exclusion, contribution to monopoly, and privilege, and provides a welfarist justification defense—is one such account. Embracing it means preserving some features of Microsoft’s treatment of the law, while setting others aside, in search of a robust and principled approach that can serve in traditional markets and on the digital frontier. The time is right to resettle and refine the law of monopolization in service of the pragmatic integration of law and economics that Microsoft, in its best dimensions, did so much to promote.

title: Housing Boom-Bust Cycles and Entrant Earnings

detail.title: Housing Boom-Bust Cycles and Entrant Earnings
detail.abstract: Are there labor-market costs to starting a career after a local housing boom turns? I use repeated cross sections from the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC) to compare entrant cohorts in high-boom states with entrants in lower-boom states around state housing peaks. Cohorts entering after the peak in high-boom states earn 5.7 percent less, and 8.2 percent less in the late post-peak window. Randomization inference and American Community Survey state-of-birth checks support the earnings result, and Quarterly Workforce Indicators new-hire evidence points to a weaker entry ladder.

title: Accumulate or Vanish: Deriving Marx's Charaktermaske from the Market Selection of Reinvestment Strategies

detail.title: Accumulate or Vanish: Deriving Marx's Charaktermaske from the Market Selection of Reinvestment Strategies
detail.abstract: Marx's capitalist is a Charaktermaske: a character mask, the personification of capital, whose purpose is imposed by the movement of value rather than by psychology. The modality of this claim has been disputed for a century: is each capitalist compelled to accumulate (the Zwang reading of Postone, Arthur, and Mau), or is the accumulating capitalist simply what survives (the filtering register of Alchian and Friedman)? We show the filtering half is a theorem. In a minimal accumulation process where each agent readvances a fraction α t ∈ [0, 1] of its capital into a circuit valorizing at rate δ, survival in wealth share is, in a population containing a full reinvestor, equivalent to ∑ t (1-α t) < ∞: survivors reinvest everything, in the full limit. Under stochastic valorization, survival against a log-optimal (Kelly) incumbent is equivalent to a finite cumulative expected loggrowth deficit; the surviving disposition is Kelly log-optimality, interior (α * < 1) under heavy downside risk, recovering the hoard as an internal moment of the capital-form. The mathematics is deliberately classical; the contribution is the bridge and its boundary. Exact survival characterizations and cash margins exist in the equilibrium market-selection literature (Massari; Drokin and Zhitlukhin; Easley, Kolumbus and Tardos); what has no counterpart there is the price-free regime of differential compounding with the reinvestment fraction as a preference-free strategy, where the Marxian claim lives. Filtering does not deliver the Zwang reading, which requires structurally enforced consequences for the individual bearer; we state this, with permutable bearers and active recapture as further candidate ingredients, as an open program. The result executes a possibility Elster conceded in 1982 and that the Marxological literature, including Mau's treatment of competition, has left without a mechanism.

title: The Bank of Canada's Communication Conundrum: How to Explain Inflation
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute, University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM) - Centre de recherche sur l'emploi et les fluctuations économiques (CREFÉ) and Queen's University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Bank of Canada's Communication Conundrum: How to Explain Inflation
detail.abstract:
• This E-Brief is the third in a series related to the Bank of Canada’s 2026 renewal of its inflation-targeting agreement with the federal government.
  • We examine the desirable properties of underlying inflation measures and assess whether the measures available to the Bank meet those criteria.
  • We find that the Bank’s current measures provide useful information about underlying inflation, but the Bank should continue exploring improved measures to help guide its policy decisions.
  • However, the measures that help policymakers assess underlying inflation are not necessarily the best tools for communicating monetary policy to the public. The Bank should place greater emphasis on its inflation forecast and policy path when explaining its decisions.

title: A Hybrid Framework for the Discount for Lack of Marketability

detail.title: A Hybrid Framework for the Discount for Lack of Marketability
detail.abstract: The most popular option-theoretic methods towards an estimation of the Discount for Lack of Marketability ("DLOM") each suffer from particular limitations that complicate their usage by practitioners. To address this, we propose a hybrid framework that formulates the DLOM as the maximum of an at-the-money vanilla put and a floating-strike Asian put (equivalently, a put on the greater of a fixed and a floating-average strike) capturing both the full extent of downside risk and some measure of lost upside potential, without recourse to the explosive discounts of a lookback formulation. We derive a closed-form analytic approximation which is bounded below by the Chaffe discount by construction. We prove that this bound survives the moment-matching approximation, holding identically within the closed form itself at every volatility and restriction period. Monte Carlo simulation confirms that the closed form reproduces the true hybrid put to within roughly a tenth of a percentage point on average, with a worst-case deviation of 1.5 percentage points confined to the high-volatility, long-tenor region of the parameter space, while producing non-explosive discounts throughout.

title: Tariffs and the Rule of Law: Is International Trade Moving Towards Legal Order or Power Politics
affiliations: and Dr. B.R Ambedkar National Law University , Sonepat

detail.title: Tariffs and the Rule of Law: Is International Trade Moving Towards Legal Order or Power Politics
detail.abstract:
In the era of rising economic nationalism, the intersection of trade law and executive power has become increasingly contentious. The resurgence of economic protectionism has strained the legal framework of international trade policy – creating cracks in the well settled global demand and supply chain.

This paper dives into the United States invocation of “““Article XXI” of the GATT”” under its “America First Trade Policy”, framing broad reciprocal tariffs as national security measures – challenging the foundational principles of international trade governance. Such unilateralism challenges the integrity of the WTO’s dispute resolution system and threatens the principle of rule of law in trade governance. The paper analyses key WTO disputes, including China’s challenge and India’s copper tariff case, illustrating how strategic unilateralism destabilizes legal predictability and undermines institutional integrity, undermining core principles such as non-discrimination and transparency.

It further investigates the economic fallout of tariff wars, including fragmentation of global supply chain. Special attention is given to India’s economic vulnerability – with sectoral impacts MSME exports. The paper also highlights shifting trade alliances and the rise of alternate trade manufacturing hubs, revealing how protectionist policies reshape global commerce. The analysis reveals how power politics increasingly supersedes legal norms, destabilizing global supply chains and marginalizing developing economies. It calls for a renewed commitment to legal restraint, multilateral cooperation, and institutional accountability to preserve the rule of law in global commerce.

title: The Manufactured Dependency: Engineered Compulsion in Games as a Service and Four Doctrines That Now Reach It

detail.title: The Manufactured Dependency: Engineered Compulsion in Games as a Service and Four Doctrines That Now Reach It
detail.abstract: For years, the claim that games built as a service engineer compulsion and profit from it was treated as a cultural grievance with no legal handle. That has changed. This article argues that manufactured dependency, the deliberate engineering of compulsive engagement and its monetization through mechanics structured like gambling, is now actionable across four independent legal vectors: negligent and defective design, consumer protection and deception, gambling aimed at minors, and contract unconscionability. Each vector is independently sufficient, and a single stretch of 2026 produced a jury verdict holding addictive design a substantial factor in a minor's injury. The article then develops a disability axis that rides alongside the four vectors. Rather than forcing a plaintiff through the statutory exclusion for compulsive gambling, it routes through a cleanly covered disability and treats the clinical picture as evidence of harm. It also identifies a judicial estoppel trap. A defendant that invokes the gambling exclusion to defeat a disability claim must characterize its own product as gambling, which is the admission the gambling and consumer protection vectors need. The empirical predicate is not incidental. The evidence indicates that loot box spending, and therefore revenue, concentrates in the players who show problem gambling behavior. The dependence is the revenue engine, not a side effect.

title: Land Interventions and Urban Vitality: Evidence from Neighborhood Traffic
affiliations: California State University, Fullerton, University of Pennsylvania - Statistics Department and University of Pennsylvania - Wharton School, Department of Real Estate

detail.title: Land Interventions and Urban Vitality: Evidence from Neighborhood Traffic
detail.abstract: How do vacant land interventions reshape neighborhood traffic during and after a severe economic shock? Using the COVID-19 pandemic as an exogenous shock to aggregate demand, we compare mobility trajectories around formerly vacant lots that were greened or redeveloped through new construction, relative to lots that remained vacant. Our matched difference-indifferences estimates are consistent with a spatial coordination game characterized by multiple equilibria. We show that the capital required to anchor neighborhood commercial vitality depends on the strength of local network externalities. For agglomeration-sensitive amenities, greening stabilizes nearby visits relative to persistent vacancy, but the rebound in visits is stronger around new construction, suggesting that durable real estate investment provides a stronger anchor for recovery. For other amenities, both interventions mitigate the decline in local visits. These results suggest that vacant land policy should match the intensity of intervention to the structure of local demand: greening offers scalable blight remediation and neighborhood stabilization, while new construction is needed where recovery depends more strongly on agglomeration-sensitive visit activity.

title: The Manufactured Line: How Nexus Doctrine and Clickwrap Enforceability Deny the Disabled and the Consumer From Opposite Directions

detail.title: The Manufactured Line: How Nexus Doctrine and Clickwrap Enforceability Deny the Disabled and the Consumer From Opposite Directions
detail.abstract: This Article identifies a single doctrinal maneuver operating across two unrelated bodies of law. In disability access law, the nexus doctrine under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act treats the absence of a physical place as a reason to deny coverage to a digital service. In consumer contract and copyright law, the rule that software is licensed rather than sold treats the presence of a physical copy as insufficient to confer ownership or control, because an amendable license governs the object the buyer holds. The two rules point in opposite directions, yet they resolve in the same direction, against the person and toward the firm. The physical and digital boundary, this Article argues, is not a neutral descriptive fact that courts discover. It is a normative lever that courts and firms deploy, and its deployment tracks power rather than principle. Part III develops the disability half through the Title III circuit split. Part IV develops the consumer half through the line running from shrinkwrap enforceability to Vernor v. Autodesk. Part V draws the symmetry and argues that the boundary's manipulability, rather than either doctrine standing alone, is the phenomenon worth naming. A short concluding Part proposes that courts treat the physical and digital line as a lever to be justified in each instance, not a fact to be honored by default.

title: Technological Asymmetry, Product Differentiation and Merger
affiliations: University of Calcutta - Department of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Technological Asymmetry, Product Differentiation and Merger

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
In a globalised business environment competition and cooperation go hand in hand. Intense competition induces firms to cooperate with one another in many ways more in strategic sense than in non-strategic sense. In an interdependent system each internalizes others’ possible reactions while making a decision. As such different types of strategic decisions have become the order of the day.

Merger is one such strategic move what firms take for a wide range of purposes, for example, to increase market share to achieve various types of synergic gains through economies of scale and scope and so on. Usually there are three types of mergers: horizontal, vertical and conglomerate. We have considered in our exercise horizontal merger. Salant, Switzer and Reynolds (1983) have shown when firms are symmetric and product is homogeneous, bilateral horizontal merger is not profitable. Perry and Porter (1985) contest their position, and they have shown that horizontal merger is profitable in the presence of synergic gain arising out of cooperation even when products are homogeneous. Deneckre and Davidson (1985) show that a merger of any size is privately profitable when firms produce differential products and compete in prices.  Singh and Vives (1984) demonstrate that in a differentiated duopoly it is a dominant strategy for each firm to choose the quantity, provided the goods are substitutes. 

The objective of this exercise is to explore in a game theoretic framework the conditions under which horizontal merger is possible in an oligopolistic market with differential products and technologically asymmetric firms. In our analysis we have combined all the fundamental results mentioned above in a single structure. We show that in an oligopoly when firms are engaged in Cournot competition there exist a range of product differentiation and technological asymmetry for which merger is profitable. It also shows that product differentiation and synergic gain are equivalent in terms of consequences for the firms to decide whether to cooperate or not.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the cultural foundations of liberty through the political thought of Friedrich A. Hayek, the constitutional principles of the American Founding, and a comparative analysis of post-communist Albania. It argues that enduring freedom depends not only on formal institutions or constitutional design but also on the civic habits, moral norms, and cultural traditions that enable those institutions to function effectively. Drawing on Hayek’s concepts of local self-government, the rule of law, and higher law, the paper contends that liberty is sustained by citizens who internalize responsibility, respect general rules, and participate in self-governing communities. The American experience illustrates how civic education, local governance, and constitutional restraint reinforced a culture capable of preserving freedom across generations. In contrast, Albania demonstrates the limitations of institutional reform in the absence of corresponding cultural development, as patronage networks, collectivist legacies, and weak civic norms continue to undermine democratic governance and the rule of law. By integrating political philosophy with comparative historical analysis, the paper argues that liberty is fundamentally a cultural achievement. Democratic institutions may establish the framework for freedom, but their long-term success ultimately depends on the moral character, civic responsibility, and constitutional habits of the societies in which they operate.

title: Seemingly Anchored Inflation Expectations
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Seemingly Anchored Inflation Expectations
detail.abstract: Empirical evidence commonly cited as indicating that inflation expectations have become better anchored includes the declining sensitivity of expectations to inflation surprises over time, particularly around the adoption of inflation targeting. These patterns are typically attributed to the influence of explicit or implicit inflation targets on inflation expectations. We show that this evidence is consistent with a model of experience-based learning in which individuals learn solely from their lifetime history of realized inflation, without anchoring their expectations to an announced inflation target. In this model, the prolonged experience of low short-run inflation persistence in the pre-COVID decades renders long-run expectations insensitive to inflation surprises, matching the patterns observed in empirical anchoring tests. A unique prediction of the experience-based learning model is also borne out in the data: the decline in surprise sensitivity since the 1980s is strongest among younger individuals. The memory of low inflation persistence experiences further explains why long-run inflation expectations remained stable in the face of the post-COVID inflation surge. At the same time, simulations indicate that the sensitivity of long-run expectations to inflation surprises would rise sharply if individuals were to experience another sustained episode of highly persistent inflation. Overall, long-run inflation expectations may be less firmly anchored than commonly believed.

title: The Cost of Industrial Destruction: Evidence from Ukrainian Strikes on Russian Refineries
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome and Masaryk University

detail.title: The Cost of Industrial Destruction: Evidence from Ukrainian Strikes on Russian Refineries
detail.abstract: We study the local economic effects of Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries, combining a manually verified event-level record of refinery strikes with quality-screened daily satellite radiance from NASA Black Marble. The analysis covers 29 large Russian refineries, 22 of which sustain verified direct hits over June 2022-May 2026. Using a monthly staggered difference-indifferences design that compares refineries after their first verified strike with not-yet-struck and neverstruck refineries, we find that nighttime radiance falls immediately and persistently after a refinery enters the strike campaign: by roughly 30 percent in the innermost measured ring around the facility and by 15-18 percent within five kilometers, with the effect attenuating until it becomes small at twenty-five kilometers. The innermost ring shows no recovery within the first post-strike year. A complementary daily instrumental-variables design uses directional wind alignment to shift strike incidence and traces the strike-day dynamic at higher frequency. Radiance rises at short horizons, consistent with a fire-related light signature corroborated by independent NASA FIRMS detections, and turns negative at a six-month horizon, with weak-instrument-robust inference. Applying the same satellite product and empirical specification to 106 non-refinery deep-strike targets produces no comparable contraction, weighing against a generic-war-disruption interpretation.

title:
The Digitalization of Sovereign Capital
A General Theory and Three Living Laboratories of Natural-Capital Sovereignty: Norway, Australia, and Costa Rica

detail.title:
The Digitalization of Sovereign Capital
A General Theory and Three Living Laboratories of Natural-Capital Sovereignty: Norway, Australia, and Costa Rica

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not required

detail.abstract:
The twenty-first century is witnessing a structural transformation in the legal architecture of sovereign capital. Historically associated with territory, extraction, industrial production, taxation, monetary administration, and physical infrastructure, sovereign wealth increasingly extends toward digitally represented systems of public value, strategic financial structures, maritime jurisdictions, biodiversity metrics, orbital infrastructure, sovereign data systems, and long-term intergenerational state assets. This paper advances the thesis that the digitalization of sovereign capital constitutes an emerging stage in the historical evolution of sovereignty itself, and that the phenomenon should therefore be examined through the combined lenses of public finance, legal governance, continuity of institutions, sovereign liquidity, digital infrastructure, and strategic state architecture (1)(2)(3)(4). The paper develops the concept of digitally represented public value and introduces the correlative notion of synthetic sovereignty: the juridical and economic capacity of a State to generate, capture, and retain value at a diminishing margin of material extraction or consumption. It argues that States are entering a period in which strategic public wealth may increasingly depend not merely upon the ownership of resources, but upon the juridical capacity to identify, represent, govern, preserve, finance, audit, and administer sovereign capital through digitally integrated institutional systems. The analysis examines sovereign wealth funds, the balance-sheet State, regulated digital assets, central bank digital currencies, sovereign liquidity systems, maritime capital, blue economy governance, data infrastructure, cybersecurity, orbital systems, artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, and representational sovereignty, and it tests these propositions against the comparative architectures of Norway, Australia, and Costa Rica (5)(6)(7)(8)(9).
These propositions are not pursued exhaustively — the field is too large for that — but are read through three living laboratories of natural-capital sovereignty: Norway, Australia, and Costa Rica. The three are chosen because each governs an exceptional endowment of natural wealth; because Norway furnishes the founding and most successful paradigm against which the others may be read; and because Australia and Costa Rica share the institutional gravitation of the Asia-Pacific. They are treated not as adversarial benchmarks but as illustrations, through which the general theory descends from epistemological reflection toward the analytical and applied registers of governance and public finance, disclosing the structural challenges and the potential benefits that the digitalization of sovereign capital entails. The central claim is not technological. It is juridical and institutional: the digitalization of sovereign capital reorganizes the ways in which public value becomes visible, governable, capable of being financed, verifiable, preservable, and transferable across generations. The comparative material also discloses a recurring paradox — that the dematerialization of value is frequently financed by an intensification, rather than a cessation, of physical throughput. The paper concludes that the future of sovereign capital may be determined less by resource abundance alone than by the legal architecture through which sovereign value is organized, disciplined, protected, and transmitted within increasingly digital systems of public administration (10)(11)(12).
