detail.abstract:
My current book project, Who Controls African Money? Currency, Empire, and the Fight for Economic Freedom, examines the politics of money as a central but often neglected dimension of Africa's developmental challenges. The book argues that monetary arrangements are not merely technical instruments of economic management but institutional expressions of power, sovereignty, and political authority. It investigates how colonial currency systems, externally imposed monetary disciplines, financial liberalisation, debt dependency, and global financial hierarchies continue to shape Africa's position within the international economy long after the formal end of colonial rule.

At the heart of the project is the argument that contemporary forms of economic dependency cannot be fully understood without examining the governance of money itself. The book explores how exchange rate regimes, reserve accumulation strategies, central banking orthodoxies, debt conditionalities, and external financial surveillance constrain developmental possibilities across the continent. It further examines the political economy of monetary sovereignty and the prospects for regional and continental financial integration as instruments of economic emancipation.

Closely connected to this work is my broader interest in the political economy of development and underdevelopment in Africa. I am particularly interested in how global capitalism, financialisation, unequal exchange, and the international monetary system interact with domestic institutions and class structures to shape developmental trajectories in postcolonial societies. My research seeks to bridge sociology, economics, political science, and history in order to produce a more integrated understanding of development processes and constraints.

title: Programmable Sovereignty: Coordinated Specialization as a Response to the N-2 Problem in AI
affiliations: Bruegel and Independent

detail.title: Programmable Sovereignty: Coordinated Specialization as a Response to the N-2 Problem in AI
detail.abstract: The dominant scholarly and policy framing of artificial intelligence (AI) power treats sovereignty as a function of production: a state is sovereign over AI to the degree that it builds, owns, and can reproduce the technological stack on which AI depends. On this view, meaningful AI sovereignty is available only to the United States and, to a lesser extent, China — producing what we term the N‑2 problem, in which every other state faces structural dependence on one or both. A separate and largely disconnected literature treats digital sovereignty as a function of governance: the capacity to shape how technology behaves through rules, standards, and market leverage, independent of who builds the underlying systems. This paper integrates these two literatures and, in doing so, makes two contributions. First, it defines programmable sovereignty precisely, as soft governance anchored by a deliberately minimal degree of hard-stack control — above all pooled compute capacity — sufficient to make governance commitments credible and dependence reversible, without requiring the costly and largely unattainable goal of full-stack AI autonomy. Second, the paper develops coordinated  specialisation as the institutional mechanism through which N‑2 states can convert individual complementary capacities into a credible and minimally self-sufficient shared coalition AI stack. We illustrate the feasibility and limits of coordinated specialisation through three existing institutional precedents (EuroHPC, India Stack, and the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework) and close with policy implications for the European Union, Asia-Pacific coalition partners, and prospective coalitions generally.

title: Are LLMs Reliable Coders of Communication Content in Economic Experiments? Working Paper #0115
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and New York University of Abu Dhabi

detail.title: Are LLMs Reliable Coders of Communication Content in Economic Experiments? Working Paper #0115
detail.abstract: Analysis of free-form communication from experiments has largely relied on manual coding by research assistants (RAs), a costly and time-consuming process. We outline an easily implemented method for coding communication data using large language models (LLMs) and propose a novel standard for evaluating the performance of LLM-based coding ("reliability"). Using data from three published articles, we find that LLM-based coding meets our two reliability conditions: (1) differences between LLM-based and RA-based coding are no larger than differences between the RA-based and original coding and (2) the LLM-based coding largely replicates qualitative conclusions from the original papers. That said, there are cases where the LLM-based coding agrees poorly with the RA-based coding or fails to replicate statistical results from the original papers. We demonstrate that these problems can be ameliorated with better prompt design. We conclude that use of LLMs can reduce research costs and time without sacrificing reliability, making content analysis a more accessible tool for experimental economists. However, only with a combination of test coding by RAs and prompt design by researchers can we avoid significant problems with LLM-based coding, highlighting the continued importance of human input.

title: Openness, Integration, and the International Monetary Order
affiliations: Boston University, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco,  and

detail.title: Openness, Integration, and the International Monetary Order

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed here are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco or the Federal Reserve System. Jingye Wang is the corresponding author of this paper. We thankPierreDeLeo,ŞebnemKalemli-Özcan, RobertKollmann,and Dmitry Mukhin for helpful comments.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a calibrated general-equilibrium model to study how different configurations of trade and financial policy reshape the hierarchy of global currencies-and the U.S. dollar's position at its anchor. Currency safety and anchor status arise endogenously from each economy's 'effective size'-the weight its domestic shocks carry in setting world prices. Tariffs reduce this effective size on the goods side; capital controls do the same on the financial side. A unifying result emerges: The economy that maintains the deepest integration with the global trading network retains the largest safety premium and gains anchor status. We use this framework to evaluate the effects of three policy levers for Europe that affect the effective size of the euro: internal harmonization and enlargement, trade openness, and capital-account openness. The stakes are large: In our model, shifts in currencies' safety can redirect global capital flows and alter sovereign borrowing costs by hundreds of billions of dollars annually.

title: Jurisdictional Bifurcation, Textual Mystification and the Question of Proper Forum for the Adjudication of Maritime Labour Disputes in Nigeria: A Search for Coherence
affiliations: Phoenix & Volge (Legal Practitioners and Arbitrators) and

detail.title: Jurisdictional Bifurcation, Textual Mystification and the Question of Proper Forum for the Adjudication of Maritime Labour Disputes in Nigeria: A Search for Coherence
detail.abstract: The amendment to the Constitution by virtue of the Third Alteration Act, 2010 made the National Industrial Court of Nigeria, a superior Court of regard with coordinate jurisdiction with the Federal High Court and the High Courts of the Federating State, and granted it, exclusive jurisdiction over labour and employment matters or causes. The same Constitution vested exclusive admiralty jurisdiction in the Federal High Court of Nigeria. However, under the extant international and domestic legal regimes, labour related matters, particularly seafarers' wages, are considered as maritime claims, which are not only intrinsic to admiralty practice, but an integral part of the admiralty jurisdiction cognisable under international law, domestic legislation and industry custom and practices. To this end, there are conflicting judicial authorities and scholarly opinions as to whether upon a proper interpretation and construction of non-obstante clause used in the both Section 251 and 254 C of the Constitution, the admiralty jurisdiction of the Federal High Court was effectively whittled down, to vest jurisdiction over maritime labour claims in the National Industrial Court, to the exclusion of the Federal High Court. The Court of Appeal recently answered the question in the affirmative, with far-reaching adverse implications. The position of the court created an absurd situation, by unwittingly unbundling the established norms and practice for the protection of seafarers. The decision specifically deprived seafarers of their right to enforce their maritime lien in respect of their unpaid wages, by taking out an action in rem, with the possibility of arresting the ship or the relevant property to secure an indemnity or security for their claims. The doctrinal method was used in this inquiry, to ascertain the palpable cause of the lingering absurdity. It was observed that the Court embarked on a cloistered construction of the text of the constitution, and largely dwelt on the legal effect of the non-obstnte clause used in the conflicting provisions, without any recourse to external aids to gain historical, contemporary and contextual perspective, in order to arrive at the true intendment of the draftsman. The court basically placed reliance establish principle for construction of statute, which in any case, has been found to be inadequate, when it comes to constitutional interpretation, which is placed on a higher pedestal. It is therefore submitted that, had the court applied the liberal and cloistered approach based on established principle of constitutional interpretation, it would have reached a different conclusion. It is recommended that, the Appellate court could reverse its earlier decision reach per incuriam, when the occasion arises, or it may be more practicable to amend the relevant provision relating to the jurisdiction of the National Industrial Court, with a rider that expressly exclude maritime labour claims.

title: Posterior Consistency and Discretization Invariance for Bayesian Inverse Problems with Score-Based Priors

detail.title: Posterior Consistency and Discretization Invariance for Bayesian Inverse Problems with Score-Based Priors
detail.abstract:
Score-based generative models are widely used as learned priors in Bayesian inverse problems, yet the posterior measure itself -- its existence in infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, its continuity in the data, and its statistical concentration -- remains essentially unstudied outside the Gaussian-prior regime.

We provide a theory for linear forward maps G in the main text; Appendix D sketches an extension to one-sided Holder-stable nonlinear G that we expect to admit a full treatment in follow-up work. We assume Gaussian observation noise and a prior defined implicitly by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE with learned score s_theta. (i) Well-posedness: Cameron-Martin Lipschitz and affine-growth hypotheses (verifiable for spectral-norm MLPs, truncated FNOs) yield a well-defined posterior, locally Hellinger-stable in y with C_R = C_0(1+R)^2 exp(eta R^2) as in Stuart (2010, Theorem 4.2); absolute continuity is handled through a finite-horizon Girsanov integrability condition. (ii) Discretization invariance: d_H(mu_N^y, mu^y) <= C(sqrt(epsilon_N^score) + sqrt(lambda_{N+1})) with identifiable score and covariance terms. (iii) Conditional contraction: Knapik et al.'s Ghosal-van der Vaart contraction template transfers to score-based priors once two local inputs are verified: Gaussian small-ball comparability at the truth and exponentially consistent tests. The contraction theorem gives the resulting sigma^{2 beta/(2 beta+1)} rate in the non-smoothing testing geometry. (iv) Identifiability: injectivity of G on the closed support of the base measure -- kernel recovery at full support and symmetry obstructions (e.g., Z/2) otherwise.

This complements concurrent sampler-focused theory. We release reproducible 1D PyTorch code and committed pilot npz files illustrating qualitative contraction; reported numerics are not a sharp-rate certification.

title: Forward Information Leakage in a Widely-Used Open-Source Chinese Financial Data Interface: A Deconfounded Statistical Audit

detail.title: Forward Information Leakage in a Widely-Used Open-Source Chinese Financial Data Interface: A Deconfounded Statistical Audit
detail.abstract:
AKShare is among the most widely-used open-source Python interfaces for Chinese A-share data (>8,000 GitHub stars), broadly adopted in academic empirical work and practitioner communities. We audit the point-in-time validity of AKSharesupplied price-to-earnings (PE) data for Beijing Stock Exchange (BSE) stocks. 
Our identification exploits an accounting identity: implied earnings, recovered as close price / PE, can mechanically change only when the data provider updates its earnings input. Under strict point-in-time construction, such updates should occur on or after a firm's earnings release. We compare the timing of genuine impliedearnings updates against China's legally mandated disclosure deadlines (Apr 30, Aug 31, Oct 31). 
We first show that the naive approach — counting jumps in the PE ratio itself — is heavily confounded: 74% of large PE-ratio jumps coincide with a large same-day price move, i.e., they are price-driven, not earnings-driven. After removing this confound and isolating the 451 genuine implied-earnings updates in our panel (181 BSE stocks, 2022–2026), 99.8% occur before the legal disclosure deadline, and 0.2% on or after. The result is stable across 10%/15%/20% jump thresholds.
We are deliberately careful about interpretation. About 56% of these updates fall in the seven days immediately preceding the deadline — a pattern also consistent with legitimate early actual disclosure, since firms typically report before the lastallowed date. The irreducible evidence of forward bias is the residual 31% of updates that land 31–90 days before the legal deadline, clustering near the fiscal period-end (e.g., H1 earnings stamped near June 30 rather than the Aug 31 deadline). No firm legally discloses that early; this residual is the signature of period-end / retrospective backfill at the upstream provider. A controlled lag experiment corroborates an exploitable magnitude: imposing a 2–3 month lag on PE in a representative BSE strategy reduces its in-sample t-statistic by 1.4–1.5 units.
We conclude that AKShare PE data is not point-in-time relative to legal disclosure for a non-trivial share of observations, that the bias is large enough to convert a marginal factor result (t≈2) into an apparently robust one (t≈3), and we propose mitigation strategies and a definitive follow-up test against actual announcementdate data.

title: Laundering in Play? eSports Virtual Economies, Skin Markets, and the Reach of the Recast EU Anti-Money Laundering Framework

authors.last_name: Faculty of Law, Palacký University Olomouc, Czech Republic

affiliations: , Faculty of Law, Palacký University Olomouc, Palacký University Olomouc, Palacký University Olomouc - Faculty of Law and Faculty of Law, Palacký University Olomouc, Czech Republic

detail.title: Laundering in Play? eSports Virtual Economies, Skin Markets, and the Reach of the Recast EU Anti-Money Laundering Framework
detail.abstract: The free-to-play business model that sustains the world's leading eSports titles rests on elaborate internal economies in which players buy, earn, and trade virtual currencies and cosmetic items. This chapter argues that those economies are not merely a consumer-protection concern but a structural money-laundering vulnerability that the European Union's recently recast anti-money laundering framework leaves substantially unaddressed. It examines how the EU's new antimoney laundering framework applies to laundering risks in eSports. It analyses the 2024 antimoney laundering package (Regulation 2024/1624, Directive 2024/1640, Regulation 2024/1620 establishing the Anti-Money Laundering Authority, and the recast Transfer of Funds Regulation 2023/1113) together with the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation 2023/1114. On that basis, it develops a typology of laundering vectors observable in the ten most-watched eSports titles of 2024 and maps each vector against the obligations introduced by the new regime. The chapter ultimately finds that the 2024 package leaves a significant gap. Because it defines "crypto-asset" by reference to the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, and because that definition depends on both technology and transferability, conventional in-game currencies, the tradable skins of the minority of titles that permit secondary trading, and most non-fungible in-game items fall outside the preventive, obliged-entity perimeter of the anti-money-laundering framework. The gap is one of preventive supervision and not of criminal money-laundering liability, which may attach to dealing in such proceeds whatever the form of the asset. The exclusion is shown to be a deliberate feature of the framework's architecture rather than a drafting oversight, and therefore far harder to remedy than the existing literature has assumed. The chapter closes by proposing solutions consistent with the Union's stated commitment to protecting players and the integrity of the financial system.

Fiscal Theory of The Price Level

detail.abstract: We present an internally consistent model in which the price level is pinned by backing with no government — a backing theory of the price level (BTPL) — that prices the issuer's whole portfolio, generalizing the valuation logic the fiscal theory of the price level (FTPL) applies to the state's claim alone: FTPL's equation is the single-leaf case ( , the endogenous book's feedback modulus), the surplus claim counted as the only asset and the endogenous inside book set to zero, so determinacy becomes a condition ( , Theorem 4.1) rather than an artifact of truncation. It answers the quantity theory's question with no quantity in the numerator — built as a valuation fixed point over the balance sheets of a stock-flow-consistent agent-based economy. Money and all claims are marked to issuer backing by a Merton (1974) structural-credit valuation placed on the network of claims and solved to a fixed point in the Eisenberg–Noe (2001) tradition — a mark-to-market network valuation in the sense of Barucca et al. (2020), not the literal clearing-payment vector — with the absolute level pinned by a real anchor. (By network we mean throughout the web of who-owes-whom: agents are nodes, and each deposit or loan is an edge whose value depends on the others.) The value of money solves , fusing the absolute-level (FTPL/backing) and network-valuation (Eisenberg–Noe/Merton) literatures with private credit and a real anchor in place of government claims. Here is the anchor's goods-value, the marked loan book, and the deposit stock (defined at §1.4). The central result is a determinacy theorem: with an exogenous anchor and bounded real collateral the fixed point has a unique positive root, while strong endogenous-anchor feedback creates multiplicity — so anchor exogeneity is a clean sufficient condition, not an equivalence. We then show determinacy and dynamic stability are separate: a reduced-form round map exhibits a leverage-driven Neimark–Sacker fragility — a slow cycle short simulations can miss —even where the level is pinned. The same fixed point yields a regime map (no anchor, floating backing, convertible par, central-bank par) in which the classical doctrines appear as restrictions of one object — a restricted, structural unification. Two signatures make it empirical: the sign of flips between convertible-par and floating regimes, and a unit root appears only with no anchor. Scope, stated up front: the components are prior art; the backing price is a read-only valuation fixed point over the model's balance sheets, not live price formation in the agent-based round (administered prices today); the dynamic result is an explicit reduced form, and its leverage-only Neimark–Sacker threshold is itself a reduced-form artifact — the structurally-bounded Merton channel is sub-critical on its own, so the bifurcation proper requires the expectational or insolvency channels (§5.4); and there is no empirical validation

title: Assessing District Elections as a Remedy in State Voting Rights Acts
affiliations: George Washington University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Political Science and Independent

detail.title: Assessing District Elections as a Remedy in State Voting Rights Acts
detail.abstract: As federal voting rights protections recede, state-level voting rights acts (VRAs) have become the principal legal tool for safeguarding minority representation in the United States. We assess what these laws can accomplish using the California Voting Rights Act, which has compelled over 150 cities to replace at-large with district elections. Applying redistricting algorithms across 109 cities, we evaluate how much district elections-and the alternative reforms state VRAs permit-can amplify Latino political influence. District elections prove to be a limited remedy: most cities cannot draw a majority-Latino district and many cannot use districts to meaningfully increase Latino electoral success, even under optimistic assumptions about turnout, cohesion, and crossover voting. By contrast, cumulative voting, ranked choice voting, and limited voting empower Latino voters without relying on favorable geography or mapmakers' discretion. We conclude that policymakers seeking to improve minority representation should be more open to reforms within the proportional representation family.

title: Monetary Transmission and Inflation Dynamics in Bangladesh: Evidence from Linear and Nonlinear ARDL Models

detail.title: Monetary Transmission and Inflation Dynamics in Bangladesh: Evidence from Linear and Nonlinear ARDL Models
detail.abstract: Import-dependent economies with managed exchange rates face a specific policy problem: identifying which monetary levers actually reach the domestic price level, so that inflation can be disciplined by adjusting those levers rather than reacting after prices have already moved. This study answers that question for Bangladesh. All three standard transmission channels-broad money growth, the lending rate, and exchange rate depreciation-are estimated jointly within one cointegration framework, using monthly data from February 2015 to June 2022. Unit root testing finds a mix of I(0) and I(1) series with no I(2) processes, so the autoregressive distributed lag (ardl) bounds test of Pesaran et al. (2001) is the correct cointegration procedure; the resulting Wald Fstatistic of 9.733 clears the one percent upper bound. Each additional percentage point of monthly broad money growth raises long-run inflation by 1.289 points, a multiplier above unity that Granger causality traces to a monetary accommodation pattern: the central bank has historically expanded the money supply after inflation rises rather than tightening pre-emptively. Exchange rate depreciation passes through almost fully, at a long-run coefficient of 1.023, a result that survives a dummy-variable check isolating the 2022 depreciation episode. The lending rate channel is statistically inert-consistent with the structural constraints on interest rate transmission documented for low-income financial systems, and sharpened here by the administrative rate ceiling introduced in April 2020. A nonlinear (nardl) extension tests, rather than assumes, the linearity built into the baseline model: all four Wald symmetry restrictions fail to reject, which validates the simpler linear specification. For policymakers, the practical implication is that price stability under the current framework requires conditioning money supply decisions on projected inflation rather than realised inflation; administrative credit constraints offer one partial, blunt mechanism for breaking the accommodation cycle in the interim.

title: What Political Favoritism Finances: Discretionary Transfers and Local Capital Investment in Romania
affiliations: University of South Florida - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics

detail.title: What Political Favoritism Finances: Discretionary Transfers and Local Capital Investment in Romania

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: A large literature has documented that political alignment between local and national governments generates favoritism in intergovernmental transfers but does not ask what the resulting transfers produce in terms of local public spending. Using detailed municipal budget microdata from Romania, we first document that aligned communes receive more in discretionary transfers and then trace that premium through the local budget: it flows predominantly into public capital investment. While municipalities have alternative uses for additional resources-goods and services, personnel costs, and local tax relief among them-roughly 70 cents of each additional unit of transfer goes into capital investment. The pattern is consistent with several non-exclusive explanations: the electoral visibility of public infrastructure; the permanent income hypothesis, under which transitory alignment-contingent income is directed to durable assets rather than recurrent commitments or tax relief; and the greater susceptibility of capital procurement to rent extraction. Within the electoral term, the windfall peaks in the election-year budget while the share converted into capital peaks mid-term, consistent with mayors timing investment to deliver visible infrastructure before the next vote.

title: Awaiting the Prompt? Generative AI Uncertainty and Firm-Level Investment
affiliations: Rutgers University, New Brunswick, Rutgers Business School, Auburn University at Montgomery,  and

detail.title: Awaiting the Prompt? Generative AI Uncertainty and Firm-Level Investment
detail.abstract: We document that firms with relatively greater workforce exposure to GenAI experience a decline in investment in the period following the release of ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. A one standard deviation increase in workforce exposure lowers the ratio of firm-level investment to lagged total assets by 0.57 percentage points, or nearly 6% of the sample mean. We argue that ChatGPT's release created a real option for firms to reorganize production around GenAI whose adoption cost, success probability, and competitive consequences were unknown at the outset. This parameter uncertainty, which scales with the firm's workforce exposure to GenAI, raises the option value of waiting and depresses current investment, when investments are irreversible. A real option model of firm investment with parameter uncertainty calibrated to bond market data (Gandhi, Lu, Pan, Plazzi, and Wei, 2026) reproduces the empirical investment response. Cross-sectional tests confirm the model's prediction that the decline in investment is concentrated in physical capital, persists through fiscal year 2025 without reversal, and is smaller for firms that have more redeployable assets. Additionally, we rule out that our results are driven by productivity substitution, talent hoarding, payout reallocation, an asymmetric-information flip, or managerial agency frictions.

title: It's Not the Technology Why Enterprise AI Fails to Create Value

detail.title: It's Not the Technology Why Enterprise AI Fails to Create Value
detail.abstract: Enterprises have invested heavily in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), yet the returns remain elusive. Across the most widely cited industry studies of 2025, only a small minority of initiatives produce measurable financial impact, while the large majority stall before reaching value. The dominant public explanation blames the technology-its tendency to hallucinate, its immaturity, or unready data. This paper argues that this explanation is largely mistaken. Synthesizing convergent evidence from three independent 2025 studies and integrating four established research streams-information-systems success and project-escalation research, technology-acceptance theory, behavioral work on algorithm aversion, and the economics of general-purpose technologies-we advance a layered model of GenAI value failure. The model distinguishes three causal layers: selection (which problem is chosen, and who is put in charge of it), organization and adoption (how work is redesigned, and whether people trust and use the system), and execution and technology (tooling, data, and integration). We argue that failures most often originate in the upper, least-scrutinized layer and cascade downward, surfacing as the technical and organizational symptoms practitioners typically diagnose. Because prevailing prioritization practice is dominated by heterogeneous, atheoretical vendor frameworks, the selection layer is precisely where rigor is most lacking. We therefore propose a selection-first framework that evaluates candidate use cases along four theoretically grounded dimensions-value, feasibility, risk, and adoptability-within a gated portfolio logic adapted from new-product-development research. The paper contributes a diagnostic reframing of a widely misunderstood phenomenon and a practical instrument for acting on it, and it sets out an agenda for the empirical validation the framework now requires.

title: Diversification all the Way Down: Multifactor Investing Within Factors, Across Factors and Across Time
affiliations: ISS, ISS, ISS and Columbia University

detail.title: Diversification all the Way Down: Multifactor Investing Within Factors, Across Factors and Across Time
detail.abstract: Diversification is applied across three dimensions. First, within factor definitions: the use of multiple signals in individual factors helps smooth individual factors' performance. Second, across factors: the multifactor portfolio earns a higher information ratio than any of its four single-factor sleeves, whose active returns are lowly correlated with one another. Third, across time: the timing overlay adds a modest improvement, generating an information ratio of 1.92 versus 1.83 for static weights over the last three years, at essentially no cost over the full 21 years (1.00 vs. 0.99).

title: Legal Speed Limits: Law, Technology Diffusion and Transformative Change

detail.title: Legal Speed Limits: Law, Technology Diffusion and Transformative Change

publicationDetails.detailsText: Utrecht University School of Law Research Paper No. 1-2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Utrecht University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of legal norms and regulatory frameworks in the diffusion of technologies, with a focus on AI and the EU regulatory landscape. Building on innovation diffusion, innovations studies, and transition literature, it develops the concept of legal speed limits (LSLs) - legal norms and regulatory requirements that affect the capacity of firms and organisations to adopt and implement new technology, operating as institutional mechanisms that can both constrain and enable diffusion. Drawing on the dynamic and non-linear character of diffusion, the paper builds on the understanding that transformative change depends not only on the pace of technology deployment but also on the breadth of cross-sectoral adoption and the depth of organisational and behavioural change. The proposed LSL taxonomy distinguishes between structural LSLs affecting pace, infrastructural LSLs affecting breadth, and organisational LSLs affecting depth of diffusion, and analyses their constraining and enabling functions in innovation adoption and implementation. The paper concludes by identifying regulatory tensions and potential blind spots that the LSL perspective helps to reveal and that can inform legislative revision and the broader policy debate on the role of law in the technology diffusion and transformative change.

title: The Variance Risk Premium Across Markets and Regimes A Downside, Crash-Conditional Risk Premium, Not Harvestable Carry

detail.title: The Variance Risk Premium Across Markets and Regimes A Downside, Crash-Conditional Risk Premium, Not Harvestable Carry
detail.abstract: We show that the variance risk premium (VRP)-option-implied minus subsequently realized volatility-is a downside, crash-conditional risk premium, compensation for a systematic tail rather than harvestable carry, and that this characterization holds in the equity cross-section, across sixteen years of market and macroeconomic regimes, and across asset classes. We assemble four free datasets: the full S&P 500 implied-volatility surface (2025-26, 440 names, one week to four months, with the one-month premium extended to a 703-name daily cross-section), a deep single-name series (AAPL, 2019-2026), the constant-maturity Cboe VIX9D/VIX/VIX3M/VIX6M complex (2010-2026), and listed volatility indices for gold and the Deribit DVOL index for Bitcoin and Ethereum. Five facts emerge. The premium is large and positive but is a downside premium: put-side model-free variance is overpriced, call-side underpriced. Its term-structure shape is regime-and convention-specific-short-end-rich in the calm 2025-26 cross-section, but on sixteen years of index data it is significant at every tenor (Newey-West t = 8-11) and rises with maturity in volatility-point terms. It is crash-conditional only in an entry-timing sense (selling volatility into a jump loses); the regime-average premium stays positive through every crisis and widens in high-stress and high-credit-spread states, when fear over-prices the volatility that subsequently mean-reverts. It is universal across asset classes, appearing with comparable proportional magnitude in gold, Bitcoin, and Ethereum. What is robust everywhere is not a tradeable premium but the implied-volatility forecast of realized volatility (cross-sectional information coefficient up to 0.84; Mincer-Zarnowitz slope below one). We frame the premium as compensation for a systematic, tail-dependent downside risk, not harvestable carry: in a calm year it mimics an annualized Sharpe above six, yet even voltargeted and overlaid it retains an irreducible left tail. All data are free and the pipeline is fully reproducible. JEL: G12, G13, G17.

title: The Lontsi Models: Adaptive Option Pricing for Markets with Frictions

detail.title: The Lontsi Models: Adaptive Option Pricing for Markets with Frictions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. This research was conducted independently and is not affiliated with or funded by any university, employer, exchange, or trading platform.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted and self-funded independently by the author.

detail.abstract: A purely frictionless option pricing model computes fair value from volatility alone, but it loses accuracy when the price-setter is a constrained dealer rather than a costless replicator. I propose a solution to this problem using an adaptive volatility input built from observable market frictions. The framework starts from the Black-Scholes pricing map but replaces static implied volatility with a Lontsi Adjusted Volatility that responds to market regime, liquidity, order-flow pressure, dealer gamma exposure, behavioral stress, and institutional constraints. From the adjusted fair value, a Lontsi Mispricing Index measures how far a market quote deviates from friction-adjusted value, and an executable-edge filter determines whether any deviation survives real costs, model risk, and capital constraints. A regime layer switches the friction weights as market conditions change, and rotation and portfolio layers extend the valuation from a single option to a full strategy. The result is a pricing system that is as simple as Black-Scholes when markets are calm, and adaptive when they are not.

title: The Macroeconomics of Sovereign Deficits Under Fiat Currency Regimes: A Synthesis of Modern Monetary Theory, Sectoral Balances, and Kaleckian Political Economy

detail.title: The Macroeconomics of Sovereign Deficits Under Fiat Currency Regimes: A Synthesis of Modern Monetary Theory, Sectoral Balances, and Kaleckian Political Economy
detail.abstract: This review article synthesizes the core theoretical contributions of Modern Monetary Theory (MMT), Abba Lerner's Functional Finance, Wynne Godley's sectoral balances framework, and Michał Kalecki's political economy to develop an integrated analytical framework for the study of government budget deficits. Conventional neoclassical paradigms typically posit a non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU), relying on structural unemployment as the primary instrument for inflation control. In contrast, this synthesis demonstrates that for a monetarily sovereign state under a fiat currency regime, the fiscal deficit is not an intrinsic source of instability or insolvency risk. Rather, it constitutes a central, highly effective instrument of macroeconomic management. The article systematically reviews the institutional and operational mechanics of fiat money, including the hierarchy of money, the state's role as currency issuer, and the interaction between the treasury and the central bank. Within this framework, it is argued that public debt issuance should be understood principally as an interest rate maintenance and monetary policy operation-facilitating the management of bank reserves and the term structure of interest rates-rather than as a financing necessity analogous to household or firm borrowing.

title: Untying the Gordian Knot: Reforming Canada’s Postal Market
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Untying the Gordian Knot: Reforming Canada’s Postal Market
detail.abstract:
• Canada Post’s financial crisis is bigger than declining mail volumes and rising costs. Drawing on economic evidence and interviews with policymakers, industry executives, and Canada Post leadership, this paper finds that the corporation’s statutory letter monopoly, universal-service obligations, and postal charter have created a rigid regulatory framework that is increasingly incompatible with a competitive postal market.
  • Economic evidence does not support maintaining Canada Post’s exclusive privilege in letter delivery. This paper argues that postal services do not exhibit the characteristics of a natural monopoly and that greater competition would improve efficiency and support long-term financial sustainability.
  • Canada should commercialize Canada Post by eliminating its letter monopoly, creating an independent postal regulator, and preserving universal service through a competitively neutral subsidy program that ensures continued service to high-cost regions.

title: A Century of Meme Stocks and the Price of Coordination

detail.title: A Century of Meme Stocks and the Price of Coordination

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No outside influence has affected this study.

detail.abstract: "Meme stocks" are known by their social-media chatter, impossible to identify before the internet age. I instead learn "memeness" from a meme-stock index fund's holdings using market data alone, so stocks can be scored back to 1926. Memeness identifies coordinated retail mispricing: prices displaced by crowds that congregate faster and more cheaply as coordination technology improves. The displacement corrects at a weekly horizon: a value-weighted five-factor-plus-momentum alpha near 10%/year (t ≈ 7), earned in two weeks and reversed within a month. It persists because arbitraging it means bearing crash risk that realizes on the crowd's timetable. Both the mispricing and its crash content emerge in force after 2000, exactly when coordination costs collapse; sampled weekly, the correction alpha holds out of sample in 2023–2025.

title: The European Commission Hits the Nail on the Head in its DMA Specification Decision Forcing Google to Allow Access to its Search Data

detail.title: The European Commission Hits the Nail on the Head in its DMA Specification Decision Forcing Google to Allow Access to its Search Data
detail.abstract: This article examines the European Commission's Specification Decision implementing Article 6(11) DMA, which obliges Google to grant third-party online search engines FRAND access to ranking, query, click and view data. Comparing the decision against the April Draft Implementation Measures, the analysis identifies substantial reinforcement of data protection safeguards: a narrowed data scope excluding highentropy fingerprinting vectors, a twentyfold increase in the k-anonymity threshold, refined mini-sessionisation limits, and a newly mandated segregated processing environment to forestall linkage attacks. These changes are situated within the unresolved debate over whether the provision's anonymisation standard equates to that of the GDPR. The article further scrutinizes the Commission's expanded eligibility criteria for accessing search data, questioning the propriety of delegating sanctions and cybersecurity screening to the gatekeeper itself, and critiques the FRAND compensation methodology for lacking independent cost verification and interim access mechanisms, thereby preserving incentives for the gatekeeper to delay or degrade data sharing.

title: Self-Exciting Preferences under Risk and Ambiguity: A Latent-State Representation
affiliations: University of Montpellier

detail.title: Self-Exciting Preferences under Risk and Ambiguity: A Latent-State Representation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic theory of self-exciting preferences under risk and ambiguity.The central idea is that revisions in risk attitudes, ambiguity attitudes, and subjectivebeliefs may be triggered, clustered, and amplified by the recent history of salient events.Instead of assuming exogenous preference changes or fixed Markov transition probabilities,the paper models latent decision states through a point process whose conditional intensityfollows a Hawkes dynamics. A salient event—such as a financial crisis, a liquidity shock,a pandemic alert, a geopolitical escalation, or a climate-related disaster—temporarily increases the intensity of future preference-state transitions. Conditional on the pair formedby the latent state and the self-exciting intensity, preferences admit a state-conditional representation involving a utility index, a set of priors, and an ambiguity aggregator. Theframework explains how locally rational preferences can alternate between periods of apparent stability and episodes of clustered revision. It provides a tractable structure for studying panic, fading disaster memory, and endogenous cycles of caution and relaxation.

title: From Principle to Doctrine: Operationalizing Human-on-the-Loop-Plus Governance in High-Consequence Autonomous Operations

detail.title: From Principle to Doctrine: Operationalizing Human-on-the-Loop-Plus Governance in High-Consequence Autonomous Operations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and Principal Investigator of Aero Shield UAS Services, LLC, the company whose Gen-1 system is used as the working case study in this paper. This work was developed as part of Aero Shield's preparation for an NSF SBIR Phase I proposal and received no external funding directed at its conclusions. The author has no other financial or personal interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This work is a conceptual governance framework and does not involve human participants or patient data. The case study concerns an autonomous technical system developed by the author, not human subjects, and therefore requires no ethics approval or participant consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was developed independently as part of the author's preparation for a prospective NSF SBIR Phase I proposal.

detail.abstract: Autonomous systems fail differently than people. They can produce confident-looking outputs while operating outside the conditions they were designed for, and the human nominally in charge often has no independent way to recognize the failure in time to intervene. In wildfire suppression, commercial aviation, nuclear operations, and autonomous driving the pattern is the same: the supervisor is legally responsible but operationally blind. This paper describes a governance approach to that problem, developed in the context of autonomous wildfire suppression and applied to the Aero Shield Gen-1 system as the working case study. The paper presents the Aero Shield swarm engagement doctrine as the working case study: how this approach plays out in a three-to-four-drone wildfire suppression operation with a dedicated overwatch drone, five abort triggers, three position-state responses, and a defined evidence package. It draws on the structural parallels in aviation Crew Resource Management and the post-Three Mile Island reforms in nuclear supervisory control, both of which arrived at similar architectural answers from different accident histories. The paper engages five operational objections to the framework directly, including concerns about authorization granularity, intervention rigidity, recording overhead, industry concentration, and litigation exposure. It names the framework's limitations explicitly, including scope, empirical status, generalizability across operational tempos, supervisor competence assumptions, and cost and concentration effects. It identifies the prototype testing program proposed for NSF SBIR Phase I research as the primary validation path, with three concrete and falsifiable validation criteria. It closes with eight design principles for practitioners working on autonomous systems in safety-critical settings, and a discussion of how these principles could be applied as performance standards in emerging regulatory frameworks, including the proposed FAA Part 108 rulemaking for routine BVLOS operations and DoD Directive 3000.09 implementation guidance. The central observation is that human supervision is only meaningful when it can be specified, trained, tested, and audited. Saying that a system is under human supervisory control is a principle. What the supervisor sees, what triggers their action, what the system is allowed to do, and what gets recorded: that is doctrine. Principle cannot be audited. Doctrine can.

title: When the Customer is an Algorithm: A Demand-Side Theory of the Machine Customer

detail.title: When the Customer is an Algorithm: A Demand-Side Theory of the Machine Customer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Commerce is undergoing a structural rupture that the dominant frameworks misread. As AI agents move from advising consumers to executing their purchases, the customer the firm must win is no longer a human but a machine acting on a human's behalf. This paper formalizes that rupture as the Shopper Schism: the structural separation, in delegated categories, of the consumer, who experiences value, from the shopper, who executes the purchase. We argue that the prevailing supply-side reading of AI in commerce, in which sellers adapt their channels and content, obscures the deeper event, which is demand-side. When an agent buys, demand itself is generated, filtered, and expressed by a non-human actor with different selection logic, latency, switching cost, and loyalty mechanics than a person. We anchor the resulting theory to a single primary construct, Agent Intent Optimization (AIO®), the practice of competing for the buying agent's selection rather than the human's attention; AIO-Commerce is introduced as the derived practitioner label for the category that AIO governs. We distinguish this discipline from search and conversion optimization, position it against the emerging industry vocabulary of business-to-AI selling and agent optimization, and derive a set of testable propositions for commercial strategy, brand equity, and governance in markets where the customer is algorithmic. The contribution is an integrative demand-side theory of the machine customer that formalizes a buyer whose existence the field already recognizes but has not theorized, and a conceptual anchor for a research stream on selling to the machine.

title: Identity Constructed Communication Architecture (ICCA)

detail.title: Identity Constructed Communication Architecture (ICCA)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares the following competing financial and non-financial interests: The author serves as Trustee and Chief Architect of the publishing Foundation (In Formation, Switzerland) and the associated social network product utilising the Identity Constructed Communication Architecture (ICCA) described in this manuscript. No external commercial venture backing or grant funding influenced the design, analysis, or writing of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research involves a theoretical and structural architecture modelled on publicly observable, macroscopic patterns of human interaction and social networking. The study did not involve direct intervention, clinical trials, or physical experimentation with human subjects or animals. No private, sensitive, or personally identifiable human data was collected, tracked, or analysed for this study; therefore, formal institutional review board (IRB) ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sectors. The study was entirely self-funded and executed independently by the author as part of the developmental architecture of the founding organisation.

detail.abstract:
Digital communication systems increasingly rely on identity centric security, yet contemporary visibility-based architectures still depend on provider observable channels metadata driven verification and behavioural trust signals [1,2]. These structural dependencies create persistent vulnerabilities in environments where visibility itself becomes a liability particularly in high risk social organisational and investigative communication. Visibility based systems assume that communication must occur within observable channels which limits their ability to eliminate impersonation inference and metadata leakage [3,4].

The Identity Constructed Communication Architecture ICCA is trustless in the provider sense; trust is established cryptographically rather than through visibility or behavioural inference. ICCA constructs communication channels directly from identity rather than from provider visible infrastructure. Using sealed identity containers and context bound permission tokens ICCA establishes momentary non persistent trust without behavioural analytics device posture telemetry or continuous monitoring. The provider operates within a blind boundary supplying infrastructure without visibility into identities communication patterns or contextual signals.

ICCA’s zero metadata transport layer eliminates IP addresses device fingerprints timestamps routing information and social-graph indicators making inference attacks and impersonation structurally impossible. ICCA is not derived from visibility-based security research and does not extend Zero Trust. ICCA provides a structural alternative to visibility‑based models by removing the assumption that communication must occur within provider observable channels and by eliminating the need for continuous verification [5]. ICCA achieves confidentiality integrity and impersonation resistance through cryptographic sufficiency rather than provider observation.

For computational law ICCA establishes a new trust geometry with implications for digital rights privacy governance and the legal status of identity in communication systems. It provides a structural model for environments where visibility metadata and provider inference are unacceptable enabling identity‑anchored trustless digital interaction.

title: Mandate Standardization, Institutional Constraint Commonality, and Equilibrium Asset Prices
affiliations: University of Zaragoza - Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Mandate Standardization, Institutional Constraint Commonality, and Equilibrium Asset Prices
detail.abstract: Institutional ownership alone need not determine price efficiency; what matters is how similarly delegated capital is constrained. This paper develops a theory in which delegated investors choose whether to adopt standardized mandate templates before trading. Standardization is privately attractive because common mandates reduce monitoring, reporting, compliance, and peer-comparison costs, but it also exposes investors to potentially crowded portfolio rules. The equilibrium adoption share generates endogenous institutional constraint commonality. When many delegated investors adopt the same rule, their marginal demands become correlated. Assets favored by standardized constraints trade at a premium and earn lower subsequent expected returns. Institutional capital has a conditional effect on price efficiency: it improves efficiency when mandates remain diverse, because delegated investors provide return-sensitive demand that absorbs nonfundamental shocks; it can reduce efficiency when standardization is high, because the same capital amplifies common constraint-induced demand. The model therefore offers a mechanism through which the asset-pricing consequences of institutionalization depend on the equilibrium commonality of the constraints under which capital is allocated.

title: Prices Are Optimal: An Information-theoretic Formalization of Austrian Price Theory

detail.title: Prices Are Optimal: An Information-theoretic Formalization of Austrian Price Theory
detail.abstract: This article presents three bounds on what centralised resource coordination through compressed signals can achieve. They were derived from an engineering audit of information-minimality in mechanism design for fifth-generation mobile networks. The formal model is constructed with maximal generosity to the central coordinator, granting settled demand types, honest reports, benevolence, known success criteria, and observable outcomes. Even under those advantages the formalism hits three bounds. The first is a floor. Any coordination on compressed signals needs signals rich enough to distinguish the situations that genuinely differ, and below that floor no refinement of mechanism recovers what compression has thrown away. This gives precise form to the informational side of the Misesian calculation argument. The second is an upper bound. Once the categorical signal captures what matters for whether coordination is working, the aggregate outcome exhausts what verification can use. Individual detail adds no value when the aggregate is directly available and strictly worsens verification when it arrives through noisy records. This sharpens the Hayekian insight about compression into a dominance statement. The third bound is on the formalism itself. The coordinating signal serves two epistemically distinct purposes, provisioning and verification, with opposed demands on granularity, and no formal criterion selects between them. The choice within the feasible range is case probability in Mises's precise sense and reaches as a lower bound the entrepreneurial function developed by Huerta de Soto. Under this generosity, the mathematics converges on the tradition's verdict and certifies its own boundary. The paper is offered as convergent testimony from outside, not as translation.

title: Identifying Stock Pricing Anomalies in Indian FinTech Stocks: A Critical Evaluation for Retail Investor
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Identifying Stock Pricing Anomalies in Indian FinTech Stocks: A Critical Evaluation for Retail Investor
detail.abstract: This study examines stock pricing anomalies in ten listed Indian FinTech companies using daily closing price data spanning diverse listing periods up to early 2026, covering a total of 7,216 firm-trading-day observations. Three categories of anomaly are investigated: (i) stationarity and unit root properties of log prices and log returns using Dickey-Fuller (DF) and Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests; (ii) explosive price behaviour and bubble episodes using the Right-Tailed ADF and Supremum Augmented Dickey-Fuller (SADF) procedure of Phillips, Wu, and Yu (2011); and (iii) calendar effects in daily returns, specifically the day-ofweek and month-of-year patterns, estimated via OLS regression with HAC standard errors and validated using Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric tests. Results indicate that while log prices are predominantly integrated of order one-confirming non-stationarity at levels-log returns are universally stationary across all ten firms, consistent with weak-form efficiency in the return space. No company exhibited statistically significant explosive pricing behaviour (all SADF values fall below the 10% critical value), suggesting the Indian FinTech sector has largely been free of speculative bubble formation during the sample period. Calendar effect tests reveal that neither day-of-week nor month-of-year patterns are statistically significant for the majority of firms, with the notable exception of One Mobikwik showing a significant dayof-week effect (F = 3.78, p = 0.005) and Suvidha Infoserve exhibiting a statistically significant month-of-year pattern. ARCH effects are pervasive across the sample, indicating pronounced volatility clustering-a finding with direct implications for risk management and derivative pricing. The results partially challenge simple efficiency narratives while offering nuanced guidance for retail investors in navigating FinTech equity markets.

title: The Page is the Unit of Authority: Content Architecture for a Machine Readership in Agent-Mediated Markets

detail.title: The Page is the Unit of Authority: Content Architecture for a Machine Readership in Agent-Mediated Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The dominant architecture of the commercial web, the multi-page funnel that routes a visitor from a homepage through category listings to a destination, was built for a reader who arrives at the front door, browses, and is gradually persuaded. That reader is disappearing on two fronts at once. On the human front, an increasing share of sessions are already shallow: many visitors land on a single page and act or leave within a window measured, for many sessions, in seconds rather than minutes. On the machine front, we theorize that AI answer engines and buying agents increasingly do not tour a site at all; to the extent that they operate as we describe, they deep-link to, ingest, and cite individual pages, and they return those pages, not homepages, as answers. This paper argues that the convergence of these two forces relocates the atomic unit of discovery, authority, and conversion from the site to the page. We name the governing construct the page as the unit of authority and specify the content-architecture principle it implies: each page must be selfcontained, carrying its own identity, positioning, proof, and call to action, and machine-legible, 2 exposing its claims in structured, verifiable, independently-citable form. We position this as the supply-side corollary of a demand-side theory advanced in prior work, in which the customer in agent-mediated markets is increasingly a machine rather than a human, and we argue that the design principle is the operational layer of Agent Intent Optimization, the practice of being selected by an agent evaluating alternatives against a delegated goal. The contribution is a contentarchitecture principle for a machine readership that bridges the conversion and user-experience literatures with the agentic-commerce research stream, a differentiating account of what it explains that search optimization, conversion optimization, answer-engine optimization, and classical information architecture do not, and a set of falsifiable propositions for an empirical program. The accessible framing of the work is building pages the machine can read.

title: Exploring the Causes of Inactive Bank Accounts in India: Evidence from the Global Findex Survey
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Foreign Trade

detail.title: Exploring the Causes of Inactive Bank Accounts in India: Evidence from the Global Findex Survey
detail.abstract: While India has made significant advancements in financial inclusion, a large portion of our population still lags behind in progress as it holds inactive bank accounts. The study aims to investigate the barriers to financial inclusion focusing on challenges faced in maintaining active bank accounts based on data from the 2021 Global Findex database. Latent Class Analysis (LCA) has been applied to classify individuals into three distinct groups based on the barriers to active banking faced by them. The results revealed that while some individuals genuinely face structural challenges such as lack of proximity, inaccessibility to financial institutions, low income and lack of digital literacy, others simply do not perceive banking as a necessary activity. Interestingly, a third group emerged that exhibited distrust towards banks discouraging them from continued banking interaction. The findings highlight need for targeted policy interventions tailored to specific challenges faced by each group of individuals with inactive bank accounts. This becomes crucial as we envision a Digital India, with increased use of formal banking, digital payment platforms, facilitate financial literacy and expand the scope of financial inclusion to the underserved portion of the population. Reviving inactive bank accounts and resolving the root issues which lead to accounts becoming inactive is the first step towards filling pitfalls in the banking channel of financial inclusion.

title: Green Bioshield to Arrest Urban Air Pollution: A Case Study on West Bengal, India

detail.title: Green Bioshield to Arrest Urban Air Pollution: A Case Study on West Bengal, India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest.

declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for the work.

detail.abstract: Introduction: Green bioshields have been proven to be effective in protecting coastal areas from storms and shoreline erosions. Use of vegetative bioshield for protecting urban areas has not been explored much. The Government of West Bengal, a state in Eastern India has taken up an ambitious project to build a three-layered green wall along its western border to protect its capital city Kolkata from transboundary air pollution. This project has provided us an opportunity to study the impact of green bioshield on urban air pollution.

title: Addressing the Gap: A Review of Fintech Literature in the Age of Finance 4.0 and Agentic AI
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Foreign Trade

detail.title: Addressing the Gap: A Review of Fintech Literature in the Age of Finance 4.0 and Agentic AI

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM), volume 5, issue 1, 2026[10.56879/ijbm.v5i1.19]

detail.abstract: As the financial industry is moves towards Finance 4.0 and Agentic AI, the FinTech landscape is undergoing a structural shift from traditional systems to advance artificial intelligence (AI), where AI now uses reasoning, planning, and multi-step actions. The existing literature on Fintech has largely focused on early-stage adoption and fails to capture this current shift. This study addresses this gap by combining a bibliometric analysis of 318 Scopus articles (2015-2024) with a narrative literature review of the most-cited and a selection of high-impact non-Scopus papers, including leading working papers and publications from high-impact journals. Our findings reveal three research streams: (1) Adoption & Innovation, (2) Market Impact & Inclusion, and (3) Regulation & Stability. We further map these themes to five foundational theories: Diffusion Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Financial Intermediation Theory, Inclusion Theory, and Regulatory Arbitrage Theory. The study provides empirical validation for established models while identifying critical gaps and future research directions.

title: Quantifying Backtest Overfitting from Information Leakage: A Walk-Forward and Embargo-Based Diagnostic Framework Applied to Deep Learning Return Forecasts
affiliations: and

detail.title: Quantifying Backtest Overfitting from Information Leakage: A Walk-Forward and Embargo-Based Diagnostic Framework Applied to Deep Learning Return Forecasts
detail.abstract: Reported backtest performance in applied financial machine learning is frequently inflated by information leakage between training and evaluation samples, yet the magnitude of this inflation is rarely measured directly. We introduce a controlled diagnostic protocol that (i) deliberately injects two common and realistic leakage mechanisms-full-sample feature scaling and globally computed rolling statisticsinto a return-forecasting pipeline; (ii) evaluates two structurally distinct deep learning architectures, a recurrent sequence model and a convolutional image-encoding model, under three validation regimes of increasing rigor (a single train/test split, non-anchored walk-forward validation, and walk-forward validation combined with an embargo period); and (iii) quantifies the resulting change in backtested trading performance at each stage. Applied to a single-asset case study (SPDR S&P 500 ETF, 2016-2023), the framework reveals that leakage inflation is large, fold-size dependent, and architecturespecific: removing leakage reduces the recurrent model's backtested return by 123 percentage points under a moderate-frequency retraining schedule and by 506 percentage points under a high-frequency schedule, while the convolutional model's apparent performance under leakage is suppressed rather than inflated, reversing in sign once leakage is removed. These findings indicate that the direction and magnitude of leakage-induced bias cannot be assumed a priori and depends on the interaction between the contamination mechanism and the model's input representation. We argue that backtest results obtained under a single validation protocol should not be trusted in isolation, and we propose the embargo period-set equal to the prediction horizon-as a low-cost, broadly applicable correction.

detail.abstract: India's financial sector has experienced a significant transformation over the last decade, driven by the rapid adoption of digital technologies, expansion of financial infrastructure, and emergence of innovative financial service providers. Initiatives such as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), Aadhaar-enabled services, Jan Dhan Yojana, and Account Aggregator framework have collectively contributed to greater financial inclusion and improved efficiency within the financial system. Simultaneously, the rise of FinTech firms, digital lending platforms, and data-driven financial services has introduced new opportunities as well as regulatory challenges. While innovation has improved access, reduced transaction costs, and strengthened economic participation, it has also created concerns relating to cybersecurity, consumer protection, data privacy, operational resilience, and financial stability. As financial services become increasingly interconnected and technology-dependent, regulators face the complex task of encouraging innovation while preserving confidence in the financial system. This paper examines the evolving relationship between financial innovation, regulation, and financial stability in India. It analyzes the opportunities generated by digital finance, identifies emerging risks, and proposes policy measures aimed at creating a resilient, inclusive, and innovation-friendly financial ecosystem. The paper argues that India's future success will depend upon a regulatory approach that supports technological advancement while ensuring prudent risk management and consumer protection.

title:
The Password Paradox:
Why the World's Least Trusted Security Tool Still Guards Most of the Internet -And What Comes Next

detail.title:
The Password Paradox:
Why the World's Least Trusted Security Tool Still Guards Most of the Internet -And What Comes Next

Where the article references the author's previously published works, these are cited for illustrative and comparative purposes only and do not represent a financial conflict of interest.

detail.abstract:
Passwords remain the primary authentication method for seventy-six percent of organizations worldwide, despite near-universal agreement among security professionals that they are the weakest link in modern cyber defense. This article traces the password's origin at MIT in 1961 through six decades of escalating attacks and defenses, examines the current data on breach costs and credential theft, and evaluates the passwordless technologies — passkeys, FIDO2, and WebAuthn — now positioned to replace them. It further examines what this shift means for the cybersecurity labor market: a global workforce gap exceeding 4.8 million positions, and a hiring landscape that increasingly rewards demonstrable, narrow technical skill over credentials alone. The conclusion is neither alarmist nor complacent: passwords will not disappear on the timeline the industry once predicted, but organizations and individuals who build layered, passkey-forward defenses today will be measurably more resilient than those waiting for the problem to solve itself.

In March 2026, an identity security firm asked more than a thousand IT and security leaders a simple question: how are you authenticating your users? The answer should unsettle anyone who has spent the last several years reading confident predictions that passwords were finally on their way out. Seventy-six percent of organizations reported that legacy passwords remain their primary authentication method. Only forty-three percent had deployed any form of passwordless authentication at all, and of those, most had rolled it out to less than half their workforce.

This is the paradox at the center of modern cybersecurity. Nearly every serious technologist agrees that the password, as an idea, is broken. It is guessable, reusable, phishable, and endlessly recycled by users who have long since stopped trying to invent something new for the fortieth account they have opened this year. And yet, more than sixty years after the first computer password was issued at MIT in 1961, we are still typing them, still resetting them, and still losing them to attackers by the billions.

title: The Impact of Professional Sports Franchise Movements on Urban Crime Rates

detail.title: The Impact of Professional Sports Franchise Movements on Urban Crime Rates
detail.abstract: While municipalities often justify large public subsidies for professional sports franchises through expected social benefits, the long-term externalities on public safety remain largely underexplored. A broad literature finds these stadiums generate negligible economic growth, making their social impact critical for policy evaluation. This paper investigates the structural effect of professional sports team entries and exits on local urban crime rates. Using a comprehensive, long-term panel of United States cities from 1985 to 2019, the study employs the Synthetic Difference-inDifferences (SDID) estimator as its primary identification strategy. The findings demonstrate that the crime externalities of professional sports are highly sensitive to market saturation. In solo markets, franchise movements generate significant and directionally symmetric shocks. The arrival of a city's first major franchise structurally increases violent (assault and robbery) and short-run property crime (burglary), whereas the departure of a sole franchise leads to a decrease in violent crime (robbery and rape). However, in established multi-team markets, the marginal addition or loss of a franchise yields no statistically significant changes in crime. Ultimately, the initial transition between zero and one team creates profound disruptions to local public safety, while subsequent movements in saturated markets have essentially no marginal effect.

title: The Influence of Fintech Integration on the Technical Efficiency of Indian Banks: A Two-Step DEA Approach
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Foreign Trade

detail.title: The Influence of Fintech Integration on the Technical Efficiency of Indian Banks: A Two-Step DEA Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency.

detail.abstract: Financial innovation worldwide has left traditional banks with no option but to provide digital fintech services, such as digital payments and peer-to-peer lending. Banks either developed digital units internally or formed external partnerships to integrate Fintech capabilities in their day-today operations. This study defines Fintech integration as the provision of digital services by banks and examines its effect on technical efficiency using a two-step Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) approach, followed by a panel regression model to evaluate the influence of specific financial variables on technical efficiency. Efficiency is decomposed into technical efficiency (optimal use of resources), pure technical efficiency (managerial effectiveness in using inputs), and scale efficiency (effects due to bank size). The data for the study comprises 21 Indian banks that implemented major Fintech initiatives, sourced from Bloomberg. The study found that persistent inefficiencies arise from suboptimal scale, input waste, and poor management. Panel regression analysis reveals that the operational impacts of Fintech integration vary significantly across the dimensions of intermediation. Larger bank size emerges as a powerful determinant of efficiency in deposit mobilisation and revenue generation, suggesting economies of scale. Also, higher loan intensity significantly accelerates the core deposit-to-loan transformation but poses a barrier to banks' interest income generation post-Fintech integration. Similarly, while high intermediation costs reduce efficiency in deposit mobilisation, they are strongly positively associated with creditprocessing efficiency, capturing the positive payoff of investments in Fintech capabilities.

title: Entrepreneurship Education and Career Trajectories
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Entrepreneurship Education and Career Trajectories

declarations.ethicsApproval: The research design was approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board (IRB).

detail.abstract: As entrepreneurship education has become increasingly prevalent in higher education, its broader consequences for students' career development have attracted growing attention. Supporters argue that entrepreneurship programs generate long-term value by cultivating transferable skills that benefit participants beyond venture creation. Critics, however, contend that such programs may crowd out other educational investments and potentially undermine academic and labor market outcomes. Despite ongoing debate over its net impact, existing research has focused primarily on whether entrepreneurship education increases entrepreneurial activity, leaving its effects on broader career trajectories underexplored. Drawing on ten years of longitudinal data from a university startup incubator, this study examines the impact of an entrepreneurship education program by comparing the post-graduation career trajectories of accepted and rejected applicants. The results show that exposure to entrepreneurship education does not necessarily increase entrepreneurial activity immediately after graduation. However, participation is associated with sustained career advantages, even among students who do not pursue entrepreneurship in the short term. Specifically, participants demonstrate better job matching, as reflected in higher earnings, longer tenure with their initial employers, and greater stability in occupational type. These findings provide empirical evidence that entrepreneurship education can generate enduring positive returns in the broader labor market. They also offer important implications for universities and organizations evaluating whether to invest in entrepreneurship programs, suggesting that the value of such programs extends beyond the creation of new ventures.

title: The Dark Side of Globalization: Quantity, Quality, and Cost-Effectiveness Enhancement of Disinformation via AI

detail.title: The Dark Side of Globalization: Quantity, Quality, and Cost-Effectiveness Enhancement of Disinformation via AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
